It responds most to phrases about introducing gases, reagents or particles into a system, such as feeding a hydrocarbon gas or admitting gases. It also responds to related process vocabulary like temperature, transport, solutions, baths, material removed from surfaces and dissolving agents.

2002.name: Later items in enumerated lists or series (comma/and/or-separated, or run-on menus and tags): the final items, the separators and conjunctions leading up to them, and the closing element of the enumeration. Activation rises toward the end of the list.

20032.name: Separators and connectives that come right after a negative or lower-bound number and lead into the next value. These include range words such as "to" and "and", commas, semicolons, inequality signs, and LaTeX integral bound markers like "}^{". Activation is strongest for range expressions running from a negative number to a positive one, e.g. "-5° to 36°" or "-1,1".

20047.name: Opening delimiters that begin a value right after a key or assignment, e.g. an opening quote following '=' or ':' in code, config and JSON/YAML (sometimes '{' or '['), and opening <td>/<th> tags that start an HTML table cell.

20072.name: Segment boundaries (periods, question marks, newlines, colons, commas) that end a sentence, title or line just before an abrupt topic shift or disjointed continuation. Activation is strongest in incoherent, spun or spam-like text where consecutive sentences are unrelated, and weaker at ordinary sentence ends or list and heading breaks.

20078.name: The token "fed"/"Fed" (also "edor"/"ed" after F), whatever it means: the Federal Reserve, "fed up", Fedora, the Fed Cup, and name fragments such as Fedorov, Federico, Feddic and Fedele. Activation is highest for capitalized "Fed" as an abbreviation or the start of a name, and weaker for the verb "fed".

20089.name: Words for soft, moldable, kneadable substances, chiefly "dough" (including "dough" within doughnut, sourdough, and the name Dougherty), along with batter, crust, clay, slurry, pulp, papier-mâché and paste. The "kne" token of knead/kneel also activates. Activation is strongest on "dough" in baking contexts.

The word "dough" (strongest, even in garbled or odd contexts like "doughnuts"), plus weaker activation on related malleable or kneadable substances and baking terms ("kne" from knead/kneel, pastry, clay, batter, sourdough, crust, Chinese 粉/胶).

20095.name: Punctuation or spacing immediately following a weekday name in date headers/timestamps (the comma after "Monday", "Friday", etc., or the space after "Tuesday,"), typically right before the day/month in blog or article dateline metadata; weakly also "Posted on"/"Updated:" lead-ins to dates.

20118.name: Tokens inside long runs of the same repeated character or token (dot leaders, dashes, spaces, nbsp, -*, ;\, repeated letters or symbols). Activation is strongest deep in the run, and a few sequence positions stand out as peaks. There are weak, sporadic activations on ordinary tokens, mostly prepositions like "in".

Tokens inside long runs of the same repeated symbol or short token (pipes, slashes, dashes, colons, asterisks, underscores, tabs, dots, arrows, etc.). The feature fires on interior repetitions once the repeating pattern is established, not on ordinary prose.

Tokens inside long runs of the same repeated character or symbol, such as whitespace, tabs, dashes, pipes, dots, invisible or zero-width characters, emojis, or repeated letters. The feature fires on tokens deep within these monotonous repetitive sequences (separators, padding, filler), not on the first occurrences.

20149.name: Negation tokens ("not", "n't", "neither", "non", "no longer", "un-") and, more weakly, the verb or condition word where a state is being checked or failing. These usually fall in descriptions of conditions or outcomes such as a file not being linked, something that wouldn't fit or work, "if not given", or "check whether X is".

20162.name: HTTP request type tokens in web code, strongest on "HttpServletRequest" (in javax.servlet.http imports or as a servlet method parameter), with weaker activation on related request/context/session types (Request, HttpContext, HttpSession) and other framework parameter types such as JoinPoint, Model and CancellationToken. Non-code text is near zero.

20184.name: Tokens in the middle of long random-looking alphanumeric strings, such as hex hashes, IDs, API keys, URL tokens and GUIDs, plus separators (dashes, spaces) inside codes and numbers. Activation peaks deep inside these unpredictable character sequences.

20223.name: Contexts about layoffs, job cuts and cost-cutting (e.g., 'pink slips to employees', 'laid-off workers', '1,000 employees… affected', reducing waste). Activation peaks on words in these workforce-reduction phrases, such as employees, workers and slips, and on the surrounding function words. Elsewhere there are weak, diffuse activations on ordinary function words in news or expository prose.

20232.name: Positive aesthetic or admiring adjectives (and related nouns/adverbs) such as "wonderful", "beautiful", "lovely", "delightful", "marvellous" and "beauty". The strongest activations are on "wonderful"/"wonderfully", weaker on "beautiful"/"lovely", and weakest on "beauty" used as a product or category noun.

Positive aesthetic/admiring words, chiefly "wonderful" (strongest), "beautiful", "beauty", and "lovely", plus similar terms like "delightful", "amazing", and "magical", used in any context to praise or describe something pleasing.

20235.name: Mentions of scheduled or time-bounded events (conferences, festivals, tournaments, ceremonies, elections, seasons, trips) and the words giving their timing, duration, or venue, such as dates, weekdays, 'two-day', 'held at', 'ends', 'last day of', 'opening'. It is strongest where an event's occurrence or ending is stated, e.g. 'The conference ends Thursday'.

2025.name: Relational/classifying adjectives (often ending in -al, -ic, -ical, -ological) placed before a noun to specify its domain or type (e.g., financial, legal, optical, emotional, medicinal, political), including word-piece suffixes that complete such adjectives.

2028.name: The preposition "of" (including capitalized "Of" and fused forms like "numberOf"), mostly in noun-phrase constructions that link a head noun to its complement, such as possessive, part-whole, attribute or title relations ("President of", "benefits of", "squares of"). Activation is highest when "of" follows a specific, technical or title-like noun.

The preposition "of" (and its equivalents such as "Of", "-of", or Chinese "的"). It fires most often where "of" links a head noun to its complement ("the Sword of", "a table of", "the odds of"), and also on the "Of" in "Of course".

20305.name: Clause and sentence boundaries in fluent, generic expository or SEO-style web prose. Activation peaks on sentence-ending periods, especially those followed by paragraph breaks, and is somewhat lower on bare newlines before headings. Weaker activation falls on commas, conjunctions like "and" and "or", and the words that begin the next sentence (It, In, She, If you, The). When the feature is strong, it spreads across many function words and pronouns (your, her, the, to), tracking the flow of formulaic text from one phrase to the next.

20314.name: Structural tokens at the start or end of a line that open or close a block or list entry: closing braces and HTML tags in code, indentation before numbered list items, section/chapter headers, and labels preceding a colon. The common thread is boundaries in structured text, where the token marks a transition between elements.

20317.name: Legal entity suffixes that end company names, chiefly "LLC" (strongest, especially after a comma or in copyright, applicant and manufacturer lines). "GmbH" and other forms such as L.L.C., PLLC and PLLP activate more weakly.

20342.name: Tokens that repeat an immediately preceding item in a run of identical elements, typically the third or later occurrence of a repeated number in lists, arrays, tables or sequences (e.g. "9, 9, 9", "10, 10, 10"). It also fires on repeated words, characters or HTML cells, and is strongest for repeated numbers in comma-separated lists.

20351.name: The first word of a message string, most strongly when that message is an error, warning, or status report. This shows up in program output and code string literals (print, log, and raise calls), and in log or error lines just after a colon. The strongest cases are error-description words right after an error prefix, like "Specified driver could not be loaded", "Unrecognized", "No suitable", and "No issue". Weaker activations land on sentence-initial words of notices or list items.

20352.name: Word-internal subword fragments in unusual or rare words, such as names, URLs, domain names, code identifiers, acronyms and technical terms. The fragment usually sits mid-word, where tokenization splits the word at an unnatural point that is not a morpheme boundary, and the word continues after it. Examples include 'pag' in pagelines, 'ib' in Unibet and 'fs' in rsfsocialfinance.

Subword fragments in the middle of an unusual, made-up or compound identifier (variable names, code tokens, odd words) that the tokenizer splits into pieces. They fire mostly on the continuation piece just after the first chunk (e.g. h|to|ffline, m|ym|ail, skill|sc|olumns), often when the identifier is a repeat of one seen earlier in the context. Common in noisy code and garbled text.

2044.name: Fires on unnatural, low-quality or garbled text. It is strongest in spun, machine-generated word salad and essay-mill prose, where it covers long runs of incoherent phrasing. It fires weakly on isolated anomalies such as typos, wrong word forms ("critical acclaimed", "filling to", "there me"), odd fragments and artifacts like "[email protected]" or mojibake.

Fires on incoherent, garbled or machine-spun text (word salad, SEO spam, gibberish identifiers), marking tokens that don't fit their context semantically or grammatically. It is strongest on long runs of fluent-sounding but nonsensical prose.

20458.name: Words in decision, approval or voting actions, especially verbs like approved, voted, signed into law, allow or permission and the prepositions or "to" that follow them, right before the object of the decision. Activation peaks on official approval by a governing body ("commission approved to").

Words describing a decision or official action by an authority, board, council, court or voters, especially "approved", along with words like "voted to", "decided to", "consider", "reject", "support", "grants" and the prepositions or articles that introduce the thing being acted on (a measure, budget, plan, project).

20459.name: Single capital letters embedded inside alphanumeric classification or identifier codes, typically following a number. The strongest cases are the letter in Mathematics Subject Classification (MSC/AMS) codes such as 34A30 or 55P42. Weaker cases include the letter after the dot in PACS codes (03.67.Bg), JEL codes (C22), patent IPC classes (G06F), and letters in part, grant or gene identifiers.

20517.name: Opening punctuation or markup tokens (quotes, brackets, asterisks, #, parentheses, HTML tags) placed right before the first word of a title, heading, quotation, or other delimited span. These usually appear at the start of a line or after a colon or label.

20563.name: Object pronouns (him, them, me, us, you, it, herself), and occasionally nouns that refer back to one, placed right after a verb or preposition. They point to a previously mentioned person or entity, usually one receiving the action (e.g., "given to us", "betray him").

Object-case personal pronouns (me, him, us, them, you, itself, myself; also Russian/Chinese/Yoruba equivalents) appearing as the object of a verb or preposition, especially after 'to', 'by', 'for', 'with'.

20613.name: Placeholder or toy values in code, math, and examples. These are typically the first in a sequence: single-letter variable names (a, x, A), sample literals (1, 'a', "hello", 'bob'), and first elements of arrays or tuples. They appear in demo code, function parameters, and abstract statements ('state A', 'if A ⊢ B').

20628.name: Function words and punctuation that come right after a topic's subject or title is introduced, usually at the start of a definition or description ("X is a…", "X refers to…", "X has…", a comma or period closing the first descriptive clause). It fires on the verbs, relative pronouns, commas and periods that build an expository opening sentence about a named entity or term, often one just given as a heading.

Function words and punctuation immediately following a just-introduced topic or entity name (usually right after a title or heading), especially the copula/verb that begins its definition or description ("X is a…", "X has…", "X (also known as …) is"). It also fires on the commas and periods that end such introductory, encyclopedic statements.

20631.name: Volume numbers in bibliographic or serial citations: the word "volume"/"Vol." and especially the number (plus surrounding period, space, comma) that follows it. Weaker activation for similar part, season, issue, edition, or book numbers in a sequence, and for the word "volume" meaning a book.

20653.name: A weak, diffuse feature that mostly fires on discourse connectives and formulaic multi-word phrases that link clauses, such as "on the other hand," "moreover," "however," "then," "in such a way that," "at the time of" and "further I will." It is strongest at the completing word of a fixed expression, for example "hand" in "on the other hand." It appears especially in SEO-style, promotional or non-native web English. It also fires on transliterated Hindi/Urdu words and scattered sentence-ending punctuation.

Markers of Indian/South Asian English: characteristic phrasings and non-native constructions (e.g. 'on basis of', 'keeping in view', 'as per your requirement', 'till date', 'as compared to', 'since…, so', redundant 'then' after 'if', 'etc'). It also fires on South Asian names, terms and contexts (Singh, Jhabak, garam masala, Rs., Sri Lanka, Delhi '011' phone codes).

20657.name: Words or symbols that link two quantities in a rate or ratio, mostly "per" (miles per hour, cost per click). It also fires on "/", "to" (debt to EBITDA), "vs", "in", "on" (return on investment) and "Per" in identifiers like samplesPer. Activation is strongest for "per" following a measured quantity.

20754.name: The end of author-affiliation addresses in academic papers. It fires mainly on the country name that closes an address (Italy, USA, France, UK, etc.) and on the newline, comma, semicolon or 'and' right after it, where the next affiliation or section begins. It fires more weakly on other line-ending punctuation in scholarly text, such as the end of a reference or caption.

2076.name: Tokens in passages where the writer announces or frames the main contribution or topic of a text, as in abstract-like openers ("this paper proposes a method", "in this paper, the authors present", "this study investigates", "we here describe a case of", "To tackle this problem", "today announced"). The strongest activations fall on these framing verbs and nouns and on the sentence boundaries just before them. Weak, scattered activations also occur on transition words and the content that follows the framing.

20777.name: The ".Web" token in code namespaces and imports. It fires most strongly on C# "using System.Web" (including System.Web.Mvc, .UI, .Http). It is weaker for other packages such as Java/Android imports (webkit.WebView, WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter) or project namespaces like SpotifyAPI.Web. Scattered prose tokens get only negligible activation.

20814.name: Units of measurement and quantity labels that come right after numbers, especially scientific or technical units (mol, mL, A, J, GB, g, oz, rpm). Activation is strongest on the unit token and often carries onto the slash or "per" of a compound rate unit (mol/m², mL/min, flops/MB). Weaker activations fall on counted nouns after numbers and on parts of ratio or fraction expressions in math and code.

20817.name: Academic citation markers, mainly the final digit of the year in author-year citations (e.g. "et al., 201[1]") and the numbers and opening brackets of numeric references like [18] or (10–12). It also fires weakly on 'et al.' and author names inside citations.

20924.name: Terms for health and well-being outcome measures, peaking on "quality of life" (especially "life") and its abbreviation QoL. It also fires on related outcome constructs and instruments (disability, health perceptions, EQ-5D, QALY, VAS), on parts of similar acronyms like QoS/QoE, and weakly on scattered other tokens.

Strongest on words naming measured well-being or outcome constructs, such as the 'life' in 'quality of life', 'happiness', 'life satisfaction', 'outcome', 'sentiment' and 'indices'. Weaker, diffuse activation falls on structural tokens in formatted or technical text, like markdown bold markers, colons after step labels, acronyms in parentheses and 'convert'.

21011.name: Nouns for a gathered group or assortment of items, chiefly "collection"/"collections", plus related words such as selection, compilation, catalog, archive, library, range, variety, collector, treasure, and curated. Activation is strongest for "collection" itself, especially for museum, library or artist collections and in the phrase "collection of".

Collective nouns for a group of gathered or owned items, chiefly "collection" (strongest, especially a personal or museum collection), plus near-synonyms such as selection, set, line, range, fleet, library, archive, stash and assortment, often followed by "of" plus the items.

21015.name: The three-digit number chunk immediately after "10." in a DOI prefix (the publisher registrant code, e.g. 1103 for APS, 1109 for IEEE). Activation is strongest for the token "110" and weaker for other prefixes like 101, 103, 108 or 109. It also fires weakly on "110" appearing in other numeric IDs such as ISBNs or user IDs.

21022.name: Diffuse, weak activation across technical/scientific and product-description prose about devices, materials, light and energy. It fires mostly on function words and descriptive tokens in phrases that characterize a device's or material's properties and performance, such as high brightness, low power consumption, long-lived, perfectly sinusoidal output, and does not suffer from. It is strongest in LED/lighting and efficiency descriptions.

21037.name: Weak, diffuse feature that mostly fires on prepositions linking a noun or verb to what follows, especially Latin/Romance-like "p"-words (par, por, per, pers, prom, porcelain) and also by, through, of, for. It is strongest on French "par" and Spanish "por" meaning "by/via". There are occasional weak hits on word fragments and paragraph breaks.

21042.name: Final word of short website navigation and boilerplate UI phrases (e.g., "Continue Reading", "Scroll to Top", "Connect with us", "Skip to content", "1 min read", "Register"). These are scraped interface labels and calls to action embedded in web text, firing most strongly on "Reading" in "Continue Reading".

21047.name: Analytical, report-style prose about trends and conditions, especially in economics, markets, energy, and policy. It fires on wording that describes change, drivers, outlooks, or the current state of things (e.g., weighed on, expected to boost, has slowed, remains, gradual, escalating, key trend). Activation is strongest in financial and market commentary such as currency forecasts and inflation.

21065.name: The determiner (mostly "the") right after a role or affiliation phrase like "director of", "member of", "spokesman for" or "scientist at", introducing the organization, institution or group a person belongs to or leads. It fires most strongly in "head of the" and "co-chair of the" titles.

Determiners (mostly "the", sometimes "a" or possessive "'s") that introduce an organization, institution, group or body after a role or membership phrase, e.g. "president of the", "member of the", "spokesman for the", "head of the". Activation is strongest after leadership or role titles followed by "of".

21066.name: Tokens describing or attaching to institutions and organizations (especially universities). The strongest activations fall on clauses, parentheticals and prepositional phrases that add affiliation, location or descriptive detail about an institution, such as "which has affiliation with", "(formerly", "located in", acronyms in parentheses, campus suffixes, and URL or email domain parts. Activation is weak on generic function words elsewhere.

21114.name: Fires on the predicate words of a clause about the remaining or alternative part of something previously described, such as "the rest", "others", "the balance", "otherwise" or "additional components". These clauses contrast that part with the main case. Activation is strongest right after such remainder subjects (e.g., "the rest failed", "others is called insolence", "the balance could be taken from", "other problems simply seemed to be exaggerated") and weak elsewhere.

21151.name: Clause-boundary punctuation and connectives (commas, periods, dashes, parentheses, semicolons, 'which', 'and', 'It') placed right after a complete statement or noun phrase, where the text is about to continue with an elaboration, explanation, or example of what was just said.

21166.name: The final token of a function, method, command or operator name right before its arguments are applied, usually the last subword of an identifier right before an opening parenthesis (e.g. make_feed_request(, url_for(, add(). This also covers math functions and operators acting on operands (f(x), ReLU(x), \div, ->, *().

21190.name: The method name in UI popup/notification calls, overwhelmingly Android's "Toast.makeText" (strongest), and more weakly similar calls such as "JOptionPane.showMessageDialog" and "Snackbar.make". These show a short user-facing message. Other activations, such as "text" in LaTeX \textsuperscript, are faint and scattered.

21199.name: Tokens at the start of, or linking to, a second parallel element that mirrors an earlier phrase with a variation, such as an alternate in parentheses, the second item of a pair or list, a repeated field label, or code lines repeating a prior pattern. The feature anticipates the text echoing a previous structure ("old and my new", "Min… ⏎Volume Range Max", "(maybe Ie7)", "die… open(").

A diffuse feature with no single topic. It fires on function words, connectives (and, to, for, unless, plus) and sentence or line-break punctuation at clause boundaries. It is strongest where the text sets up a parallel, contrastive or repeated structure that echoes earlier wording, such as 'origin and destination', 'not my favorite books', 'carrier sheet', 'compare them to the same edges' and 'second-to-last dimension'.

21269.name: The head word (often the final subword of a name) of a noun phrase acting as the subject at the start of a new sentence or paragraph, usually a definite or anaphoric re-mention of an entity already introduced (e.g. 'The report', 'The currency', a surname, a team or country), right before its verb.

21288.name: Closing delimiter tokens that end a nested or paired span, most strongly doubled closing braces "}}" in LaTeX subscripts, \text{}, \frac, \sqrt and template expressions. It fires more weakly on other closers: markdown bold "**", closing quotes, generic-type ">>" or ">", ")}", "})" and HTML closing tags.

21291.name: Function words that come right before a name, label, description or quotation is applied to something, most strongly "as"/"as a" after verbs of naming or describing (referred to as, known as, describing it as, called). Also covers similar connectors such as "called", "a" after calls/calling, and the colons, commas and opening quotes that introduce quoted characterizations.

21295.name: Weak, diffuse activation in tense or alarming narrative contexts, peaking on words describing fear, panic, worry or desperation (e.g. 'Panicking I began to try', 'heart dropped as she', 'feared', 'desperate') and on the reaction clauses around them. Elsewhere it fires faintly on function words, commas and verbs in emergencies, illness or death, urgent waiting or rushing.

21374.name: The word "email" (also "e-mail", "Email", "inbox") and related contact or identifier terms such as phone, IP, ZIP and username. It fires most strongly on "email" in form or contact contexts like "your email address", sign-up prompts and registration fields.

21431.name: Boilerplate legal and licensing text, such as copyright notices, Creative Commons license statements, permission and reproduction terms, disclaimers, and repository archive descriptions. It is strongest on the 'distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License, which permits unrestricted use...' formula.

21436.name: The last digit of a year inside citation keys (author name + year + title word, e.g. \cite{liu2017smart}, @article{Howell2016...}), firing on the digit that completes the year right before the title word. It is strongest in LaTeX \cite{} keys. A weak secondary response shows up on boilerplate web phrases like "Related questions" and "save at Amazon".
The final digit of a publication year inside a BibTeX citation key (e.g., the last digit just before a disambiguating letter like 'b').

Tokens at boundaries between a main text and its boilerplate or metadata, especially the final year digit in citation keys (e.g. "zeros2010", "Lowe2018"), which activate most strongly. It also fires on the word "questions" in Q&A site footers ("Related questions") and on trailing whitespace before comment-section boilerplate.

21439.name: Nouns and verbs for things a person says, records or produces that can be held against them or used as evidence, such as statements, confessions, testimony, remarks, recorded conversations, communications, photos/images and fingerprints. Contexts are often legal, investigative or reputational. The strongest activations are on confession, statement and self-incriminating phrases like 'incriminate herself'.

21458.name: The start of a second predicate in a coordinated clause: the verb, participle or predicative adjective (often with its preposition, e.g. "consists of", "works as", "ranged from") that comes right after "and", "but" or an auxiliary ("and is", "and was") and continues talking about the same subject without restating it.

The verb, or start of the predicate, in a second coordinated clause whose subject is omitted and carried over from earlier, usually right after "and" (sometimes "and is", "but", or "then"). Examples include "and resides on", "and hosted", and "and is teeming".

21479.name: Narrative biographical text about a person's career, especially athletes and fighters: their records, upcoming bouts and matchups, preparation, achievements and final roles (e.g. 'coming off a 41-0-1 record that includes 30 knockouts', 'was slated to face… champion', 'after his fifth, and final, role'). Function words and clause connectors in these career-history sentences activate most; scattered weak activations appear elsewhere.

2149.name: Fires on the noun that names the authority or governing document in legal, licensing and copyright boilerplate. It peaks on "License" in the Apache phrase "in compliance with the License". It is also strong on "author", "publisher" and "terms" in phrases like "without the consent of the author" and "consult the publisher's version". It fires weakly on other words in similar permission or usage text.

21542.name: Segments of file system paths and URLs, particularly server directory paths in PHP/CMS error messages (e.g., /wp-content/plugins/, /sites/all/modules/, /themes/), with the strongest activation on the directory components after the site root. Weak, scattered activations also appear on other code-like or technical identifiers.

21551.name: Fires on word-piece tokens inside the term "microtubule", most strongly on the "ub" right after "microt", with weaker activation on related cytoskeleton words (tubulin, cytoskeleton, filaments) and on microtubule-targeting drugs (paclitaxel, docetaxel, colchicine, taxol). There is faint spillover onto other "t-ub" pieces such as "tuberculosis".

2162.name: Numbers in running text, whether written as digits or words (cardinal or ordinal), that give a count, quantity, amount, percentage or ranking. The leading number of a phrase activates most, and statistics such as sports tallies activate strongest.

Cardinal numbers (digits or spelled-out words) used as quantities or counts in running text, especially the first number of a phrase. Activation is strongest for sports statistics and tallies such as scores, vote counts, sacks, touchdowns and saves.

21708.name: Academic/scientific prose, especially introduction and background sections that review prior work. Activations peak on literature-review framing such as "recent studies have", "researchers have found", "previous measurements", and "recent advances". They also fire on citation numbers and years and on discourse transitions at sentence starts ("For", "A", "On", "In").

21714.name:
Tokens that close an opening tag or block header and add a line break (e.g. "> ", ""> ", "{ "). They mostly follow HTML opening tags such as , ,
and

, and mark the point where nested child content is about to start.

21723.name: Binary operators (+, -, =, ==, /, ·) in math formulas or code, usually right after a product term or closing parenthesis, e.g. xy + ..., ps-qr, f(z))/. A few weak activations land on other separator tokens such as bullets, periods and commas.

21753.name: Error and failure messages, especially software, system, or network error output such as "failed", "connection refused", "error", "could not be loaded", or "too many arguments", along with error codes and the punctuation inside them. It fires weakly on nearby tokens about things breaking, being rejected, or not working.

21780.name: Separator (mostly a comma, sometimes a newline or ").,") that follows a department/lab/sub-unit name in academic author affiliations, right before the parent institution (e.g. "Department of Physics, University of…"). It fires most strongly after "Department of X". Weak activations appear on similar separators in addresses, citations and other text.

21825.name: Nouns naming the features, functions or capabilities something offers, most often a product, software, app or system (e.g. "features", "functionality", "functions", "capabilities", "properties"). Activation peaks on "features"/"functionality" and sometimes carries onto a following "that", "of" or "are".

21836.name: Words and phrases describing conduct, behavior or the manner and course of action: how someone acts, lives or behaves. Examples include the actions people take or avoid, ways or approaches of doing something, staying within or transgressing bounds, and doing right or wrong. Typical cases are 'act and behave', 'walk in the', 'how they live', 'doing nothing wrong', 'in such a way that', 'strategies' and 'trying to be'.

21846.name: Tokens that close a unit, typically right after an enumerated list or series of items: final punctuation, closing brackets/quotes/braces, line breaks, or the word right after the list ends. Activation is weak and diffuse, peaking where a list or bracketed/quoted group closes (")", "\"]", " }").

The token right after a list or enumeration of items ends (closing parentheses or brackets, periods, commas, dashes, quotes, newlines, or a connecting word like 'to', 'as', 'and'), marking where the series closes and the main sentence or structure resumes.

21928.name: Short value-like content tokens in math, code and structured data, such as numbers, single-letter variables, string literals and dictionary keys. They often sit right after =, (, quotes or currency symbols. Many repeat or are determined by earlier context (e.g. a repeated bid amount, a variable or answer value), though there is a weak scattering of ordinary words too.

Fires mainly on the first operand or term in math, code, and logic expressions: numbers, variables, or operators that begin an equation, list, set, comparison, or computation step (e.g. the first number being compared or added, the first element of an output list or set). It fires weakly on scattered other tokens such as answer colons in multiple-choice questions and sentence-ending periods.

21944.name: Sentence-ending punctuation fused with a paragraph break ('.⏎⏎', '?⏎⏎', '".⏎⏎') at the end of a news article's main body, right before unrelated boilerplate such as 'Related news', 'Latest News', 'More news:', or another story's headline. A mid-paragraph period gets weaker activation, and other tokens barely register.

21945.name: Whitespace tokens (spaces, trailing spaces, newlines and paragraph breaks) that come right after sentence-ending punctuation and mark the boundary before a new sentence, paragraph, heading or list item.

21975.name: Language that cites earlier research or past work, as in the related-work sections of academic writing. It fires most on perfect and passive verbs and nouns like "has been studied", "have been proposed/developed", "was shown in", "literature", "studies", "previous", "recently" and "many authors", which signal that a topic has already been investigated.

21981.name: Line-break and line-continuation tokens that fall mid-sentence: newlines (and following comment markers like ///, *, //, or indentation) that hard-wrap a sentence before it is finished, often right after a word that needs a continuation (articles, prepositions, adjectives, 'and', 'the'). Strongest when the newline splits a grammatical phrase.

22003.name: The LaTeX citation command name "cite" (including variants like \citep, \citealt, \newcite, \textcite) right after the backslash, which marks references to literature in academic text. Activation is highest for repeated citations in a list. There are weak activations on other LaTeX reference commands like \secref and on scattered unrelated tokens.

22047.name: Expressions of quantitative comparison or relative magnitude, especially in technical and scientific text. Typical forms are "comparable to", "larger than", "much greater than", "of the same order of magnitude" and "≫". The words "than" and "to" in these comparisons are usually the strongest tokens. Weaker activations fall on nearby size, scale and quantity terms such as widths, intensities and velocities.

22088.name: Strongly fires on ".Collectors" in Java "import java.util.stream.Collectors;" lines. It responds weakly to related collection/utility tokens in code, such as Rust ".collect()" on iterators, ".ContextCompat" and "Itertools" imports, and to the "202" year prefix in dates.

22129.name: Templated, machine-generated boilerplate text (citation headers, metadata records, product/listing pages, database-generated sentences), firing on the fixed scaffolding between variable slots: newlines and punctuation that end a filled-in field (name, place, date, number) and the stock template words that follow, such as "She was born", "and arrive at", "followed by", "is".

Tokens that repeat or complete a pattern seen earlier in the same context, where the token is predictable by copying a previous occurrence (e.g. a repeated variable suffix, a repeated word after the same preceding word, or repeated symbols). This is induction-like copying of earlier tokens, not tied to any particular meaning.

22176.name: The subword token "ube" (and variants like "UBE", "ubes", "ubectl", "kube") inside larger words, mostly names and proper nouns. It is strongest for Kubernetes terms (Kube, KubeCon, kubectl) and the province Hubei, and weaker in personal names (Rube, Dube, Steube) and words like lube. Occasional weak activations appear on bullet points and short function words.

22201.name: Fires at the end of a sentence's subject noun phrase (often a proper name or organization, especially in headlines and opening sentences) and on the verb or auxiliary that immediately follows it (has, is, are, warns, gives, appears to), i.e. the subject–predicate boundary.

22257.name: Separators (mostly semicolons, also commas, periods, newlines, braces and bullets) that end one field of a document's metadata and begin the next. The strongest cases are the semicolons in academic article history lines ("Received …; Revised …; Accepted …"), especially right after the year of the revised date. Weaker cases mark field boundaries in citation records, copyright/license notices, credit lines and similar boilerplate.

2233.name: A weak, diffuse feature with no single trigger word. It fires on the core content of explanatory or defining phrases: the words that say what something is, what it does, or how it works. These phrases typically follow a setup cue such as "i.e.", "that is,", "occurs when", "By that I mean", "governs", "are the", "need to" or "built for". Examples include "an elastic material deforms through a small opening", "how long your armour lasts when" and "do not accommodate naturally the notion of a secret key". Activation is strongest in the middle of such a functional or definitional description, especially on its main noun or verb.

Tokens inside clarifying or definitional phrases that restate or explain what something means or does, typically right after "i.e.,", a colon, an opening parenthesis, or a relative pronoun ("that", "where", "who"). Examples include "relationship is actually linear", "modify the original list" and "how far the object is from the axis". Activation is highest on the core predicate of the explanation, mostly in technical or instructional text.

22331.name: Fires on the word-piece ending in "-all" that precedes a suffix, mostly "crystall" (alone or the "all" after "cryst") in crystalline/crystallize/crystallization, and more weakly "metall" in metallurgy/metallizing. It fires most on scientific and materials usage.

22339.name: Fires weakly and diffusely on ordinary words inside direct quotations and reported speech, such as interview remarks ending in “,” he said. Activation tends to grow over longer spans of quoted spoken language, especially conversational or opinion-giving phrasing. Some activations appear outside quotes but are weak and scattered.

22343.name: Language of public opinion measurement: polls, surveys, approval ratings and popularity, and the phrasing used to report their results (e.g. "polls showed", "72 percent disapprove", "is above 50%"). Activation is strongest on poll/approval/rating terms and the reported percentages. It weakly extends to related rankings, market share, odds and consensus.

2239.name: Temporal-perspective words that relate a thing's state to a different point in time than the one being narrated, usually the present or a later moment. The strongest is "now", especially in "what is now" and appositive "now a ...". Weaker ones include "today", "to this day", "later", "eventual", "will become", "still", "current", "future" and "retroactively named".

22402.name: Segment-boundary tokens, mostly sentence-final periods and also commas, colons and newlines, that end a clause or list item just before an abrupt shift. It fires most strongly on periods in incoherent, spun or SEO-style filler text (e.g., essay-writing spam), where the next sentence is an unrelated non-sequitur. It fires weakly on separators in lists, metadata and boilerplate.

22433.name: Nouns for external threats or unwanted agents that something defends against, removes or fights off (enemies, invaders, attackers, predators, pests, viruses, disease, asteroids, dust, toxins), usually the object of verbs or prepositions like "against", "combat", "protect from", "remove" or "filter out". It is weaker on other things a system takes in or acts on (food, glucose, sauces, the environment).

Nouns naming the threat, enemy or harmful agent that something defends against, fights, or is protected from (invaders, predators, viruses, foreign substances, enemies, attacks, disease, danger), usually the object of verbs like protect from, stop, fight, kill or intercept. Weak activations appear on unrelated object nouns.

22443.name: Prepositions (mostly "of", "in", "to", "for", "on", "about") that come right after a noun, adjective or verb and introduce a prepositional phrase. Strongest when the phrase ties a head word to a following noun phrase ("members of", "efforts in", "to all"), and it often extends onto a following "the".

22446.name: The strong activations are on the bodies of anonymous C/C++-style union and struct declarations: the opening brace, the indentation, member types and names (e.g. "float all[", "long long", "double d"), and the closing ";" or "};". Weak activations elsewhere fall on structural and list markers such as numbering, bullets, braces, newlines and indentation, plus occasional connective words.

22495.name: Boundary tokens that close a title, name, or header-like field in structured or semi-structured text. These are mostly newlines (often double) right after a page/article/namespace/class title or metadata value. Closing HTML tags, quotes, braces, file extensions/domains, and the ' on' after an author name in code headers also fire. The activation marks the end of a label just before new content begins.

22522.name: Second-level segments of dotted namespace/package paths in code, mostly ".Runtime" after "System" in C# using directives, ".gms" after "com.google.android" and ".minecraftforge" after "net" in Java imports. Activation is strongest in import/using statements and weaker in inline references or documentation.

22564.name: Affiliation markers placed right after author names in academic paper bylines: superscript numbers, letters, or symbols (1, ¹, a, †, *), including LaTeX \textsuperscript arguments. The first affiliation marker ("1"/"¹"/"a") activates most strongly, while secondary markers (2, ‡) and separating commas activate weakly.

22574.name: Tokens right after a 'Returns'/'Output'/'@return'/'Value'/'Result' label in docstrings, API docs, and problem statements, i.e. the colon, newline, indentation, bullet or opening words ('the', 'A', 'Print the single number') that begin the description of what is returned or output. It also fires weakly on commas after sentence-initial words like 'Finally' or 'Eventually' and on similar section-heading punctuation.

22618.name: Tokens that mark conditioning, i.e. what something is computed or evaluated relative to. This covers the conditional bar in probability notation like P(A|B), which activates most strongly, plus similar bars and separators in math or code (restriction, set-builder, random-effect bars, ~). It also covers words like "given (the)", "assuming", "subject to", "constrained", "considering", "based on" and "from".

22621.name: The access modifier "protected" at the start of a method declaration in object-oriented code (Java, C#, PHP), along with the words right after it ("void", "override", "function"). It is strongest right after an @Override annotation in Android code such as "protected void onCreate(Bundle savedInstanceState)". Other method modifiers like "public" or "private void" fire weakly, and the few prose examples are only trace activations.
The invisible variation selector (U+FE0F) that follows an emoji such as 🌤, forcing emoji-style rendering. Here it appears in emoji-heavy, code-like markup text.

22680.name: Sentence openings and connective phrases in the results and conclusion parts of scientific abstracts. Activation is highest on sentence boundaries and on the subject-plus-reporting-verb frames that follow them, such as "The results ... confirm", "our analysis reveals that", "We observed" and "values are".

22751.name: Separators between consecutive entries in academic citation lists, chiefly the semicolon after a year in author–year in-text citations (e.g. "Smith et al., 2005; Jones, 2007"), where activation is strongest. Weaker activation falls on commas, "and" or "&" between cited works or authors, and occasionally on words leading into a cited author name.

22756.name: Postal address unit designators that come right before a number, most strongly "PO Box" and its variants (P.O. Box, BP, C.P., GPO Box, CP), plus the following space. Weaker activations occur on similar address labels such as Suite, Room, Apt, #, Street/Highway, and UMR.

22761.name: Language about change or development over time, especially present-perfect phrasing describing how things have shifted, grown, evolved or been transformed since some earlier point. Typical forms are "has changed since", "have grown", "evolved over the years", "huge changes have begun" and "in the meantime". The strongest activations come from explicit descriptions of change since a past reference point. Weaker activations land on scattered nouns and verbs nearby.

22766.name: The "public" access modifier at the start of a top-level type declaration (usually "public class"), typically in Java, placed right after imports, comments or annotations. It is strongest when unindented at the start of a line and weaker for indented C# declarations inside namespaces or "public" inside URLs.

22794.name: Parameter/key names in key=value syntax, mostly keyword arguments in code function calls (e.g. delimiter=, encoding=, fontsize=, cls=) and also BibTeX fields (author=, title=) and URL query keys. Activation peaks on the argument name right before '=', especially after a comma or opening parenthesis.

22854.name: Statement-terminating tokens in code, typically closing parentheses, semicolons or brackets fused with a newline (");⏎", ";⏎", "))⏎"). They most often end the last statement inside a block, right before a closing brace or dedent (e.g., after error handling, throw/exit/fail calls). Weaker activations appear on similar line endings in HTML tables and Python.

22856.name: Words that name a particular time point when something happens, mainly "day" (also night, year, hour, date, holiday names like Christmas Eve or Thanksgiving), typically in phrases like "the same day", "that day", "launch day" or "the night before" that anchor an event to a specific occasion.

Words naming a specific day or point in time, mostly "day" (strongest in "same day", "first day", "that day", "Christmas day"), plus related time units and occasions such as night, morning, week, year, date, today, and holidays. It also fires on date fragments like ordinal suffixes and day numbers, usually within time-reference phrases such as "on the ___ of".

22878.name: Tokens in academic, scientific, or technical prose that mark scholarly discourse: research and expertise vocabulary (theory, method, study, explanation, foundations, perspectives, expertise), researcher actions (we prove, argue, uncovered, solve this problem), and citation or reference formatting such as titles in quotes, journal abbreviations, and citation counts.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on tokens in technical, academic or methodological contexts, such as text about research, engineering, models, theory, scientific methods and expert explanations. It tends to activate near words like 'models', 'sciences', 'theory', 'engineers', 'research', 'technical' and 'proof and simulation', and on function words inside those passages. It is driven by the expert or scholarly register of the surrounding text rather than by any specific word.

2289.name: Words expressing attempt, effort, ability or goal toward an action, most often the infinitive "to" after verbs like try, able/unable, managed, working, aim, along with "can", "if you can", and "as ... as possible". The common thread is striving or capacity to accomplish something.

22978.name: Punctuation and connectors inside taxonomic author citations that follow scientific species names, such as the comma or space before the year, the closing parenthesis or period after an abbreviated author name, and joiners like '&', 'et', or 'ex'. It fires weakly on similar separators in ordinary author-year literature citations.

23033.name: Words inside natural-language explanations embedded in technical or code contexts, firing most strongly within code comments (e.g. after //, /*, #, <!--) and descriptive identifiers such as test method names. Activation is weak and diffuse in ordinary prose.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no single token trigger. It fires on scattered mid-sentence words, mostly content words and function words inside explanatory or instructional prose. The text is typically technical documentation, code comments, recipes, how-to steps, notes and forms, and the tokens usually fall within phrases describing what something does or what to do.

23058.name: Tokens at the start of a new sentence or clause, mostly the opening words of a statement such as "There are", "Most of us", "While", "Although you may", "As" and "In the case of". These framing phrases set up a general claim or the next point in expository prose, often right after a period or paragraph break.

2308.name: Symbolic operators and connector symbols, especially arrows and relational tokens (=>, ->, \to, \rightarrow, >, >=, ±, ×, \circ), along with other special symbols like ©, ####, and emoji. These are tokens linking two operands or marking structure, mostly in code, math/LaTeX, and formatted text; arrows activate most strongly.

23133.name: Content tokens in technical, scientific or research writing (methods, materials, research aims, specs, job/tech requirements). It fires on domain terms such as instruments, compounds, organisms, software and techniques, and on whole phrases describing research goals or findings. Activation is broad and moderate rather than tied to one word.

23148.name: Relative pronouns (mostly "where", also "which"/"whom") that open a non-restrictive relative clause right after a named place or institution (school, university, city, company). The strongest cases follow educational or employer names, as in biographical text.

23188.name: The LaTeX command name "label" right after a backslash, as in \label{...}, typically placed after \section{...} headings or inside equation, align and figure environments. It fires most strongly when \label starts its own line. Similar LaTeX commands such as \tag and \be activate weakly, as does indentation whitespace in Chinese text.

2322.name: Nouns (or noun modifiers in compounds) naming the functional role, purpose, use, or domain/sector of something, often following phrases like “used as a”, “as a”, “for”, or “in the”. Examples include “tool”, “laboratory”, “food source”, “investment”, “medical applications”, “drinking water”, “training aircraft”, “entertainment world”, and “side dish”.

23262.name: Tokens that come right after a newly introduced named entity, usually a product, system, method, species or acronym, and begin describing it. These are mostly commas, closing parentheses or periods, and verbs like "is"/"was" or relative pronouns like "which"/"that"/"a" that open an appositive or definitional clause. Activation is strongest on the comma or parenthesis right after the name.

23274.name: Function, method, or command names that execute or invoke something, mostly in code. The strongest cases are calls like os.system, runString, run, and search, which execute commands, code, or strings. Weaker hits include shell commands, macros (try!, html!, assert_eq!), asm blocks, and words like "execute" or "Type" in instructions. Activation usually falls on the method or call token just before its arguments.

23280.name: Line breaks and trailing punctuation (e.g. ".", "!", ")", ";" followed by newlines, and occasionally markers like "###" or "<td") at a boundary where one document, section or list item ends and an unrelated one begins, typically just before a new title, headline or heading.

23344.name: Institution names in author affiliation or address lines, especially the start of a new segment after a comma or line break. It fires most strongly on "University (of)" and its foreign equivalents (Universität, Université, Universidad), and also on Department, Faculty, School, College, Institute and the first token of named universities.

23404.name: Inner subword fragments of biomedical terms tied to calcium regulation and endocrinology, with the peak on "athy" in "parathyroid". Weaker hits come from "calc" in hypercalcemia and cholecalciferol, "mod" in calmodulin, "yst" in homocysteine, and calcitriol. Faint, noisy activations also appear on unrelated tokens such as commas and name pieces like "Sathy".

23415.name: Leading/partial tokens of variable or identifier names in code, especially at the beginning of a line or statement where a previously defined variable is being reassigned or used (e.g., the first subword of a multi-token identifier like "waiting_time", "test_files", "cleanArticleID").

23441.name: The pointer asterisk in Go method receivers, e.g. "func (s *Type)", and more weakly in pointer parameter types. Activation is strongest when the * follows a short receiver variable name. The other low activations are scattered noise: sentence-initial "However"/"Furthermore", German "vorhand(en)", and "GTA" in username lists.

23463.name: Standalone punctuation or symbol tokens, often combined with newlines (e.g. "---", "…", ":", "/", ".", "{"), that act as separators or filler at section and document boundaries. They typically appear where one text segment ends and an unrelated one (a new heading, a scraped fragment, a code block) begins.

23492.name: Garbled or corrupted spots in noisy text such as OCR errors, spun or scraped spam, redaction blocks, censored swearing, stray symbols and digits inside words, and misplaced punctuation or spacing. It fires on the anomalous token that breaks the expected word or sentence, especially digits or symbols standing in for letters (s6ances, a9tion, ma&us, i8go) and censorship or redaction marks.

235.name: Word-initial fragments, usually capitalized or space-prefixed, that begin a longer word split across tokens, such as name parts (Ver, Char, Mel), abbreviations (Rev., prof., Std) and truncated stems (Ex, dist, rep, def, Comp). Activation sits on the first piece, which predicts the rest of the word; full short words like obj, err and Pro also fire.

Word-initial fragment tokens: the first subword piece of a longer word that is split across multiple tokens (e.g. "param"-etric, "Rec"-all, "Lib"-elle, "Met"-roid, "dir"). They also include truncated identifiers and abbreviations in code (len, int, del, _prod). The feature seems to mark an incomplete word stem that predicts a continuation, and it shows up most in noisy, technical, or garbled text.

2351.name: Separator tokens (commas, spaces, ampersands, pipes, slashes) between items in repetitive lists, arrays, matrices, tables and other sequences of numbers or symbols, strongest in long uniform patterns like LaTeX matrix '&' cells.

23533.name: Punctuation that ends a clause or sentence (periods, commas, question/exclamation marks, colons, dashes, Chinese 。, line breaks). It fires most strongly in non-English text such as German, Dutch, Catalan, Hindi and Portuguese, and at boundaries where the next clause or sentence begins.

23561.name: Statistical labels inside parenthetical results in scientific writing, mainly 'n =', 'P/p =' or 'p <', 'r =', 'OR', 'CI', 'AUC', plus the following '=' or '<' and sometimes the leading '0' of the value. The label letter is the strongest part; weaker hits fall on other labels placed right before a number (level, Km, Rs., table <td> cells).

23582.name: Words that introduce the result or product of a transformation, conversion, reaction or formation: prepositions and verbs such as "into", "to", "to form", "produce", "yielding" and "create" placed right before the resulting substance or form (e.g., "converting X into", "react to form", "reduced to"). Activation is strongest for chemical and physical reaction contexts like "react to form" and "decays to form". Weaker activation falls on list conjunctions joining multiple products.

Words marking the result or output of a transformation, conversion or production process. Most often "into" after verbs like turn, convert, transform or change, but also "to", "as", "produce", "generate", "release" and "get". The word links a source to what it becomes or yields.

2363.name: The negation word "not" (sometimes "Not" or, weakly, similar words like "never", "even", "without") when it stands without an auxiliary verb and negates a phrase, clause, or contrast. Typical cases are "not only…but also", "but not X", "not just", "not least", and sentence-initial "Not". Activation is strongest at the start of sentences or clauses, and weak when "not" simply follows "is" or "has".

23719.name: Android/Java "Context" objects in code: the Context type and its context variable (field declarations like "private Context context;", constructor parameters, calls passing context). It is weaker on context-like stand-ins such as passing "this" or getActivity(), Application, env, plugin, request, and imports of android.content.Context. Activation peaks on declared Context fields and variable names.

23721.name: A diffuse, low-specificity feature with weak activations spread across varied text. It is most consistent at structural boundaries where a new segment begins: paragraph breaks and newline/indentation runs (especially after forum headers like "Homepage" or before a reply), sentence-ending periods followed by newlines, list numbers and bullets, and commas separating list items. It also fires on scattered clause-initial or continuation words ("There", "These", "should", "like", "may then") and on some emotionally descriptive phrases.

23731.name: The word "victim" and its forms (victims, victimhood, Victim No.), usually as a noun for a person or thing harmed by crime, disaster, attack, disease, hacking or predation. A following "of" gets weaker activation. Related roles like prey, survivors, sufferers, casualties, perpetrators and beneficiary activate weakly, as does the name fragment "Vict" (Victor).

23737.name: Technical terms for operations, transformations or mappings applied to something (function, operation, unitary transformation, map, gate, transition probabilities, update, applying), strongest in math notation defining a function "f: X \to Y"; weak elsewhere in technical/code text.

23738.name: A diffuse, weak feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires on mid-phrase continuation tokens such as prepositions, verbs after a subject, the second word of a compound noun, word-suffix pieces, and code or LaTeX syntax fragments. These appear mostly in technical, code, math or documentation text. The strongest activation is on the second word of a short label inside code ("Front End" in a print call).

23762.name: Place names, mostly cities, towns and neighborhoods. Activation falls on the token that completes the name, often a suffix fragment such as "ington", "ville", "ley" or "burg", or the second word of a multiword name like Santa Barbara or Orland Park. These names usually appear in addresses, datelines or institutional affiliations.

Place names, mostly cities and towns (often US college or mid-sized towns), with activation landing on the token that completes the name, such as the final subword or the second word of a multi-word name (e.g. "ston" in Evanston, "Haven" in New Haven). Activation is strongest in locative contexts like "in X" or "based in X". It occasionally also fires on venue names, university domains and person names.

23827.name: Administrative boilerplate covering access, permissions, contact details and usage terms: tokens in instructions about whom to contact, how to obtain or use material (accounts, licenses, membership, availability, restrictions), and disclaimers or correspondence notes. Activation is strongest on directive phrases like "are required to contact" or "are urged to consult".

Words in formal boilerplate or notice-style text about access, availability, permission, restrictions and contact procedures (e.g. 'available from', 'contact … by writing to', 'requires a special permit', 'may not be copied', 'with permission'). They are mostly function words and predicates that link a resource to how, where or under what conditions it can be obtained or used.

23834.name: The subword "toc" (or "oc" after T), strongest as the middle of "oxytocin" and in "toc" as a table-of-contents marker (e.g. {:toc}, toc = false, @[toc]); weaker for tocopherol, Tocqueville, Tocantins, and TOC.

23844.name: The word-piece "hemorrh"/"orrh" (as in hemorrhage, hemorrhagic, haemorrhage, hemorrhoid), firing most strongly in medical bleeding contexts and also on figurative uses like "hemorrhaging staff". It fires weakly on "orrh" in mycorrhizal and on related blood terms such as "hematoma" and "bleeding".

23851.name: Words for travelling to, visiting, attending or staying at a place or event, such as visit/visiting, trip, journey, travel, stay, attend and "you're in [place]". It fires most strongly on "visiting" and attendance or stay phrases. It also fires weakly on related activity nouns like purchase, sale, ride and experience.

23879.name: Fires on function words that link phrases mid-sentence, mostly prepositions ('of', 'in', 'to', 'on') directly after a noun or verb, plus commas, 'and'/'or' and articles. It is strongest in stilted, formal or translated-sounding prose, often by Spanish or Portuguese writers, where runs of connective phrasing light up together.

23896.name: Opening punctuation that starts a citation or source attribution right after a quoted or stated claim, mostly " (" before author/page/verse/source references, plus "[" for numbered footnotes, "Source:" colons, and numbering periods or braces in reference lists.

23941.name: Text on dark matter and hypothetical particles in physics (WIMPs, axions, gravitons, relic density, indirect detection, particle stability and mass). It peaks on phrases describing dark matter candidates and their properties, with weak, diffuse activation on other scientific or technical text.

23943.name: Separators that come right after a URI scheme or resource prefix, mostly "://" (http, https, ftp, s3, postgresql, res, gs). Also fires on related prefix delimiters: ":" in jdbc:/dbi:/jar:/steam:, "mailto:", and "\\" or "//" at the start of a path. Activation is strongest for less common schemes such as postgresql, res, ftp and s3, and weaker for ordinary http/https.

23998.name: Hyphen/minus/dash characters and tokens naming them, usually as literal symbols in code strings, math, identifiers or separators (e.g. '-', "--", -*-, minus sign). The strongest hits are words for such punctuation ("hyphens", "hyphenated", "underscores"), with weaker hits on related naming conventions like snake_case and camelCase.

Dashes, hyphens, underscores and similar separator or filler punctuation ("-", "_", "---", soft hyphens, combining marks). These usually appear in noisy, garbled or code-like text, and the feature also fires on the word "hyphens"/"dash" and on character classes like [-+].

24029.name: The comma (or semicolon) right after a surname in inverted "Surname, Given-name" form, as in author lists, citations and bibliographies. It also fires weakly on other separators after a leading name or term ("Place, Region", "Term, qualifier").

Commas placed right after a surname (often an unusual or foreign one) in "Lastname, Firstname" inverted order, as in author lists, citations, bibliographies and obituaries. Sometimes the following initial or first-name token fires instead, and weakly the comma after a place name or other proper noun.

24051.name: Fires on text about visual formatting and layout of web pages and documents: CSS properties such as font-size and px values, HTML header and h1 tags placed at the top of a page, colors, typography size and image dimensions. The strongest activations come from descriptions of where or how titles and headers are styled or positioned. Weaker, scattered activations fall on markup and code syntax and on assorted function words.

24056.name: Names of news outlets, wire services and publishers given as source attributions, especially in datelines like "CITY (AP) —", after "told" (told Reuters), or in bylines and credits. It also fires on the labels "Press Release" and "News Release". Activation is strongest on agency names inside dateline parentheses such as AP, Reuters, IANS and Xinhua.

24139.name: A standalone space token that sits right before a number (a year, address number, ID, count, time, percentage, list index), usually following a comma, colon, dash, slash or the end of a name or title. It also fires on the leading space before bullet points or list items in metadata-like text such as citations, addresses, dates and listings.

24140.name: Variable or symbol references in math expressions and code, especially a variable appearing again after it was already used (e.g. the x in “x = 0.6x”, “2x”, “self”, array indices). It fires most strongly on single-letter variables that follow a coefficient or operator. Weaker activations fall on pronouns and determiners that refer back to an earlier subject.

24345.name: The direct object (usually a noun or noun phrase) that immediately follows a transitive verb, especially gerunds and imperatives, as in UI commands and titles, e.g. 'Transfer money', 'measuring gamma rays', 'Engineering enzyme', 'cooking dinner', 'Stop leak'. The activation is on the object token(s), not on the verb.

24360.name: Numeric indices inside Lie/symmetry group names, especially gauge groups like U(1), SU(2), SU(3), O(3) (the number and its closing parenthesis/subscript), with strongest activation on U(1) and Standard Model gauge groups; weaker activation on related physics concepts such as electromagnetism, conserved quantum numbers (baryon/lepton number, R-parity) and other group subscripts.

Tokens in technical math/physics contexts, chiefly small numeric parameters inside group or interval notation (SL(2,Z), SO(2,1), Z_2, (-1,1)), plus physics terms about charges and forces (charge, electromagnetism), with the strongest activation on 'electrom'.

24439.name: Words about explaining or accounting for something, giving a cause or reason for a phenomenon. "explain" is the strongest, especially after modals or hedges ("may explain", "partly explain", "would explain"). Related forms ("explanation", "explained"), "account for", "understand", "makes sense", "reason" and "why" activate more weakly.

24441.name: Binary operators that combine sets or functions, mostly set intersection: the LaTeX \cap token (strongest), the ∩ symbol, and the words "intersection" and "union". Weaker activations go to related operators such as \cup/∪, \circ (function composition), ∧, Python & between sets, and .intersection. Isolated non-math tokens (e.g. "Pages", "the") activate only faintly.

24442.name: Separator tokens (colons, equals signs, opening quotes or braces, spaces) right after a property, parameter or field name and just before its value is written, especially color values in CSS, plotting and code (e.g. 'color:', "col = '", 'background-color: #'). It also fires more weakly on the space before a number in prose.

24448.name: The final token(s) of long alphanumeric strings such as IDs, hashes, URL shortener codes, hex addresses, part/serial numbers and numeric values. The activation lands on the last chunk of these random-looking sequences, right before a delimiter like a slash, quote, newline or space.

245.name: Weak, diffuse feature on the token immediately following a number or completed noun phrase, usually a connector or separator leading to the next item: range and comparison words ("to", "and", "than", "more"), math operators (+, =, ×, )/( ), dashes, spaces, commas, newlines, and units. It is most common right after numeric values in ranges, equations, dates and measurements.

Separator or connector tokens that come right after a number (or a numeric or other item) and link it to a following value. Typical cases are hyphens, dashes, slashes, plus signs, ±, commas and line breaks in scores, records, ranges, page spans and table cells, e.g. 3-0, 15 - 10, 9st 4lb / 130lb. Weaker activations fall on short words that play the same linking role after an item (in, and, at, than, for).

24573.name: Content of formal, journalistic or official-report prose, especially clauses reporting attributed claims or findings about government, military, intelligence or security actions (e.g. sources saying an attack was intended to cause harm, that malware was used against agencies, or that officials attempted/created a program). Weaker activation is spread across function words in similar documentary/historical report text.

24632.name: Website metadata and labeling boilerplate, mainly the tagging of posts. It fires most strongly on "ged" in "Tagged", especially in "Posts Tagged" archive headers. It fires weakly on "Tags:", "tagged", "Tagged as/with", "Filed Under", "Posts by" and "archive for", which introduce the category, tag or author labels of a blog or forum page.

24647.name: Number chunks (usually three-digit tokens like "000", "130", "700") inside the suffix of DOI identifiers. They tend to fall in the middle of the article number after the journal or year prefix, not at the start or end.

24653.name: In academic citations, the space, opening parenthesis, or bracket right after an author name (e.g. "et al.," or "Smith and Jones") together with the first digits of the publication year that follows ("200", "199", "201"). In short, the point where an author name gives way to the citation year. Activation is highest in lists of several references.

The space (or opening parenthesis) right before a year number, and the first digits of that year ("198", "200", "201"). It fires most strongly inside academic author–year citations such as "et al., 2013" or "Smith (1994)". It fires more weakly on years in dates and in lists.

24660.name: Terms for biological or physical specimens collected for testing or analysis, chiefly "blood" and "samples" (blood tests, blood work, serum, saliva samples, specimen, biopsy, tissue, swab), plus verbs of collecting or sampling. Activation is strongest on phrases like "blood samples" and "saliva samples".

24738.name: The "pom" letter sequence across words and languages: whole tokens like "pomp" (pompous), "Pom" (Pomodoro, Pompidou, pom-pom) and Czech/Slavic "pom" (pomalu, pomáhají), plus "om/ome/omer/um" pieces right after a split-off "P/p" (Pompeo, pomegranate, Pomeranz, pummeled). Activation is strongest on "Pom"/"pom" tokens.

Word-piece tokens for the sound "pom"/"om" (and similar "um"/"omm"), mostly right after a "P" (or L/G) at the start of a word. Activation is strongest for a capitalized " Pom" opening a proper noun (Pomona, Pomsky, Pompidou, Pomodoro, Pomc) and for "Pompe"/"pomp", and weaker for mid-word fragments like p-ome-granate, p-um-meled, L-om-ax and G-om-el.

24740.name: The letter pair "GL" (any casing or prefix: " GL", ",GL", "/GL") as a token, nearly always in an uppercase acronym, abbreviation or code: GLP, GLUE, GL(n) groups, GLaDOS, GLA, postcodes, IDs and random strings. It is strongest when GL begins an acronym or follows an opening parenthesis. There is weak firing on similar tokens such as "GH" and "gh".

24747.name: The subword token "uz" (and close variants such as "Suz", "Luz", "uzz", "z"), mostly found inside proper names and foreign words like surnames, place names and brands (Suzuki, Soyuz, Fuzhou, Kreuz-). Activation is strongest when it falls mid-word in an unfamiliar name.

The subword "uz" (and close variants like " Luz", " Suz", "uzz", "z", "Z", "ž", Cyrillic "з") appearing inside words, mostly proper nouns such as surnames, given names and place names (e.g. Kuznets, Guzman, Luzon, Suzie), plus slang spellings like "cuz"/"duz".

24819.name: The category noun (head of a reference class) in classifying or superlative statements like "the most common X", "one type/form of X", "X% of all X", saying where something ranks within or belongs to a class. It fires most strongly on disease terms, especially "cancer", "tumor" and "malignancy".

24849.name: Job titles and occupational roles, especially the head noun completing a position name after a modifier (e.g., editorial assistant, acquisitions officer, security guard, Audit Senior, DevOps expert), plus occasional work-related nouns or activities.

Job titles, occupations and professional roles, with activation on the head noun or final subword that completes the role (e.g. clerk, driver, designer, attorney, gunner). It also fires weakly on related work or field nouns (management, design, instruction). Activation is strongest in job-posting or hiring contexts.

2485.name: Separators and coordinating conjunctions (commas, "and", "or", "&", "/or", "such as", "including") that join items in coordinated lists or pairs of nouns, especially enumerations of proper names, platforms, or technologies. Activation is strongest late in longer lists, at the final ", and" or "and".

24887.name: A weak, diffuse feature with low activation that does not track any particular word. It fires on tokens inside clauses that express contrast, comparison, negation or evaluation, such as "but we weren't the only ones", "not even", "instead of", "more real than", "easier and more likely", "right or wrong" and "aren't". It also picks up some of the function words that carry these argumentative turns.

24898.name: Words that name an intervention or change in something's presence or level (loss, lack, knockdown, lesions, blockade, addition, overexpression, suppression, removal, deficiency). They usually take an "of" object and set up a cause-effect claim about what that manipulation does, mostly in scientific or experimental writing. The strongest are phrases like "Loss of", "knockdown in" and "blockade of".

24923.name: Subword fragments inside personal names, mostly non-English given names (especially Chinese, Korean, Thai and other Asian names) in author lists and bylines. It fires most strongly on the middle or later pieces of multi-token or hyphenated given names (e.g. "-Ki", "-Ho", "ih", "h").

24931.name: A weak, diffuse feature firing on structural boundary tokens where one unit ends and a new one begins: sentence-final periods, paragraph and line breaks, stray spaces, list and line numbers, markdown and closing markup such as ** and , and code delimiters such as ```, $$ or (['. It peaks slightly in code and markup contexts, but overall reflects text-segmentation positions rather than specific meaning.

24936.name: Words naming prisons and the penal/correctional system, especially as part of facility or agency names (Correctional, Corrections, correction officers, jail, prison, penitentiary, Shawshank, San Quentin, Department of Justice). The strongest are 'correction(al)' forms. Other institution-name heads (Hospital, Convalescent, College of Education) fire weakly.

24954.name: Tokens that are a name or identifier stem immediately preceding an index-like suffix, usually a digit (e.g. value→3, decorator→1, Part→2, R→1, Profile→7), but also Roman numerals, letters or subscripts (Walker B, Science IV, Villa Wagner II, n_i). Common in code variable and function names, labels, part or section numbers and model/catalog codes. The feature anticipates an upcoming number or label.

24957.name: Line breaks, bullets, spaces and closing punctuation that separate fields in boilerplate or structured web and document text, such as metadata, HAL IDs, radio player widgets, bid listings, HTML tables and citation footers. Activation peaks at the newline that ends one metadata item and comes right before the next item.

24967.name: Dot leaders (runs of periods/ellipses, sometimes spaces or table cell tags) that fill the gap between an entry title and its page number in tables of contents, indexes and similar listings. Activation is strongest on the final dot tokens just before the page number.

25012.name: Scientific journal names and their abbreviations in citations, especially the "J" in ApJ/EPJ bibcodes and "Journal" after "Astrophysical"/"Astronomical". Also fires on other journal abbreviation fragments (Sci, Natur, PhysRevLett, RMP, CQG, ApJS).

25058.name: Words that refer back to a set of several items named earlier, often quantifiers or demonstratives such as "these/those", "both/all of which", "respectively", "the two", "each" and "the latter". The activating words are anaphoric or distributive and point to multiple entities already introduced in the text.

25132.name: Tokens inside URLs, file paths and web addresses (domains like .com/.org/.uk, github.com, path segments such as /blob/master, /uploads/2018/05, relative ../ paths), especially image/link sources in markdown or HTML. Strongest on domain names and path components. Weaker hits fall on source or credit attributions (website, publisher or organization names, e.g. 'CBC', 'Facebook', 'Survey').

25173.name: Words for entry points and ways in or through: entrance, entry, gate, door, access, portal, gateway, intake, ingress, mostly physical but also figurative. Activation peaks on "entrance", especially "the entrance (of/to)", and the following "of" or "to" also fires.

Words for entry and threshold points of a place, such as entrance, entry, gate, gateway, door, lobby, foyer, exit, front and access, plus verbs like enter. It is strongest on "entrance", especially "entrance to/of" a physical place like a mine, tunnel, station or restaurant.

25182.name: The ".Linq" token in C# using directives ("using System.Linq;", also System.Linq.Expressions / System.Xml.Linq), within the import block at the top of a file. Activation is strongest for the plain System.Linq import.

25214.name: Initial tokens of proper names, chiefly Scottish/Irish "Mc" surnames and brands (strongest on "McDonald", especially the restaurant chain; also McKinsey, McLaren, McCormick). Weaker hits on other name-start pieces like "Maurit" (Mauritius/Mauritania), Kellogg, Tiffany and Suzuki, and on fast-food words.

Strongest on the name "McDonald", especially the fast-food chain McDonald's, and weaker on other "Mc"/"Mac" surnames (McConnell, McKinsey, McGuire). It also fires on related fast-food words ("fast food", Happy Meal, burger) and on brand or place names that look like surnames (Tiffany, Kellogg, Buckingham, Coventry).

25249.name: Nouns for retail establishments, mainly "store"/"stores", plus "shop(s)", "retailer", "bookstore", "supermarket" and Chinese 店. They often follow a modifier naming what is sold (grocery, toy, comic book) or a brand name (Honeywell Store). Activation is strongest for "store", weaker for "shop", and also fires on the idiom "in store".

Nouns for retail establishments, mainly "store" and "shop" (plus plurals and compounds like bookstore, storefront, boutiques, in-store). They cover physical and online stores (App Store, iTunes store), and occasionally storage senses such as evidence stores, ammunition store, or the code term Store/load. Activation is strongest for "store"/"stores" in the retail sense and weaker for "shop".

25260.name: Tokens that begin a continuation line in multi-line math derivations: new display-math openers (\[, $$) or alignment characters (&, &=) and line breaks (\\) immediately after a previous equation closes, usually followed by '=', '\le', '+', or '⇒' chaining the next step.
