Weaker activations appear on declarations, config syntax, the variable-introducing "Let ..." in math, and formulaic document structure like tables of contents, academic affiliations and forum headers.

30469.name: The main verb (often a copula or auxiliary like is/are/was/has/would/can) that comes right after a long, complex subject noun phrase, especially one containing prepositional modifiers ("the X of the Y"). It marks where the subject ends and the predicate begins. It sometimes fires on a comma or "to" sitting at the same subject–predicate boundary.

30495.name: Tokens that fuse a leading punctuation mark or symbol (parenthesis, quote, bracket, asterisk, hyphen, slash, dollar sign, @, period) with the first letters of the next word, e.g. "(T", ""C", "[s", "-user". They mostly appear at the start of a line or a parenthetical or quoted span, where the tokenizer splits the following word oddly.

30499.name: Opening delimiters or spaces that come right before an inline value (a math variable, number, or code literal), usually after a noun that the value names (e.g. 'the complete graph on $n$', 'set to 1 inch', 'port 3333'). Strongest on the opening LaTeX '$' or '\(' of inline math; weaker on backticks, quotes, and the space before a bare number.

30518.name: Words built on the root "collaborat-" (collaboration, collaborate, collaborative, collaborator, including split pieces like "Coll|abor|ating"), covering joint work, partnerships and co-authored efforts. Near-synonyms such as "cooperate" and "team effort" fire only weakly.

30570.name: The final digit of a DOI's publisher prefix (the "10.xxxx" registrant code), right before the slash that starts the suffix, sometimes including the slash. Weak activation on similar URL path segments such as "/embed" or "/articles".

30614.name: Discourse boundaries in expository or news-style prose: sentence-ending punctuation, paragraph breaks, and the words that open a new sentence or clause ("The", "A", "In", "One of"). Activation is strongest where a report, study or source is introduced or attributed, as in "The report said", "X notes that", "which conducted the survey" and "said".

30616.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on tokens in hard-to-predict, high-entropy text rather than on a particular word. Typical contexts are random alphanumeric strings, hashes, IDs, URLs, IP addresses and numeric lists or codes. It also fires on rare non-Latin scripts, garbled LaTeX, and incoherent spam or machine-generated prose.

Fires in garbled, incoherent, or machine-generated-looking text such as gibberish, broken code, spam, and mixed-language noise. It most often lands on word fragments or subword pieces that repeat or complete a string seen earlier in the same context (e.g. a repeated name, acronym, number or code token), suggesting a copying/induction behaviour within low-quality text.

30619.name: Line breaks (and trailing markers like *, }, superscript-number syntax) right after the author-name list in academic paper headers, marking the transition to the affiliation block (Department, University, \textsuperscript{1}, "Affiliations:") or to the abstract. Weaker activations occur on similar header and metadata breaks.

Boundary tokens (newlines, bullets, spaces, superscript markers, LaTeX braces) that come right after an author list in academic paper headers and lead into the affiliation lines. They are strongest on the line break or marker that separates the last author name from its numbered affiliation, such as "1 Department of…" or "University…". Weaker activations occur on similar structural separators in other metadata or markup.

3062.name: A diffuse, weakly activating feature that mostly fires on clause and phrase boundaries: commas, periods, paragraph breaks and connectives such as "and", "in" or "with a" right after a completed clause, just before the narrative continues. The strongest hits come from event-reporting text like sports results or historical accounts (e.g. "heats, … Time, and"; "Rohit was on hand to"), where the boundary leads into the next action or outcome.

30662.name: The first token of a word, name or compound that the tokenizer splits into several pieces, so the word is unfinished at that point. These are often single capital letters or short prefixes that begin acronyms, brand names, chemical or technical terms, usernames, or hyphenated compounds (e.g. E-skom, P-glycoprotein, she-wolf, Co-founder).

30695.name: Words for empathy, sympathy and compassion toward others' feelings or suffering (empathy/empathetic, sympathetic, sympathy for, pity, feel sorry for, compassion, mercy), with weaker activation on related warm attitudes (understanding, solidarity, admiration, caring) and on look-alike fragments such as 'path/athetic' in parasympathetic, apathetic and telepathy, or 'merc'.

Words for feeling for or with others, especially "sympathy"/"sympathetic", along with compassion, empathy, mercy, pity, condolences and solidarity. Weaker activations go to related emotional-attitude terms (admiration, affinity, apathy, heart, support).

3074.name: The ".widget" token in Java import statements, chiefly "android.widget" (and android.support.v7.widget), the package that holds UI components such as Button, TextView and Toast. Similar UI-component packages in other frameworks (SWT ".widgets", JavaFX ".control", libGDX ".ui") activate only weakly.

30744.name: The preposition "on" (and equivalents like Dutch "op", "starting") introducing a temporal expression — a date or weekday — especially after event or publication verbs (took place, born, launched, posted, submitted). It fires more weakly on locative or platform uses of "on".

30774.name: Words about creative authorship and composing, especially writing and composing music and songs (songwriter, composer, writing music, song-writing), plus related terms for writers, playwrights, designers, and creators. Activation is strongest for music and song writing.

30828.name: Fires on "thereby" (strongest) and related consequence/means connectives that introduce a resulting action or the mechanism of a preceding clause: "whereby", "hereby", "thus", "thereupon", and the Chinese "从而". Activation is highest when "thereby" is followed by a participle describing the result ("thereby increasing…").

30930.name: Coordinating conjunctions (mostly "and", also "or", occasionally a comma or slash) that join two nouns or adjectives into a coordinated phrase, especially right after a noun or modifier, where another item of the same kind is about to follow (e.g., "pain and dysfunction", "wires or cords").

30945.name: The second item in a coordinated pair of descriptors, usually after "and"/"&": a further role, profession, or title given to the same person or thing (e.g. "actor and director", "historian and author", "singer and songwriter"). It also fires weakly on other second-coordinate nouns or adjectives.

Role, title, or descriptive nouns (e.g., owner, CEO, chairman of, author, host of, former…) that follow a conjunction like "and" in a coordinated description of one person or entity, the second item in an appositive list of roles or attributes, usually just before the person's name.

30966.name: Adjectives and participles describing something left in an unfinished, unresolved, unaddressed or not-yet-acted-upon state, most often un- words (unanswered, unchecked, untreated, untapped, unexplored, unborn, unknown), plus related ideas like outstanding, open problems, loose ends, missed, pent-up and undercooked.

31039.name: Pieces of abbreviations, acronyms and initialisms (e.g. TFA, CTA, IMHO, OOP, PO Box, B/L, VoIP, RTL), typically the token right after the first letter of an uppercase acronym, plus some shorthand fragments such as 'vols', 'thx', '24/7' and 'ra'.

31048.name: Weak, diffuse activation across text discussing proposed solutions, policies, plans or approaches to problems, often political or argumentative commentary. The strongest hits are on nouns and phrases naming the proposal or its proposer (e.g. "policy proposals", "proposed by the", "Solutions", "Experts"). Function words and punctuation around such claims also fire at lower levels.

A diffuse feature in news and political or policy writing, firing on words in clauses about government plans, proposals, bills, initiatives and ideologies, and on how they are announced, compared, supported or debated. Typical spans include 'suggesting the administration has yet to decide on a final plan', 'Trump's plan… compares with', 'With Labour having committed to' and 'the plan also'. It also fires weakly on clause boundaries, such as periods and commas, within such discussion.

A weak, diffuse feature in expository news, policy, and argumentative prose. It fires most on nouns for proposals, policies, plans, or ideas (package, compromise, framework, plan, bill, ideas, demands, Solution, concepts) and on the tokens that open the claim about them: predicate starts like "is/has been/was a", relative "which", reporting verbs like "stated that it" or "experts note", and the punctuation or sentence boundary that begins a new assertion.

31062.name: Tokens that repeat an immediately preceding token or short pattern. The feature fires on the second and later copies in runs of identical words, symbols, numbers, or cells, such as "H H H H", "+ + +", "Unlimited Unlimited", "agree agree", "7 7 7" and "NA NA". Activation tends to grow the longer the repetition goes on.

31067.name: Author surnames in academic citations, firing mainly on the final subword pieces of the name and on the "et al." that follows it. These typically appear in parenthetical or inline references such as "(Smith et al., 2010)" and "Smith and Jones (1994)". It fires weakly on other proper names.

31120.name: Punctuation or function word right after a citation or reference to a source (patent number, paper [1], author et al., journal, institution, URL, date), marking the boundary where the citation ends and the text goes on to describe what that work did. Strongest on the comma or period directly after a patent or reference (e.g. 'JP20033078A,' and 'incorporated by reference herein in its entirety. In').

31149.name: Verbs and nouns for making, creating or preparing something (cook, make, build, prepare, bake, mix, craft, grow, manufacture), plus the words right after them such as the object or a following article/preposition. Activation is strongest for food and drink preparation (cooking dinner, making applesauce, preparing dishes, homemade cookies).

Verbs and words about making, creating or preparing something, especially food (cook, make a meal, cooking, kitchen skills, blend). Tokens like create, make, build, grow, produce, and 'your own' usually come after 'to' or 'can'. Activation is strongest for cooking and meal preparation.

Verbs and nouns about making, building or preparing something oneself (create, make, build, compile, cook, DIY, crafts, homemade). Activation is strongest for hands-on, do-it-yourself production such as cooking, DIY projects and compiling code yourself.

31195.name: Structural and formatting tokens inside tabular or grid-like layouts, such as cell separators (|, &, <td>), row starts after newlines, alignment whitespace runs, and dotted or dashed filler in markdown, HTML and LaTeX tables or matrices and ASCII-art blocks. Activation is strongest at the start of a new row or line within these structures.

31220.name: Promotional, corporate or marketing-style language about benefits and value, such as verbs like help, enhance, deliver, streamline, reduce and drive, and phrases like achieve business goals, productivity, performance, customer satisfaction or reduced costs. Activation is strongest in value-proposition phrases describing what a product, service or technology enables users to achieve.

31254.name: Ranges, most often year or date spans like 1945-1948 or 1830 and 1860. It fires on the separator (hyphen, en dash, "to") and the end-point number that closes the span. It is strongest on dash-joined year ranges, and weaker on page or chapter ranges, times, and decades such as 1950s.

31261.name: Expository news-style prose. Activation peaks on the core clause of a sentence that introduces who did what, most often at the start of a new sentence or paragraph. Typical spans are the subject (a named person, organization or "The former couple"), the main verb, and the source-attribution phrasing that follows. Examples include "The attorney for … says in court papers", "According to a report produced by", "announced the split with" and "trimmed its … ownership in". Function words linking these elements (to, the, in, of, commas) are also marked, while scattered weak activations appear elsewhere.

31273.name: The name "Roger" and similar-sounding name fragments. The first name "Roger" fires most strongly, especially before a surname or initial. The surname "Rogers"/"Rodgers" and fragments like "Rog" or "ogers" fire moderately. Weaker activations appear on phonetically similar name pieces such as Peggy/Peg, Siegel/Nigel ("-igel") and Berger.

31316.name: A diffuse, weakly activating feature with no single clear trigger. It fires mostly on tokens that complete a content-word noun or compound term, especially in technical, scientific or product-description text. These include head nouns of technical noun phrases (processor, algorithm, ions, timezone, holder) and final subword pieces of longer words (-etry, -osity, -iddle, -urg, -fish). It also fires occasionally on nearby connectors or closing parentheses inside such terms.

31402.name: Encyclopedic or travel-guide passages about the history of buildings and landmarks (churches, chapels, temples, cathedrals, palaces, statues, terminals). It fires on the building nouns and the historical narration around them, such as construction, dates, past locations, renovation or replacement, and later use, for example "was built in 1851 at the", "replaced a previous version", "redesigned", "(now the".

31412.name: Tokens that open an anonymous function or closure definition in code: Python "lambda", Rust closure pipes "|" / "(|" (often after .map), C++ lambda "[]", JS/R/PHP inline "function", arrow-function parameter parentheses, and Fn/Function types. Strongest for lambda passed as an argument or assigned to a variable. Weak hits on math function names like f/F.

31413.name: Fires most strongly on the space-prefixed double-colon token " ::". It appears as a separator in titles and labels ("Gaia ::", "JQuery ::", "Free Shell Accounts ::") and as a code operator for Rust paths, Haskell type signatures, Fortran declarations and C++ scope. It peaks on leading-path cases such as "= ::std". Weaker activations go to other separator-like tokens ("•", "|", ")" inside DOIs) and to Arabic/Persian word-initial " ا".

31421.name: The first word of a new sentence or line, mostly after a period or line break, that opens a new section or instruction. It is strongest for "For" (especially "For more information" and "For other purposes") in boilerplate such as repository notices, copyright statements, and contact or reference lines. Other openers like "To", "See", "Other", "On" and "In" activate more weakly.

31460.name: Code statement boundaries where an object, widget, or variable is being instantiated or assigned. The strongest activations fall on the closing parenthesis, semicolon and newline (");\n") that end constructor calls such as new X(...) or Widget::new(...). Weaker activations fall on the class names and variable names involved in these creation and assignment lines, especially for GUI components like labels, toolbars, shells and boxes.

Code where an object is created or assigned (e.g., document.createElement(...), new X(), Flask(), handler = ...). Activation peaks on the closing punctuation/newline that ends the creation statement, such as '");\n' or ')\n'. It is also strong on the next use of the newly created variable name (poster., handler., app, arrow.) as a method or property is set on it.

31463.name: A diffuse feature found mostly in scientific and technical prose. It fires on words inside clauses that describe processes, changes of state, or goals: reaching a steady state, finding or obtaining solutions, transforming, distinguishing, varying over time. Activations usually fall on the verb or object right after purpose or result phrases such as "to", "leads to" and "in order to".

31518.name: The last token of a person's name, most often the surname after a first name or title, strongest for well-known political leaders (President Obama/Trump/Biden, Roosevelt). When the surname is split into pieces, the final subword fires (e.g. Gorbache-v, Hickenlo-oper), usually where the name is the subject about to say or do something.

31562.name: Tokens that begin a metadata or key–value field line in structured or boilerplate text, typically right after a line break. It fires most strongly on "ms" in Microsoft-docs front-matter keys (ms.date, ms.topic, ms.author). Weaker activations come from other field labels and prefixes such as "Document Version", "Molecular Weight" and "Job Type", page boilerplate, and the "ms" unit.

31630.name: A diffuse, low-level feature that fires mainly inside technical and procedural text. It is strongest on statement-level code inside loop or conditional bodies, especially variable assignments and updates (e.g. "resA = *it1", "v = Vec::new(); for", "flips += 1") and the indentation tokens before them. It fires weakly on operators and expressions in math, and on scattered content words and phrases in explanatory prose describing methods or steps, which appear to be noise.

31674.name: The final token(s) of a product or model name, especially vehicles (Toyota Supra/Prius/Corolla, Laguna, BMW R24) but also gadgets, planes, guns and spacecraft. Activation lands on the name suffix or model number that completes the name after the brand. Generic vehicle-type nouns (van, sedan, wagon, minivan) also activate, with car names strongest.

31693.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature in scientific and technical prose. It fires on the key terms of technical noun phrases and method descriptions, such as model parameters, processes and components. It is strongest where items are paired, coordinated or contrasted, as in "X and Y", "both … as well as", "horizontal/vertical" and "possibility/impossibility".

31822.name: Fires most strongly on the ".bind" segment of Java import paths (org.springframework.web.bind, javax.xml.bind) and on ".HttpServlet" in javax.servlet.http, i.e. a package segment within repeated import statements. Weaker activations occur on the optional-plural marker "(s" in form-style labels (Genre(s), Subject(s), Programme(s)) and on separators in repetitive boilerplate lists (semicolons in OEIS link lists, list dashes).

31837.name: A sparse, weak feature that fires on structural or delimiter tokens in mixed or technical text. Its strongest hits are the period or space right after a list number ("1.", "2.", "3. "). It also fires on separators such as " /" and "<![", and on spaces between English and Chinese text. A few scattered fragments activate too, such as pieces of hex hashes, timestamp digits and occasional English words. Chinese characters themselves essentially never activate it.

31843.name: The integer part of a decimal number, i.e. the digits just before a decimal point (prices, measurements, percentages, coordinates), especially when a similar number appeared earlier in the context. It occasionally fires on plain integers.

31859.name: Diffuse, weak activations on tokens in noisy, low-coherence or structured text: garbled/encoded strings, ASCII art, ID and part numbers, URL encodings, tables, list bullets, and run-together or spam text. It fires mostly on repeated or fragment tokens (numbers, single letters, symbols, bullets) where the next token is hard to predict. No clear semantic meaning.

31864.name: The path or namespace separator segment that follows a library or package name in code imports and qualified references (e.g. ".api", ".Framework", "::", ".core" after junit, NUnit, assertj, failure). It fires most strongly on testing-framework imports such as org.junit.jupiter.api, junit.framework and NUnit.Framework. It also fires weakly on "add" after paket.

31865.name: A diffuse, weak feature centered on normative or value-laden phrasing about what is best, right or beneficial for someone, such as "do what's best for your story", "the best fit for their team", "seek their greatest happiness" and "what is right". It also fires faintly on surrounding advisory or concessive language ("but", "take your time", "there is no").

31869.name: Expressions of equality, sameness or comparison: equals signs and == operators, words like "equal", "equality", "identical", "same", "agreement", "equivalences" and "resemblance", and equality-test functions such as Assert.Equal and cmp. Activation is strongest on explicit equality terms like "equal sign", "==", "identical" and "equality".

Words and symbols expressing equality, sameness, matching or comparison: "same", "equal", "equality", "identical", "match", "agreement", "unity", "unchanged", and the "="/"==" operators in code and math. Weaker activations land on comparison-linking words like "with", "to", "like", and on fragments of such concepts in other languages (ÉGALITÉ, 平).

31889.name: Anaphoric determiners that point back to something already mentioned, chiefly "said" used in the formal/legal sense of "the aforementioned" (e.g. "the said drawings", "aforesaid"), along with Chinese 该/該 ("this/the said") and "aforementioned". Activation is strongest in legal or archaic "the said X" constructions. Weaker hits come from other uses of "said/Said" (speech verb, the surname).

31904.name: Abstract head words in formal or literary multiword phrases, especially nouns heading an "of" construction ("the point of", "the part of", "the consequences of", "the close of the year", "the number of"). It also fires on intensifying or degree modifiers (full, utmost, total, very much, precisely) and time or quantity expressions (some time, just before, at three). Activation is broad and weak, peaking on "the point" and "the part".

3191.name: Word-internal and word-final subword fragments (suffixes, inflectional endings, continuation pieces) of words split across multiple tokens, mostly in non-English or uncommon words (Latin, Slavic, Icelandic, German, Portuguese, Arabic, transliterations, rare names). The strongest activations fall on inflectional endings of heavily inflected languages.

31929.name: The double-slash token "//" in any role: code comments, integer division, URL and path separators, XPath, and decorative separators in bylines or headers. Activation peaks where it joins a URL or template placeholder (e.g. "{{site.github}}//") or appears as a quoted string literal. Weak activations also land on unrelated tokens.

The double-slash token "//" (often with a leading space or attached to brackets, quotes, or "="), used as a code comment marker, Python floor division (//, //=), URL fragments, separators, or long runs of repeated slashes. Activation is strongest in noisy, malformed, or out-of-place contexts, such as junk text, broken URLs, and decorative slash runs.

31931.name: A diffuse feature that fires weakly across ordinary expository and explanatory prose. It lands mostly on clause-continuing words such as verbs, abstract nouns and function words. It peaks on discourse transitions and connectives that link or extend ideas, like "for example", "In addition", "Ultimately", "but", "as ... famously put it" and "result from".

31933.name: Output/print statements in code across many languages (print, println, printf, cout <<, Console.WriteLine, echo, System.out.println, warn), firing on the print function name and its accompanying syntax such as the opening paren/quote, format specifiers (%d, {0}, \n), stream operators/endl and the closing paren/semicolon. Weakly fires on a few output-like prose words.

31980.name: A diffuse, low-specificity pattern. It fires mostly on punctuation, operators and short connector tokens (commas, colons, parentheses, '&', '+', '/', arrows, '%>', '$(') that separate elements in structured or noisy text such as code, LaTeX, chemical formulas, file names, mojibake, spam and transliterations. It occasionally also fires on a function word or word fragment in ordinary prose where the next token is hard to predict.

Punctuation and symbol tokens acting as delimiters or separators in structured, code-like or noisy text: brackets, braces, quotes, colons, dashes, equals signs, URL separators (://, ?), and format markers. They usually appear at boundaries between fields or segments, with the strongest activations on opening brackets/braces and quote combinations such as ({, (", ":{".

32.name: Mainly code: the identifier that begins a called expression, usually right after '=' or 'return' or at the start of a statement, such as a module, class or function name preceding '.method(' or '(' (json.dumps, numpy.array, plt.gcf, Activator.CreateInstance, Ray::new, substractWords). Elsewhere, in prose, math, URLs and LaTeX, activation is weak and scattered.

32005.name: Weak, sparse feature for anomalous or obfuscated text. It fires mostly on single Cyrillic look-alike letters swapped into Latin or Greek words (e.g. a Cyrillic 'с' in 'topic' or 'confirmo'). It also fires on spaces just before words written in homoglyph scripts. Other weak hits are odd tokens in spun or garbled text (misplaced 'often', 'simply just') and leading list numbers like '1.'. Text written entirely in a foreign script mostly does not trigger it.

32015.name: The token "ID" (also " ID", "-ID", "IDs", occasionally "I.D"/"iD"), the identifier abbreviation, most often as a suffix to a noun naming an identifier field or label (Job ID, Patient ID, polygonID), and usually followed by a number or colon.

32022.name: Head nouns that name an academic or research unit in institutional affiliations, chiefly "Department"/"Dept", plus Institute, School, Faculty, Division, Centre, Laboratory and University, along with their non-English forms. They usually begin an affiliation line in a paper's author block, often right after a superscript number or after an author's name, and are typically followed by "of". Activation is strongest for "Department" at the start of a numbered affiliation line and weaker for mentions inside running prose.

32050.name: The word-start subword token "rhe"/"Rhe" (as in rheumatoid, rheumatism, rheology, rheometer, Rhein). It fires most strongly in "rheumatoid arthritis" medical contexts. Weaker activations occur on "he"/"whe"/"hes" fragments after an h-cluster letter (diarrhea, wheeled, wheezing, rhesus, Phe).

32084.name: The token that comes right after a noun for a table or other structured display (table, chart, figure, diagram, template, box, list, tree, field, Table class), most often in tabular contexts. Usually this is a function word or punctuation continuing the phrase (to, for, in, are, be, comma, colon), or the markup that follows a table opening tag: '>' plus newline after <table, or ']' and '\' after \begin{table}. LaTeX table environments activate most strongly.

3209.name: Mostly weak activations on scientific and technical writing about modeling and analysis. The strongest are on names of approximations, frameworks and analytical methods (e.g. "within the Bogoliubov approximation", "framework of MCT", "Approximate Evaluation", "quasi-linear", "asymptotic techniques"), and on words describing simplifying assumptions or idealized models such as linear, classical, continuum, assumption of independence, simplified and predictable.

32093.name: Technical and engineering descriptions of physical apparatus, instruments and their specifications. It fires weakly and sparsely on words naming components, dimensions, units and physical properties (sensor, telescope, chamber, diameter, temperature, kg, KB), and most strongly on spans describing a device's construction or makeup (e.g., 'operates two 17 m diameter Imaging...', 'composed of particle identification suites including...').

32142.name: The word "elite" and its plural "elites", both as a noun for a privileged ruling group and as an adjective meaning top-tier (elite squad, elite performers, elite colleges). Weaker matches are related ideas of exclusivity and high status, such as aristocracy, ruling class, exclusive, select, inner circle and esteemed.

3215.name: Coordinating conjunctions (mostly "and", also "or", "as well as", and occasionally a comma) that follow a completed noun phrase or clause, marking where a second coordinated item or predicate is about to be joined. The conjunction is sometimes paired with the next word ("and the", "or your", "and especially").

32190.name: Tokens that end in a backslash (often fused with preceding punctuation like :\ .\ }\ '\), which begin an escape sequence, LaTeX command or file path (e.g. \n, \033, \t, \label). They fire most strongly in code string literals just before newline or ANSI escapes.

32440.name: The main-clause subject and its first verb, coming right after an introductory modifier phrase (participial, adjectival, or prepositional, e.g. "Born in Chile," or "Due to its simplicity,"). These are often pronouns (he, they, it, we, I) or short noun phrases. Activation is strongest when the subject is the entity the fronted phrase describes.

The subject (and often its main verb) of a main clause that comes right after an introductory phrase, usually a participial, prepositional or appositive phrase set off by a comma, e.g. "Recently painted, this home offers" or "A native of Winnipeg, Jeremy". It also fires on the main verb that follows a long subject noun phrase. Names and nouns like "game" or "it" get the strongest weight.

32458.name: Imperative instructions or prompts aimed at a user, as in UI/form text, input() prompts, button labels and directions (enter, select, input, submit, add, press, specify, "please …"). They appear across many languages, e.g. 'Digite', '请输入', 'зарегистрируйтесь'. The strongest signal is on the verb that starts a prompt string requesting user input.

32479.name: Fires very strongly on "imgur" in image-hosting URLs (especially ".imgur" in i.imgur.com), and somewhat on similar site-name pieces of URLs such as "reddit" in reddit.com. All other activations are faint: the leading space or bullet at the start of list items, numbered-list digits, and paragraph breaks.

32541.name: Boilerplate legal or policy text such as disclaimers, copyright notices and terms. It fires on the subject entity (organization, publisher, author) and the verb phrase that follows, stating its responsibility, rights or obligations. It is strongest on disclaiming phrases like "does not", "will not be responsible", "assumes no" and "offers no warranties".

32556.name: Fires on the first token after an abrupt, incoherent break in the text, where one sentence or topic is cut off mid-flow and unrelated content begins. This is typical of spliced, scraped, or spam-generated text, such as "Amazon.com|Before you can sell…", "in|While recuperating…" or "pickup|Popular Mechanics". The activating token is often capitalized, starts a new clause, and follows no punctuation.

32561.name: Words that open a slot for an upcoming object or complement: transitive verbs (exploit, achieve, destroy, count, display, automate) and relational prepositions or nouns (of, to, on, with, for, near the, quality of) that come right before the noun phrase or pronoun they govern. That following argument is often 'the …', 'them', 'it' or 'that …', frequently pointing back to something mentioned earlier. The strongest activations fall on longer predicate spans, such as 'to recover the original color of', 'assigned to' and '(or'.

32562.name: The final digit of a year marking the end of a lifespan or period, usually a death year in a birth–death range like "(1921–1981)" or after "died in/on". It also fires weakly on other death-related words such as "died", "passed away", "d." and "dies at".

3259.name: The final element of a location or postal address, typically a country name (or a state/region abbreviation or the end of a postal code) that closes a comma-separated address string. It fires most strongly in academic affiliation and contact-address lines.

32609.name: Words that come just before a noun for a person or group of people (trainer, team, professionals, staff, specialists, artists, users). These are mostly prepositions and determiners such as "by", "with", "of", "our", "a" and "the", plus descriptive adjectives such as "skilled", "experienced", "talented", "licensed" and "medical". The phrases often name the people doing, helping with or collaborating on an action, e.g. "guided by a local", "consultation with a licensed", "team of skilled".

Function words (by, of, to, with, a) and modifiers that come right before a noun naming a person, group or agent, often an expert or authority (a qualified healthcare provider, a panel of experts, a second engineer, a mentor, industry practitioners). Typical frames are agentive or relational phrases such as 'reviewed by', 'advice of', 'talk to a' and 'work with'.

32689.name: Final tokens or subwords that complete a multi-token proper name, especially titles of games, films, albums, products or series. These are often sequel numbers or subtitles ("2", "VI", "Fallen Kingdom", "Jr"), and the model predicts them once the name's opening is recognized.

3269.name: Nouns (and their preceding prepositions) naming the recipient entity that some agent acts on, lives in, or interacts with, especially biological hosts or targets such as a host plant, host cell, cell line or test animal. The strongest case is a pathogen's host ('in interaction with rubber tree'). Weaker activations fall on general targets, substrates or locations ('onto a building', 'into the gut', 'invasion of the Soviet Union').

3280.name: Function, method, class and library identifiers in code, especially the name being called or imported (often right after a dot or ::, before an opening parenthesis), e.g. .get, .write_all, sprintf, WriteLine, Mutex, info. Weaker activation on similar call-like tokens such as LaTeX commands (eqnarray, limsup), shell commands (curl) and URL domain parts (.com, .org).

Function, method and command names in code or code-like text, especially the identifier right before a call's opening parenthesis (.slice, .insert, .find, input, pow, open, switch, -gradient, AVERAGE). Activation is strongest on method names after a dot. It also fires more weakly on keywords, CLI subcommands such as 'startapp', and code-like words in prose.

32828.name: Boilerplate method signatures in Java/C# code (Android onCreateView/onCreate, servlet doGet/doPost, C# event handlers). Activation falls mainly on the commas that separate parameters, the continuation parameters (ViewGroup container, Bundle), the alignment whitespace and the closing ') {' plus the first line of the body. It is strongest for the standard onCreateView(LayoutInflater inflater, ViewGroup container, Bundle savedInstanceState) pattern, with only weak, scattered hits in prose.

32836.name: A weak, diffuse feature about limits, thresholds and repeated occurrences: quantities, frequencies, durations or patterns of activity being capped, measured or restricted. It fires on words like limits, period, times, years, consecutive, streak, bursts, peak demand, chatter and bounce. It also fires on rate-limit and anti-abuse contexts, such as spam filtering, reporting requirements, chasing losses and repeated identical samples.

32842.name: First element of a coordinate pair or tuple, plus the comma after it, mostly in code and math (e.g. Point(50f, 50f), [0, 1], (3, 4)), with the x-coordinate activating most strongly. Weaker activation appears on other index or coordinate tokens inside arrays and point lists.

32861.name: The Java unbounded wildcard generic token "<?>" (and " ?>"), as in Class<?>, AdapterView<?>, List<?>. It fires most strongly on AdapterView<?> in onItemClick callbacks. Other activations on ordinary prose tokens are negligible.

33073.name: The final digit chunk(s) of long numeric identifiers such as article, document, product, ISBN/SKU, paper, case and cable numbers, usually in metadata headers or URLs. The completing tokens of the ID string are the ones marked.

33074.name: The punctuation that ends a news dateline or source credit and comes right before the article body begins. It is most often the closing parenthesis after an agency name, as in "(AP)" or "(Reuters)", and fires most strongly there. It also fires weakly on other dateline separators such as dashes, colons, brackets, periods and line breaks that follow a location, date or byline.

The punctuation that closes a news dateline or wire-service credit at the start of an article, just before the story body begins. Typical cases are the closing parenthesis after an agency name such as (AP), (Reuters) or (UPI), the period of a state abbreviation (N.H., Calif.), and the following dash, slash, colon or line break. Activation is strongest on the ")" after a wire-service name.

33106.name: Grammatical particles, case endings and inflectional suffixes in non-English text, especially Japanese particles (に, と), Korean postpositions (에, 로, 으로) and case or verb endings in agglutinative and inflected languages (Azerbaijani, Turkish, Russian, Latin). Activation is strongest on Japanese に and Korean 에.

3311.name: Weak, diffuse feature that fires at positions where a number is about to follow, especially the standalone space token before a numeral. It is strongest in ranges, dates, years and numbered sequences ("to 90.0", "November 2019", "1997 to 1999", list indices). It also fires more weakly on separators and first digits within such numeric patterns, such as dashes, periods, "%", commas and "or".

A weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly on the token just before an expected number: standalone spaces before digits ("Windows 7", "Java 5", "of 2011"), and operators or separators such as =, ×, x, $, commas and dashes inside math, code and numeric lists. Its activations elsewhere look like noise.

33136.name: Website boilerplate headers for comment, answer, review or result sections (e.g. "4 thoughts on", "8 Responses to", "Leave a Reply", "0 comentarii", "1 Answer", "Results 1-1 of"). The feature fires on the word just after the count/label, usually a preposition like "on", "to" or "for" that introduces the post title, or a plural ending. It is strongest for "N thoughts on “Title”".

33158.name: Tokens at the start of repeated import/include lines in source code (Python "import"/"from", C/C++ "#include <" or "\"", Rust "use"/"::", C# "using"), firing on the keyword or delimiter that opens each successive dependency path. The strongest activations are on the "<" after #include. There is weak, sparse activation on other repetitive list-like structure, such as category separators, bullets, and repeated command flags.

33188.name: Words naming infrastructure, utilities, public services and institutions that serve a locality or community (government services, post/mail, courthouses, police, hospitals, railways, wastewater, outlets, area codes, banks and companies operating in a town), plus phrases describing what connects to or supplies a place (e.g., 'railway reached Putney', 'blood supply from the artery'). Activation is strongest in local-geography or civic-amenity contexts.

33193.name: Fires in birth-date contexts, mainly on the space token right before the day or year number that follows "born", "b.", "born on", or a month name in a birthday entry. It also fires on the word "born" itself in parenthetical "(born YEAR)" notes. Occasional weak hits appear on unrelated tokens.

33254.name: Practical travel‑guide and consumer‑advice prose: tips about transport, journey times, fares, prices and costs, and conditional advice ("depending on", "unless", "check", "buy a SIM card", "use local bus/taxi"). Activation peaks on concrete logistics details such as durations and prices.

33270.name: Indefinite or narrative time expressions, especially the noun completing a phrase like "one day", "next day/time", "someday", "ever", "once", "in the middle of the night". Activation peaks strongly on "day" in "one day" used to introduce a story event or an unspecified future time.

Time-unit nouns (especially "day", also night, time, morning, week) completing indefinite or narrative temporal phrases, strongest for "one day" introducing a past anecdote or a hoped-for future ("one day I…", "the other night", "on a Friday morning").

33280.name: Class names of I/O stream, reader and writer objects (InputStreamReader, StreamReader, FileWriter, PrintWriter, BufferedReader wrappers) in code, mostly right after the "new" keyword in constructor calls. Activation peaks on InputStreamReader nested inside new BufferedReader(new ...).

33299.name: Tokens containing the dollar sign "$" in any role: currency amounts, LaTeX math delimiters, shell prompts, and variable sigils in code (PHP, Perl, R, Rust macros, template ${...}). Activation runs highest for code and shell uses such as R's "\$" accessor, Perl comments, terminal prompts and PHP variables, and is weaker for plain currency and math.

Dollar-sign tokens ($, $$, ${, $output, $data) used as variable or template sigils, math delimiters, or stray symbols, mostly inside garbled, code-like or mixed-language text. Other odd punctuation and symbol tokens (backticks, #, %, curly quotes) activate weakly.

33396.name: A diffuse feature found in expository, advisory or policy-style prose about practices and processes, such as healthcare, management, public engagement and wellbeing. It fires on words that name means or approaches for achieving an outcome: nouns like methods, measures, steps, ways, tool, factors, involvement, engagement and communication, and action verbs like help, create, streamline, enhance, implementing and focusing. It also fires on nearby function words like "to", "in" and commas within those purpose and benefit statements. Activations are strongest on terms for participation and engagement and on tools.

33421.name: The preposition (mostly "of", sometimes "in"/"the") right after purpose-type nouns such as aim, goal, objective, purpose or focus, in phrases like "The aim of this study is to...". It is strongest in academic or research statements of intent.

33443.name: Function words and nouns in website navigation and boilerplate text that invites users to search, find, browse or look up information or resources (e.g. "search for", "find something about", "list of", "reviews", "archive", "websites"). The strongest activations come on the prepositions and objects in these search-and-find calls to action.

33506.name: Line-ending tokens that close a structural or delimiter element in code and markup, typically at the start of a file, such as the end of a comment banner or separator line (---⏎, **⏎, #⏎), the closing ">⏎" of an HTML or XML tag, header guards and blank lines after includes. The token marks the transition from boilerplate or formatting into the actual content. Activation is strongest at the ends of long dash or asterisk comment borders.

Tokens at the start of a code or formatting block, chiefly the language tag after opening triple backticks (python, plaintext, javascript) or the backtick/newline that closes the fence. Also fires weakly on other structural line-break tokens in code-like or markup text, such as trailing-whitespace newlines, comment markers, separators and function-header colons.

33528.name: Names of data serialization/parsing formats and libraries in code (pickle, json, csv, XML, serde_json, XmlSerializer, struct, DataStream), strongest for 'pickle' and 'json' as Python import targets; weaker for other type/parse names (Integer, int.Parse).

33541.name: Tokens inside proper names of institutions, especially hospitals, medical centers, universities and research institutes. Activation falls on the name-continuing words or word pieces after the first word (e.g., 'Hospital', 'Medical Center', 'Health', 'Museum', or the rest of a split name) and is strongest for hospital and medical-center names.

33546.name: Function words and verbs in descriptions of how something was made, assembled, decorated, or equipped: materials, added components, and methods (e.g., "made out of", "with a", "and added", "attached to"). Activation is strongest on crafting narratives that list added elements ("added a piece of ribbon and lace to").

33592.name: Words referring to a written work or study being discussed, mainly papers, articles, reports, studies, books and reviews ("this paper", "the study in question", "the report notes", "this article is well written"). It also fires on nearby discourse boundaries, such as the punctuation, commas and line breaks after author names, citations or sentence ends that lead into a summary of what the work found or claims.

3361.name: City names and the state/country parts that follow them in place references. It fires hardest in formal postal addresses and academic affiliation lines, on the city, its commas, the state or province abbreviation and the postal-code start, e.g. 'Santa Rosa, CA 954' or 'Columbia, Missouri'. It is weaker on cities mentioned inside ordinary sentences.

33620.name: The word "stroke" and its pieces ("st-roke", "strokes", "stroked", "keystrokes", "breaststroke"), plus some weaker look-alikes with "stro" (strode, Stroop, Stokes). Activation is highest for the medical sense, cerebrovascular stroke, especially when it is listed beside heart attack, heart disease or hemorrhage. Other senses (brush strokes, golf strokes, keystrokes, caressing) activate more weakly.

33668.name: The word "City" as the final part of a multi-word place or team name (e.g., Kansas City, Salt Lake City, Manchester City, Vatican City). It fires most strongly for Kansas City, and occasionally on the abbreviation "KC".

33678.name: The word "the" coming right after a question opener or task verb ("What is", "What was", "Determine", "Calculate", "Find", "Give", "Write"). It introduces the noun phrase naming the thing to be answered or computed, as in quiz, homework and FAQ questions. Activation is strongest in math and science problem prompts.

3369.name: Citation and reference numbers in academic or technical text, mainly numeric reference markers in brackets, parentheses, or superscripts (e.g. [1], (3–5), ^1,2) that follow a claim. Weaker activations appear on other citation-like digits: the last digit of years in author–year citations, author affiliation numbers, figure/section numbers, and LaTeX \cite.

3373.name: Speech and attribution verbs (mostly "said", also says/told/wrote/added/reports), plus the pronoun or speaker right before them, that credit a quote or reported statement to its source. Activation is strongest for "said" right after a closing quotation and a speaker's name or pronoun in news-style quotes, and weaker in narrative fiction or for other reporting verbs.

33736.name: Scientific (especially spectroscopy/astrophysics) terms for measurable spectral features or tracers; strongest on "emission lines", "lines", "peaks", "bands", and ion/element notations like [OIII], O+, i.e., spectral lines and signals of chemical species.

33761.name: Tokens that introduce a function's or program's return value or output. These are mainly the word "return(s)/returning" in documentation prose and the return-type arrow "->" in function signatures (Rust/Python), along with similar markers such as VB "As", "@return" and "Returns:". Activation is often strongest on 'returns', and some weaker activation falls on the returned value that follows (0, True, False, a status code).

Return values of functions in code and documentation. It fires most on the word "return"/"returns" (including @return and <returns> doc tags, "and return" in comments, Rust "->", the Chinese 返回) and weakly on tokens naming what is returned, such as "true", "Result" or "(".

33772.name: The first token of a new noun phrase, usually an entity or proper name (often only the first subword fragment of a multi-token name like Qu|attara, Bay|rd, Fat|ih). It appears right after a preposition, verb, clause boundary or line break, where the entity is introduced as subject or possessor. It is frequently followed by a possessive 's or the rest of the name.

33776.name: Journalistic news-story prose, strongest on attribution and narrative-reporting phrases (e.g., ',” said X while attending…', 'he concluded, as reported by', 'shared:', 'Reportedly,') and clauses describing what a public figure did or is doing in celebrity, sports and news reports. Activation is weak and diffuse on other tokens.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no single clear token type. It lights up on scattered mid-phrase tokens such as function words, punctuation, date digits and code identifiers, often in noisy, garbled or synthetic-looking web, code or multilingual text. It is strongest on factual or news-style claims about real-world entities: who won an award in which category, someone's net worth as of a year, a headline saying 'leaks suggest' something, or a company explaining in a blog post.

33820.name: Fires on the verb, gerund or claim noun (often with a following "that", "to" or "of") that names an action, statement or belief whose rightness is being judged. Typical frames are "was right in revealing", "correctly found", "wrongly stated that", "justified in refusing to", "mistaken if you believe", "rejected her argument that" and "determination that". The judged acts are usually assertions, decisions or stances.

Verbs or action nouns naming a specific act, statement or decision that the surrounding text judges as right, wrong, mistaken, controversial or justified (e.g. 'right in asserting', 'mistake of quoting', 'correct that', 'decision to hire'). Activation sits on the act being evaluated, often a speech or decision verb, or a 'that'/'to' introducing the evaluated claim.

33834.name: Fires right after a C# "using System;" import line. It is strongest on the ";⏎" that ends "using System" and on the next token, usually the following "using" (or "namespace"). It responds weakly to other import/line boundaries in Python code.

33852.name: The leading number in a quantity expression (digits or spelled-out words, often the part before a comma, decimal, or unit) that gives an amount, duration, price, or measurement. It fires most strongly on prison sentences and other durations ("sentenced to 15 months", "70 lashes") and on dollar amounts.

The leading digits or number word of a numeric quantity in running text. It fires on the number that is about to be followed by a unit, scale word or counted noun (million, years, percent, days, ,000, -foot), often after $, "up to" or "to". Activation is strongest for durations and sentence lengths, e.g. "six years in prison", "six months", "seven years".

33911.name: Stray whitespace tokens (a lone space, or spaces plus a newline) at line or paragraph starts after line breaks, marking a section or content shift. Whitespace-only lines in Markdown and code fire most strongly.

33913.name: Words referring to letter case, such as uppercase, lowercase, capitalization, caps, case-sensitive, camelCase, .upper(), and equivalents in other languages (mayúscula, maiúsculas, регистр). Strongest on 'uppercase' and 'capital(ized)' in password, naming, or formatting rules. Weak hits on loosely related words like 'capitalize on' or 'capitalists'.

33933.name: Fires on the token "embry-" and its forms (embryo, embryos, embryonic, embryology), peaking on the "embry" piece in "embryonic". The match is by spelling, so it also fires on unrelated "Embry"/"emb" fragments. Weaker activation on related early-life and developmental terms: developmental/development, neonatal, fetal, blastocysts, trimester, seedlings, larval, intrauterine.

33960.name: Academic and research administrative boilerplate covering funding acknowledgments, ethics and review approvals (ethics committees, IRBs, IACUC), regulatory and supervisory bodies, trial registrations, and author/affiliation metadata. Activation lands on the function words and nouns that link to the approving or funding body ("approved by the", "funded", "support from", "Council", "Ethics Board") and is strongest on ethics and oversight terms.

33962.name: The second term in a slash-joined pair or alternative (X/Y), marked on the word or word-completion right after the slash. These are usually closely related alternatives or co-equal options such as left/right, arrival/departure, iPhone/iPad and elements/words. Weaker activations appear for similar pairings joined by hyphens, 'and', or commas in a list.

33998.name: Tokens that begin a new component inside a compound identifier or multi-part term, typically right after an underscore, hyphen, or camelCase boundary (e.g. in snake_case function or variable names, file paths, API names), and often only a partial-word subtoken. Activation is strongest in code identifiers; in prose it fires more weakly on the next word of a multi-word compound or name.

34025.name: The noun "point"/"points" (and similar discrete-location nouns like "dots", "node" 点), especially in the geometric/mathematical sense of a location or data element (each point, a single point, data point, at point A). It is strongest in technical contexts and weaker for score points or other senses.

The noun "point"/"points" (incl. midpoint, timepoints, -point), mostly meaning a location or position, as in geometric, data, or physical points in space, also other senses like point guard, decimal point, stock points. Weak firing on similar nouns (dots, pin, notes). Strongest in mathematical/geometric contexts ("another such point", "about a point").

34045.name: Chess move notation: fires most strongly on square coordinates and captures (e.g. 'e6', 'dxc4', 'xf2', 'g5', 'O-O-O') in game records. It also fires weakly on moves and actions in other play-by-play accounts (card games, poker, board/war games, sports, fights).

34048.name: A diffuse, low-specificity feature firing on mid-sentence connective tokens, mostly prepositions, determiners (especially "the" after a preposition or verb) and verb/preposition complements, that open or continue a phrase leading to an upcoming noun object (e.g. "in the development of", "targeted by the", "find out the"). It has no clear semantic theme.

A diffuse, weakly selective feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires on ordinary mid-sentence tokens, mostly function words such as determiners, prepositions, pronouns and auxiliaries, and occasionally on a content word. Many of these sit right after a verb, preposition or connective and begin the complement or noun phrase that continues the clause (e.g., "after a", "exposure to this", "resulted in", "difference from"). The contexts are typically expository or explanatory prose.

34055.name: Mostly in math formulas and code, the token that completes a binary operation, i.e. the right-hand operand directly after an operator such as /, *, ^, + or %. This is typically a denominator, divisor, multiplier or exponent (numbers, variables, slash-variables like /n or /M). Activation is strongest when that operand ends a parenthesized or bracketed sub-expression, just before the closing ) or }. There are a few weak, scattered activations on ordinary prose words.

3407.name: Discourse transition points where a new clause or section begins, most strongly the contrastive connective "However/however" (sentence-initial or parenthetical between commas). Weaker hits fall on other boundary tokens that open new content: sentence-starting "There" or "Let", the comma after "said" before a quote, numbering periods, list-item spaces, and structural markup such as "thead" or "\begin".

34100.name: Fires on the last word of a verb or noun phrase (e.g., happen, received, take place, overexpressed, stable, thrive, -inch) when it is immediately followed by a locative or temporal prepositional phrase such as 'in X', 'at X', 'during X', 'off X' or 'near X'. In effect it anticipates a 'where/when' modifier coming next.

34124.name: Terms for isolated software or development environments, chiefly "virtual environment", "virtualenv"/"venv" and "Python/dev environment", with weaker activation on related concepts like chroot, sandbox, dev-container, VirtualBox and requirements files. The strongest activations fall on "environment" and "env".

34149.name: Places where a term, symbol, variable or abbreviation is being defined or expanded. It fires on the defined symbol or acronym and on the linking token that follows it ("=", "means", "where", "is", a dash, comma or parenthesis), as in glossaries, table footnotes, keyword lists and variable definitions in equations. The strongest case is "SD = standard deviation".

3419.name: Words about creating or initializing something, strongest on programming object lifecycle terms (constructor, destructor, initialization, created, setter). It also fires weakly on sign-up and registration wording and scattered tokens in technical text.

Object-creation vocabulary, mostly in programming: by far the strongest on "constructor(s)", and weaker on related terms like create/creating, instance, instantiate, builder, factory and copy. Faint, noisy activations also appear on unrelated words, such as section headers and "Commentary".

34200.name: Narrative news-report prose describing events, scenes and reactions in the past tense (who did what, where, and how people responded). The strongest activations fall on main-clause verbs, auxiliaries ("were", "was", "had"), collective subjects such as people, groups or communities, and scene-setting phrases about circumstances or aftermath. Sentence boundaries followed by paragraph breaks also activate.

A diffuse syntactic-boundary feature: it fires on the token that completes a phrase or clause just before a new constituent begins. These are often the head noun closing a noun phrase (e.g. streams, basin, echoes, members), clause-ending punctuation or commas, and, in code, line-ending tokens such as ':⏎' after except/if statements or '.")⏎' closing a print call. It appears across prose, code, lists and non-English text, with no clear semantic theme.

34205.name: Clause and sentence boundaries in expository, documentation- or tutorial-style prose. It fires on transition points such as punctuation and paragraph breaks, and on clause openers that set up an explanation ("You can", "To access", "If", "Whether you are", "As a", "The syntax of… is"). These tokens mark where the text moves from stating a topic to explaining how something works or what the reader can do.

Clause and sentence boundaries in explanatory, technical or instructional prose. It fires most on periods, commas and line breaks that end one statement, and on the words that open the next one ("This is", "In this case", "If", "A", "You", "However"). It also fires on linking verbs and connectives inside definitional or descriptive statements ("are called", "is", "will", "that", "to").

34206.name: Diffuse, low-strength activation on the content of embedded verb-phrase complements that spell out an intended action, purpose or effect. These tokens typically follow a setup word such as "to", "of", "through", "efforts", "willingness" or "help". Examples include "to provide users with", "efforts to develop a field-based test", "to figure out how to make" and "how climate change will affect sea level". The strongest activations fall on the verbs and objects in the middle of these purpose or goal clauses.

34219.name: The word "property"/"properties" (also Chinese 属性), firing most strongly on its programming sense of an object attribute or field (code, XML, config, APIs). It fires more weakly on scientific or mathematical attributes and weakest on real-estate or proper-name uses.

34300.name: Personal names, especially first names (and the start of full names), of authors, reporters, photographers, or people being quoted. These often appear in bylines, credits, or contact lines after cues like "By", "Author:", "Photo:", or "said". Activation is strongest on the given name, weaker on surnames and on surrounding punctuation or initials.

Personal names, chiefly first names and the early part of full names, in author/byline or attribution spots (after "By", "—", "@author:", "name:", photo credits, or a name standing alone on its own line before text). Feminine first names often activate most strongly. There is weak activation on list/answer starters such as "1.", "**", "*".

34304.name: Leading indentation whitespace (spaces/tabs) at the start of a code line, especially the first line of a newly indented block after a colon, brace, or control statement; weaker activation on line-break/delimiter tokens that separate statements or sections in code and math text.

Whitespace indentation tokens (runs of spaces or tabs) at the start of code lines, especially inside nested blocks, along with line-ending punctuation plus newlines (e.g. ");\n", " {\n"). In prose it fires weakly on clause or sentence boundaries such as commas and periods, essentially marking structural boundaries where a new statement or line begins.

34305.name: Whitespace runs and filler/separator tokens in structured or tabular text (column padding, alignment spaces, empty HTML table cells like , LaTeX & separators, underscores/dots), plus boilerplate web text such as "Sponsored" and "Jump to"; strongest for long space runs that pad columns.

Runs of whitespace (spaces, tabs, sometimes followed by newlines) used for alignment or padding inside code, tables, ASCII art, and other formatted or structured text. Activation is strongest for long space runs separating symbols in ASCII diagrams and aligned columns.

34322.name: Mentions of a class/struct's own type name inside its definition or methods in code, e.g. constructors and destructors (Command(), Game::~Game), return types (-> Self, -> Scorekeeper), self-typed parameters (const Rational&, Node*), and impl headers. It also fires weakly on recursive self-references such as a function calling itself or d[i] = d[i-1].

34334.name: The word stem "electric" (electric, Electric, electricity, electrician, electrically), strongest for the adjective "electric" in technical or physical senses (electric field, current, charge, motor, grid). It is weaker for "electricity" and weakest for the figurative "electr-" in "electrifying".

34337.name: Words for a first public appearance, launch or introduction, most strongly "debut" (especially debut novel, album or film), along with premiere/premiered, breakout, inaugural and opener. More weakly, related words for a leading or notable start such as flagship, career and opening.

3437.name: Word-initial fragments beginning with a vowel plus p/b (mostly "hyp"/"Hyp", with weaker "imp", "hip" and "yp"), firing on the first subword of words like hypotension, hypertrophic, hyperspectral, impressive and impacts. "hyp" fragments activate most strongly; whole words and unrelated tokens activate only weakly.

34462.name: The first three-digit chunk of a four-digit year (e.g. "164" in 1645), firing most strongly on pre-modern dates (11th–18th centuries) in historical prose and weakly on 19th–20th-century years or other numeric strings.

34524.name: A diffuse, mostly structural pattern. It fires on tokens at segment boundaries or at the start of a new unit: paragraph breaks after a sentence (the strongest), bullets, table and line-break tags, and statement-initial code keywords inside a namespace or class block ('using', 'internal', 'private'). It also fires on sentence-opening connectives ('However', 'Furthermore', 'If', 'The company'). Isolated tokens such as 'assigned' or 'mathrm' also activate, with no clear semantic theme.

A diffuse, low-level feature firing on structural boundary tokens, mostly in code or noisy/garbled text. Typical hits are line-start indentation, newlines, braces and parentheses that open blocks, sentence- or line-ending punctuation, list bullets, and tokens that begin a new statement or clause (e.g. "However", "In addition"). It is strongest on C# "using" directives at the start of lines inside a namespace, and on opening "((" in JavaScript.

34556.name: Inner subword pieces of medical/anatomical terms, firing most strongly on the 'ch' in bronch- words (bronchitis, bronchial, bronchodilator) and on 'b'/'bo' in thromb- words (thrombosis, thrombocytopenia). Weaker activations occur on similar mid-word fragments (papill-, glomerul-, cervix) and on the '<tr' tag that starts each new HTML table row.

34577.name: Words describing fullness, crowding, or capacity: something being packed, clogged, congested, cluttered, flooded, overstretched, backed up, busy, filled to the brim, or in high demand (and occasionally its opposite, emptiness or lack of space).

Words about capacity, fullness, and limits: being full, filled, crowded, empty, sold out, maxed out, capped, overloaded, limited, or taken. The feature fires on adjectives, verbs, and particles that describe how much something is occupied or saturated, with the strongest activations on words like 'full', 'sold out', and 'capped'.

34663.name: Words that set up a comparison or matching criterion, typically in questions or selection phrases like "which/the one that best describes, fits, matches" or "closest/nearest/similar to". The feature fires on the relational word, most often "to" after closest/nearest/equal, "than" after comparatives, or verbs such as fits, matches, describes and makes true. It is strongest for "equal to" and "nearest/closer to".

34778.name: Tokens where arguments or inputs are being specified. Activation is strongest inside function and method signatures and parameter lists, such as C, C#, Java and Perl prototypes. It peaks on opening parentheses, parameter types and names, and the commas or newline indentation between parameters. It fires more weakly on usage-syntax option brackets. It also fires weakly in procedural instructions where the user is told what to supply or choose ("choose the", "fill in the", "add the recipient", numbered step markers, bullets).

Tokens marking a slot where an input, argument, or parameter is expected next. The strongest cases are function signatures and parameter lists ("=function(e", "open(", "(enum mode, uint", "(int"). The pattern also covers API descriptions such as "expects an", "takes a" and "given by the arg". It appears in UI instructions to supply a value ("Enter your", "enter a name", "type in a number for", "Choose a") and in form field labels followed by a colon or asterisk.

34799.name: Fires weakly and diffusely on tokens, often mid-word subword fragments or function words, in text that is non-English (French, German, Spanish, Romanian, Polish, Korean, Persian, Greek, Welsh, Russian) or unusual and nonstandard English (archaic or Scots spelling, Shakespearean contractions, ungrammatical or machine-translated phrasing). It seems to respond to language or orthography that departs from ordinary modern English rather than to any particular meaning.

A diffuse feature that fires on tokens where the English is unexpected or non-standard, often right after a verb or preposition. This covers misspellings and odd word splits (sup-r-ised, b-ing, anounce), awkward machine-translated, non-native or spun text ("tour to Odisha", "I am purchase the Find"), and foreign-language words. It also fires on stiff, formal announcement or notification phrasing ("has the honor to enclose", "I inform the House", "glad to announce you, that").

34875.name: Website navigation and boilerplate UI text, such as links for Previous/Next post or page, Home, Return/Back to, page-number lists (1 2 3…), arrows and separators, skip-to-content and table-of-contents links. These typically sit between or after main content.

Website navigation and boilerplate text, such as "Home", "Previous", "Next", "Back to Gallery", "Page X of Y", "«", "Jump to", and "You are here". These usually appear at line starts between scraped page content and the main text. It also fires on similar words like "Previous" or "Home" in ordinary prose at the same positions.

34921.name: Weak, diffuse activation on boilerplate web text such as site descriptions, cookie and browser notices, newsletter or subscription prompts, repository and access notices, and product blurbs. It fires on function words and generic service phrases like "to ensure you have", "for the latest updates", "with your name and password", "uses ... that" and "for further information".

34968.name: A weak, diffuse feature found mostly in personal, profile-style or promotional text such as bios, dating or classified ads, and self-descriptions. It fires on list connectors (commas, "and", "or") and on first-person words ("I", "am", "your") in enumerations of hobbies, traits or interests, e.g. "hiking, adventuring, and cuddling" or "hardworking, motivated and determined".

3497.name: Opening markup tag names and commands, mostly HTML table cell tags (<td, <th) plus <p, <strong, <br, <sub and LaTeX commands like \frac, \caption and \textsuperscript, marking the start of a formatted element just before its content.

34972.name: Tokens inside long random-looking alphanumeric strings such as hex hashes, UUIDs, session IDs, URL query tokens, DOIs, and other identifier codes. Activation is strongest in the middle of high-entropy character sequences, especially mixed letter-digit runs.

34975.name: Descriptions of a person's or entity's body of work or output, especially counts of creative or scholarly works produced (e.g., "authored more than 700 papers", "author of six previous books", "his films include", "third novel"). The strongest activations fall on the quantity phrase and the work noun ("more than 30", "articles", "papers", "books"); weaker ones appear on general catalog or listing language about works, publications, or items.

3501.name: Separator tokens that sit between two paired or listed values: commas between coordinates, function arguments, or list items; hyphens in ranges; ' x' in resolutions; slashes and colons in ratios; 'and', 'to', or 'of' joining two terms. Most often numbers, especially in code and technical text. It is weak, firing a little more on commas inside coordinate or argument pairs.

35068.name: The last word (or final subword piece) of a short heading, section title, or page/UI label, usually a generic noun like Information, Details, Reviews, search, content or features. It typically follows a newline and comes just before another line break or colon, as in web boilerplate and document headers.

35169.name: Words for rounding numbers (round, rounds, rounded, rounding, round off/up/down to), used for numeric approximation in math, programming and data reporting. Related terms like 'nearest', 'approximation' and the Russian 'округление' fire weakly.

35196.name: Function words and punctuation (prepositions, conjunctions, articles, commas, relative pronouns) that come right after a complete noun phrase or clause and introduce a continuation such as a modifier, appositive, prepositional phrase or list item. The activation marks the boundary where the sentence is extended beyond a finished constituent.

35205.name: Diffuse, low-level activation across formal scientific and technical prose such as abstracts, papers, reports and specifications. It fires most on structural and functional tokens: sentence-ending periods, paragraph breaks, citations and reference numbers, and section headers like Introduction. It also picks up methodological phrasing in the body text, such as "we developed an analysis method", "newly developed", "these tools are developed within" and "basic design".

35210.name: A diffuse, low-level feature that fires in technical prose about web development and programming, such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript, markup and rendering. It mostly lands on function words, clause boundaries and punctuation in explanatory sentences around those mentions, not on the technical terms themselves. It is strongest where the text describes writing or needing code to make a page work, e.g. 'CSS will be needed… This is some simple CSS that will' and 'code it up and'.

35317.name: A weak, diffuse feature on structural and formatting tokens. It fires most strongly on decorative comment banners and boxed headers in code: runs of # or *, "//" and "|" borders at line ends, and "<!--" openers. It also fires weakly on markup scaffolding such as HTML table tags (td, tbody, br, p), LaTeX commands, markdown fences and dividers, and line breaks between list or table items.

35327.name: Language about climate change and global warming: terms like "warming", "climate", rising temperature, CO₂ emissions, sea level rise and human-induced environmental change. It is strongest on "warming" and "temperature increase" phrases, and weaker on general change or increase words (prices, risk, losses) in scientific contexts.

35379.name: Words describing investigation, discovery and evidence-gathering, such as searching, finding, examining, tracking down, suspecting, proving or identifying something. These show up mostly in police, crime, legal or detective contexts, e.g. interviewing, finding sufficient evidence, or information leading to identification. Activation is strongest on the action verbs and on 'evidence/information' phrases.

35387.name: A diffuse, weakly firing feature found mostly in technical text such as math, physics, code and data tables. It fires most on named variables or quantities being defined or compared: the variable name in a definition like 'R =', a repeated 'width' in a ratio, symbols like rho and mu, indices and subscripts, and parameter or field names like 'x:', 'href' and 'Unit'. It also responds weakly to surrounding syntax and to some ordinary words in explanatory prose.

35412.name: The word introducing a reference to a numbered figure in scientific/technical writing ("Fig", "Figure", "figure", "Figures"), typically after phrases like "as shown in", "see", or at sentence start before a figure number. It fires more weakly on similar references to tables or equations ("Table", the "(" in "Eq. (1)").

35431.name: The subword token "raf" inside words, firing most strongly on the middle of "zebrafish" (zeb-raf-ish). It fires only weakly on "raf" in other words such as Musharraf, Ashraf, Trafalgar and dabrafenib, and weakly on other fragments of model-organism or fish names.

35474.name: Mentions of saints and other revered religious figures: "Saint", "Blessed", "holy Elder", guru and canonization, feast days and devotion/commemoration. Activation is strongest on the title words themselves ("Saint", "canonization", "Feast Day"). Weaker activation spreads to the honorific and hagiographic context around such figures, including piety, mystics, honoring legacies and the names of revered people.

35476.name: The word "continent" and its forms (continents, continental, subcontinent, Continental), plus weaker activations on related large landmass terms like peninsula, mainland, plains, and planet.

3557.name: Language reporting quantitative changes and statistics, especially in financial or news reports: words and phrases describing increases, decreases, or levels ("dropped by 3.4 per cent on last year", "increased to", "stood at", "down almost 5%"), together with the attached numbers, percentages, currency amounts and reporting-period dates. Weaker activation appears on scattered numeric or technical tokens such as years and spec figures.

35576.name: Concepts of legitimacy and formal recognition of status or authority: words in contexts where something or someone is acknowledged, declared, installed, elected or proclaimed (a leader, government, spouse, heir, independence), or where legitimacy is questioned (illegitimate, illegally occupied, annexation). The strongest activations are on 'legitimacy', 'acknowledge … independence' and 'installed … government'.

3558.name: Code annotations, attributes and decorators that modify following declarations, such as Java @Subscribe (strongest), Rust #[derive(...)], #[allow], #[test], Blade @if and mentions of decorators. Weaker activations fall on boilerplate page and document metadata labels, e.g. 'Skip to content/navigation', 'Corresponding author', 'Open Access', 'Opinion' and 'Location', plus similar header or structural tokens in code.

35594.name: Gravitational lensing, firing most strongly on "lens" (and "ensing" in microlensing) in astrophysics text. Weaker activations appear on related light-distortion and astrophysical terms such as bend/bent, mirage, mirrors, redshift, shear, Shapiro delay, curvature, polarization and clusters.

3565.name: Weak, diffuse activations on nouns and short phrases that name ready-made, reusable things provided for others to adopt or build on: templates, libraries, building blocks, predefined sets, reference implementations or architectures, guidelines, protocols, and product solutions or offerings. Nearby enabling phrases like "helps you to", "enable you to", "to choose from" and "to use" also activate, with the strongest responses in software and technical descriptions.

Weak, diffuse feature in technical/assistant-style text (mostly programming and instructions). It fires on nouns and phrases for generic tools, templates, examples or artifacts being offered or used, such as code, sample, example, prompt, framework, template, placeholder, dataset and Material UI/Tailwind CSS. It also catches nearby helper verbs like provide, craft, use and help. It is strongest on terms for sample or ready-made code and resources.

35662.name: Mid-word subword tokens inside scientific names of pathogens and organisms, strongest on the malaria parasite genus 'Plasmodium' ('mod'/'ium'). It also fires on 'falciparum', the 'imal' in 'antimalarial' and 'alar' in 'malar', and other Latin genus names such as Borrelia, Babesia, Cordyceps, Oryza and Flaviviridae. Occasional weak activations on unrelated punctuation and line breaks.

35668.name: The tag name inside a closing HTML/XML markup tag, i.e. the token right after "</" (div, li, span, button, label, etc.). Activation is strongest for common HTML elements like div, li and button. Elsewhere it fires only weakly and sporadically on prose tokens.

35674.name: A mid-word subword token, usually starting with 'e' or another vowel, that follows a token ending in a vowel, so a vowel pair (oe, ae, ue, ee, ie, au) is split across the token boundary. It appears mostly in rare proper names and foreign or German/Dutch-style words (Roebuck, Glaessgen, Oestermann, Shoenfeld, Aesop). It fires most strongly on oe/ae combinations in surnames.

35705.name: Words expressing ending, leaving, exiting, or going back, such as close, quit, exit, finish, halt, terminate, return/back, done, and bye. They often appear as UI or menu commands (Close, Back, Done, OK), program control (KeyboardInterrupt, break, Disconnect) or step-by-step instructions.

358.name: A weak, diffuse feature with no single clear meaning. It fires mostly on the opening piece of multi-token names or unusual terms (e.g. the first fragment of a rare word, place name or software name) and on label-like tokens in structured or boilerplate text, such as citations ("et al.", "eds", PMCID), affiliations, photo credits, numbered list entries, and code or notebook markers.
