It fires more weakly on company or brand names in front of a product (Amazon Echo, Nintendo Switch, Toyota Supra) and on place names in front of organizations or newspapers.

51143.name: The word "being" and closely related welfare terms: strongest on "-being" completing "well-being" (and "wellbeing"/"wellness"). It fires more weakly on "being(s)" as a noun for an entity or existence ("human beings", "living beings", "state of being") and on "welfare".

The word "being" used as a noun, peaking in "well-being"/"wellbeing" (health, welfare sense). It also fires more weakly on "being(s)" meaning an entity or existence (human beings, magical beings, one's being) and on related welfare words like "wellness" and "welfare".

51228.name: Words inside parenthetical, non-restrictive modifiers that interrupt a main clause: tokens just after a noun followed by a comma (appositives, 'which/who' relative clauses, participial phrases like 'used in', 'based in', 'inspired by'). Activation peaks at the start of the inserted descriptive clause (verbs, prepositions, adjectives) before the sentence returns to its main predicate.

51232.name: Citation and reference markers in academic or encyclopedic prose: the opening bracket/parenthesis and the digits of reference numbers (e.g. [13], (2), .[19]) and of author–year citations (e.g. (Mark, 1985; ...)), firing most strongly on the final year digit. It also fires weakly at points where a statement ends and a source or attribution follows, such as punctuation before a speaker's name or words like "previously" and "below".

Citation and attribution markers right after a claim or statement: academic references (opening parentheses, author-year dates, et al., bracketed footnote numbers like [5] or .[3]), plus similar source cues such as "according to", "he said", closing quote-comma before a speaker, and URL fragments. The year digit or footnote number activates most strongly.

51279.name: The preposition completing a source-attribution phrase, mainly "to" in "According to" and also "per" in "As per" or Dutch "volgens". It is strongest when "According to" opens a sentence and introduces a named source such as a person, organization or publication, and weaker after a lowercase mid-sentence "according".

51302.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires mostly on tokens that complete a phrase or clause, typically the head noun ending a noun phrase (e.g., platform, market, rotor, happiness), and on the punctuation that follows, such as periods, commas or newlines. Occasionally it spreads across short continuation spans right after a sentence boundary (e.g., "The chart suggests", "The benefits ... from CBD is greatly affected"), suggesting a general clause-boundary or phrase-closure signal.

A diffuse, weakly selective feature with no clear lexical target. It fires at low levels on scattered function words, sentence-ending punctuation (often a period before a line break), and occasional content nouns in ordinary running prose. Its strongest activations come as long contiguous spans across whole clauses in conversational, instructional or promotional sentences, for example 'colors for your convenience... are saved', 'conclude that if they can't finish it on normal mode' and 'is to be the leading trusted online source'.

51324.name: Fires on clause/sentence boundaries (periods, commas, paragraph breaks, and the conjunction or pronoun starting the next clause) right after a statement about excess, avoidance or prevention. Typical preceding words are overload, overwhelmed, overboard, too much, avoid, prevent, waste and criticise. The feature marks the end of such a cautionary or limiting clause.

51329.name: Words about carrying, holding or transporting goods: cargo, freight, loads, contents, packing, containers and vehicles (trains, wagons, lorries, boxes, stuffed or full). Activation is strongest on "cargo", "load" and "full of".

51378.name: Diffuse, weak activations spread across scientific/technical prose (physics, plasma, astrophysics abstracts and reports). The highlighted tokens are mostly function words and generic noun-phrase pieces such as "the", "of", "amount of", "effect", "nature" and "confinement", often inside descriptive phrases about physical quantities and processes. There is no single specific word; the common thread is academic scientific register.

51406.name: Structural and attribution tokens in news or journalistic prose: sentence and paragraph boundaries (period plus double newline, headline-ending newlines), the first word of a new paragraph, and reporting or attribution words such as "said", "according to", "announced", "stresses" and "found". It also fires on the punctuation around quotes, source names, datelines and photo credits. Activation is strongest on "said" after a quote and on paragraph breaks.

51492.name: Text inside error, warning or status messages from software and systems (e.g. "No address found", "failed to destroy network for", "Access Denied", "Operation timed out", "Prototype mismatch"), especially quoted or logged failure strings. The strongest activations fall on the failure words themselves (found, failed, denied, mismatch). Many weak activations are scattered over unrelated technical or code tokens.

Text of error, warning and system status messages: words inside quoted or reported software errors and failure notices (e.g. "invalid input syntax", "could not connect", "no longer supported", "unable to save", "cannot be empty", "not found"). The strongest responses are on negations and failure terms ("not", "invalid", "error", "No"). There are weaker hits on boilerplate website notices ("you're using an unsupported browser", "you already have an account") and scattered technical tokens.

51505.name: Language that expresses predictions, expectations or intentions about future outcomes. It is strongest on modal and forward-looking phrasing such as "will/'ll be", "expect that", "hoping to get", "sure to", "promises to be" and "primed to", especially in sports previews and forecasts. Activation peaks on the auxiliary or infinitive "to" that sets up the anticipated event.

51536.name: The "cellul" / "ul" / "ulos" subword pieces of cellulose-family words (cellulose, hemicellulose, nitrocellulose, cellulosic, cellulase, celluloid, cellulite, cellulitis). It is strongest for " cellul" in cellulose. Other sugar or chemical fragments (xyl-, -lose) activate only weakly.

51568.name: The word "affair(s)" (incl. French "affaire", "Public/Home Affairs", "state of affairs", love affair, all-day affair) is the strongest trigger. Weaker hits go to near-synonyms for general domains or concerns after a modifier, such as matters, issues, business, relations and things.

The word "affair(s)" in all its senses: a domain or field (public, foreign, rural, world, current affairs, often in department or job titles), an event or occasion ("an all-European affair", "a messy affair"), and a romantic affair. It fires most strongly on "affairs"/"Affairs". Near-synonyms for a subject or business, such as matters, relations, liaison, business and fiasco, fire weakly.

51630.name: Separator or lead-in tokens (commas, 'and', 'or', pipes, table-cell tags, bullet/bold markers, newlines, indentation, 'The', 'a') that come immediately before the next item in an enumeration, glossary or definition list, especially one naming technical, programming or vocabulary terms (imports, keywords, language constructs, acronyms). The feature anticipates that a new term or list entry is about to be introduced.

51644.name: Internet laughter or reaction slang in casual writing, mainly "lol"/"LOL", along with "haha", "kek", "OMG" and emoticons. It fires most strongly on a standalone "lol" placed at the end of a clause or sentence. It also fires weakly on look-alike letter strings such as "Lol" in "Lollipop", "Lolwe", "Lollapalooza" and "LOL" as in League of Legends.

Internet slang laughter/reaction interjections in informal text, chiefly "lol"/"LOL" (strongest), plus variants like "lulz", "LMAO", "haha", "hehe", and weaker "OMG"; often the final token completing the acronym, typically placed at the end of a sentence or clause.

51675.name: The subword token "del"/"Del" (and close variants like "dele", "delic", "deline", "el") at the start of a word that it only partially spells, as in delve, deliver, delirious, deleterious, delicacy, delineate, or names like Delphine, Delly and Delin. Activation is strongest for a capitalized " Del" beginning a proper name or sentence-initial "Delve"/"Delivered".

51716.name: Fires at structural boundary tokens that end one segment and precede new content. These include question marks or newlines right before an answer, the period after a multiple-choice letter before the option value, and spaces or colons before a numeric value. It also covers paragraph breaks before a new heading or section, and web-page boilerplate labels such as "Leave a Reply", "Write a Review", "Sponsored", "BrainMass" and "Author".

51801.name: Words naming the hoped-for, uncertain, or prospective outcome or endpoint of an action or process, usually verbs and nouns after modals, 'to', 'will', or 'able to'. Examples are success, conquer, save, be passed, get fixed, elect, failure, champion, and breakthrough. They mark the goal or result that might or might not be achieved.

51807.name: Continuation subword tokens inside proper names and foreign or uncommon words, especially personal names, places, institutions and non-English or non-Latin script terms. Activations are weak and diffuse; they are slightly stronger for distinctly foreign character sequences such as Czech, Polish, Russian, Chinese or Romanian.

51829.name: Tokens inside long runs of the same repeated token or short pattern, such as dashes, asterisks, quotes, stars or "true". Activation builds the longer the repetition continues, peaking in decorative separator lines. Ordinary prose words fire only weakly.

51832.name: The word "sustainable"/"sustainability" in any form, including other languages (German Nachhaltigkeit, Turkish sürdürülebilirlik). Weaker firing on related ethical or long-term terms such as responsible, renewable, holistic, inclusive, eco, lasting and security.

51851.name: Tokens in code and command-line text that end an argument, string or path, mostly closing quotation marks (often fused with ')', ',' or ';'), closing brackets, file extensions like .zip/.yaml/.diff, and line-continuation whitespace. They fire where a literal or argument finishes and the next argument or code resumes.

51866.name: Repeated package-name tokens in sequential Java import lists, chiefly " android" (and the "import" before it) in Android import blocks. Activation builds the deeper into the list it gets, peaking around android.widget/android.view imports; it also fires weakly on the next "import" line once the android imports end. Weak scattered activations appear at list or section transitions, such as an abstract's closing period before its keyword list.

Structural punctuation and separator tokens (commas, spaces, '=', LaTeX '\(') in technical or structured text, such as code import lists, numbered Q&A, and math notation. It fires mainly where a token repeats an established pattern, e.g. later items in a comma-separated list, a second function definition, or a repeated 'Question N' header.

51915.name: The first token of a direct object or argument: a determiner, opening quote or parenthesis, or the first piece of a multi-token name or identifier. It typically follows a verb, preposition, or function call (e.g. print(lst, open TEST, into conf, the + noun). Activation is weak and diffuse, and is somewhat stronger for code identifiers and function arguments.

Tokens that open a noun phrase or multi-part name/identifier right after a verb or preposition, where the following token completes a specific entity. These include determiners after instruction verbs in recipes ('add the', 'whisk together the', 'cutting your'), first subword fragments of names or codes ('Ch|aitanya', 'R|ijiju', 'K|ARB', 'i|Red', 'Sim|Cash'), hyphens inside alphanumeric labels ('RM-131', 'carbon-13') and labels like 'Step'/'Group' that precede an index.

51922.name: The word "enterprise(s)" (and cross-lingual equivalents like 企业, empres-), meaning a business or organization. It is strongest in the corporate IT/software sense of large organizations (enterprise applications, enterprise IT, Enterprise plan) and weaker for general business ventures, social enterprises, or company names.

51928.name: Sentence-ending punctuation (mostly periods, sometimes with newlines, colons, ?/!) at abrupt boundaries in incoherent, spammy or machine-generated text, where the next sentence is unrelated to the previous one. Activation is strongest after citation-like fragments (years, page numbers, journal references) that are followed by an unrelated topic.

51937.name: Biographical or profile-style text: fires at the points where a description of a person (or organization) moves on to the next fact about them, especially on the subject pronoun, name, or verb that opens a new clause or sentence ("He was", "She is", "who served as", "has been a", "I publish") and on articles introducing a role ("the author/director of").

51973.name: Tokens immediately preceding a multi-component value such as a coordinate pair, vector, tuple, dimensions (e.g. 640x480, 2.4m by 3.6m), grid size or array index. These are mostly opening brackets or parentheses ('[(', '((', '=[', ' (', 'vec![', 'new Point'), colons or spaces right before the first number of the group. The feature anticipates an upcoming tuple or dimension list of numbers.

5200.name: Whitespace tokens (often unusual or non-breaking spaces) immediately preceding a special Unicode symbol such as an emoji, ℃, ω, ⌚ or ‹. More weakly, the feature fires on stray formatting and encoding artifacts like Â, €, BOM or directional marks, combining diacritics in kaomoji, bullets (•, ·, ●) and list-number punctuation.

Weak, diffuse activation on unusual or non-standard characters and encoding artifacts: special Unicode symbols (bullets, emoji, zero-width/invisible spaces, BOM, variation selectors, braille blank), odd whitespace before non-Latin text, mojibake fragments, HTML entities, and escaped unicode sequences.

52011.name: The capitalized token "Json" (mostly ".Json") in code, peaking in namespace/package imports such as Newtonsoft.Json, System.Text.Json and javax.json.Json. It fires more weakly on Json in class or identifier names (JsonUtil, JsonParser). Faint activations on unrelated function words and punctuation are noise.

The token "Json" (capitalized JSON), mostly embedded inside camel-case code identifiers, class or file names (e.g. DoseJson, Wiki2Json, SimpleJsonWSItem). It also fires weakly on a few unrelated tokens.

52035.name: The "/wp" path segment (WordPress) in URLs and file paths, usually right after a domain or directory and before "-content", "-includes" or "-json". Weaker on standalone "wp"/"WP" tokens (e.g., "wpb-js-composer" CSS classes) and other URL path segments like "/media", "/node" and "/product".

52043.name: Nouns naming a property or attribute category in descriptive or spec-style text, often as section headers (Personality, Screen, Voice, Inhalation, Spore Print). Activation is strongest for sensory terms, especially taste and smell (flavor, notes, inhale/exhale, odor, aroma, bite).

52064.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on tokens where the text becomes unexpected or incoherent. Typical triggers are spliced or spam-inserted phrases, duplicated words ('the the', 'like like'), typos ('firewords'), OCR and formatting artifacts (ligatures, broken citations, stray numbers or spaces) and abrupt topic shifts. It often lands on the noun or term right at the point of disruption.

52073.name: Tracks state that changes step by step, especially quantities being reduced over time. In code it fires on loop-state variables and their updates: while/if conditions, mutated variables (n /= i, x = x - 2, self.position +=) and the statements that follow them. In prose it fires on remaining or diminishing amounts, such as supply dwindling, the remaining error being smaller, days remaining, or 'this leaves eighteen'. Activations are mostly weak and diffuse.

52079.name: The ".slf" token in Java logging package paths (org.slf4j, lombok.extern.slf4j), especially in import statements. Related logging-package tokens like ".log" in org.apache.log4j get weak activation. Other tokens only fire faintly.

52115.name: The verb or predicate that follows a noun phrase naming a qualification, item or action and judges how desirable, required or acceptable it is, as in "is a plus", "would be desirable", "is a must", "preferred", "would be appreciated" or "can help". It is especially common in job requirement lists and in requests or guidelines. Activation is strongest on the copula or modal ("is", "would be") and on evaluative words like "plus" and "must".

52123.name: Empty parameter lists opening anonymous functions or lambdas in code, i.e. the "()" or "(()" token right before an arrow (=> or ->). It is strongest when it is passed as a callback argument, as in setTimeout(() =>, new Thread(() ->, or useFactory: () =>. It fires weakly on related placeholders such as "_" in for-loops, Rust "(move" closures and Fn() bounds, and on scattered commas in lists.

52142.name: Words about the release format, version, or edition of a media product, such as edition, version, copy, remake, re-release, HD, Blu-ray, resolution, recording, or review. Activations are weak and diffuse. They peak in product and review listing contexts like 'Review by', price lines, Blu-ray/720p, and remake.

52176.name: A diffuse feature that fires on the opening words of an expository sentence that comes right after a heading, bullet label, colon or title. It mostly lands on the subject and main verb or connective that introduces the description ("is believed to", "emphasizes that", "Go to", "is assigned to", "A one deck version"). In other words, it tracks the start of the body text that explains or defines the labelled item.

52205.name: Incomplete word fragments, mostly stems or prefixes of longer, often technical or academic words, where the next token supplies a derivational suffix such as -ation, -ity, -ment, -ance or -ize (e.g. polar|ities, mobil|isation, reint|roduced, co|ales|cence). A few whole words that begin a compound or phrase also activate weakly.

52208.name: The opening brace plus newline, and the indentation that follows it, at the start of a struct or enum definition body (mostly Rust `pub struct/enum Name {`, also Go `type X struct {`), right before the first field or variant is listed. It fires weakly on other structural separators such as list indentation, colons, and table cells.

52259.name: In scientific and technical prose, this fires weakly to moderately on words just before or between mentions of observation and measurement methods, especially imaging types and electromagnetic bands (radio, infrared, thermal, VHE emission, nm ranges, RF/IF, radiography vs sonography, fMRI). The activating tokens are often connectives and modifiers such as 'and', 'or', 'of', 'at', 'both', 'multiple', 'conventional' and 'functional'. The strongest case is 'observed at radio wavelengths at very late times'.

52335.name: Fires at the very start of a document on leading boilerplate or list formatting: indentation spaces, bullet points (•) and numbering like "1.", plus the first word that follows. These are usually navigation menus, breadcrumbs and list items. It responds weakly to other opening structural markers such as runs of newlines, section commands, separator lines and stray header or menu words like "Stations".

52346.name: Tokens in scientific and technical writing, mostly abstracts and methods sections, that describe a material, device or method being made, prepared or studied. The strongest hits are the words that name or connect the material and its preparation, such as synthesis, polymer, nanoparticles, deposited, coated with, obtained by, and "the synthesis of a". Weaker hits fall on connectives and component lists in materials and method descriptions.

5237.name: Numbers and operands (or the spaces before them) appearing in arithmetic expressions, especially the second operand right after an operator like ×, /, *, ^, = or a comma in function arguments, as in calculations, equations, code, and table cells. A few weak activations fall on unrelated words.

5238.name: The word "New" (and equivalents like "new", "Nieuwe", "新"), strongest when capitalized as the first word of a multi-word proper name, especially places (New York, New Delhi, New Hampshire, New Zealand) or titles (New Labour, New Scientist, Newbery). It fires weakly on lowercase "new", code constructors (::new), and similar name-opening words like "Los" (Angeles), "Long" (Beach), and "Young".

5241.name: Tokens that mark a first item or starting position in a sequence: the index/number "1" (or 0) after Chapter, Week, Part, No., or array brackets, plus words like "first", "start of", "opening", "begun with", "prior", "elder", "front-ended", "N-terminal", "early season", "left side", "lower end". The common thread is the beginning or front end of an ordered series.

52443.name: Words and word pieces expressing permanence, endlessness or long duration (eternal, enduring, perpetual, lasting, perennial, timeless, immortal, endless, infinite, lifelong). "Eternal" fires most strongly, and related mortality and age terms fire weakly.

Words expressing permanence, endless duration or timelessness (eternal, timeless, forever, enduring, lasting, lifelong, posterity, immortal, endless, infinite). Activation is strongest for "eternal" and "timeless", and weaker for related ideas of longevity, great age, or transience (ephemeral).

52453.name: Fires on tokens beginning with or containing a "u"/"ur" sound, strongest on "Ur" words and names (Ur, Urmas, Urmia, Urbana, urgencies, uit). It also fires often on the word "out", both alone and as a prefix (outplayed, outwit, out-of-the-ordinary). Weaker hits come from other U-initial capitals and acronyms (UT, UF, UCS) and stray tokens like "url" or "uh".

52457.name: Titles, roles and honorifics (Dr., Mr., Prof., Gov., Ir., President, General, leader, engineer, son, owner) placed directly before a person's name, with the trailing period of abbreviations often weighted most. The same pattern covers other labels that introduce a following proper name or identifier, such as 'Grant', 'Chapter' or 'Student:'. Also fires weakly on 'main' in 'Skip to main content'.

52517.name: A weak, diffuse feature firing on structural and symbolic tokens rather than words. The most common triggers are the final digit of four-digit years (often in citations like "(Author, 201X)" or bibliographic dates), closing parentheses and brackets, and assorted symbols such as &, $, #, |$, and censor marks like *@. The strongest activations are on unusual symbol sequences, such as OCR-garbled "()" and censored profanity.

52532.name: Tokens forming a person's surname (and sometimes middle initials or particles), mostly the first subword pieces of multi-token, often foreign or uncommon surnames. These usually come right after a first name or initial, as in author bylines of academic papers and in news attributions.

52630.name: The word "egg"/"eggs" in any sense (food, biological ova, laying, Easter eggs, place names) plus related pieces like yolk, ovum, 蛋, and stray "gg" subword fragments (veggie, Deggendorf). Strongest when eggs are food items in lists or recipes.

52645.name: Language about the movement and flow of air, water and other large-scale physical systems, especially weather and oceanography: winds, currents, air masses, pressure systems, ocean circulation and weather patterns, plus the verbs and prepositions saying where they move ("blow from", "extend to", "into the weekend"). Activations are strongest on meteorological terms such as "high pressure is expected to extend", "pattern", "air" and "currents". Weaker hits fall on loosely related flow and direction words in technical or scientific text.

52686.name: A weak, diffuse feature. It mostly fires at clause and sentence boundaries (commas, periods, newlines, a following "The/He/I") that come right after scene-setting phrases naming an event, place or time, such as "at a funeral,", "conference, in New York.", "this week," and "on my aunt's wedding day,". It also fires on words that lead into what happened or what was observed: see, find, what they hear, had, was. Overall it marks the transition from framing context into the narrated content.

A diffuse feature in news-style or narrative prose, firing weakly on sentence boundaries (periods, paragraph breaks) and the subject/auxiliary/main verb that opens the next clause ("was attended", "will be looking for", "were told", "is"). It often appears right after an event, meeting, conference or person has been introduced, where the text moves on to report what happened or how people reacted.

52700.name: Possessive markers, meaning possessive determiners (our, your, its, my, their, his, her) and the possessive 's. They usually come right after a preposition or verb (of, to, for, with, about) and introduce the noun that is possessed. Occasionally a subject pronoun in a similar slot is marked too.

52702.name: Mainly function, method and constructor signatures in code: the declared function name, opening parenthesis, typed parameter lists and generic template parameters (C#, C++, Java, Rust, TypeScript, Python), with the strongest activations on parameter names, types and separators. It fires weakly on other code tokens (variables, operators) and on prose, especially formulaic SEO-style conclusion phrases such as "By understanding the…" or "Whether you're…".

52739.name: Website and document boilerplate addressed to the reader: calls to action, contact and feedback prompts, and instructions such as "let us know", "click the button below", "subscribe", "visit us on", "should be sent to", and "please check". Activation is strongest on the action verbs and the phrases that direct the reader to a contact point or action.

52828.name: Continuation and final tokens that complete a multi-token named entity or fixed noun phrase, most often titles of creative works (films, TV shows, songs, books) and other proper names (brands, organizations, places, characters), plus some compound nouns. Activation is strongest in lists of an actor's credits, where it falls on the title words and closing quotes.

52837.name: Pronoun subjects (it, I, we, they, you, she, he, there) and the auxiliary or copular verbs right after them ('s, 're, was, is, can, will be) that begin a new clause. Activation is strongest on contractions like "it's" and "I'm" in conversational or quoted speech.

Sentence-initial subject pronouns (it, they, we, you, he) and the auxiliary/copular verbs or contractions right after them ('s, are, have, was, 're), mostly in quoted, conversational speech. The activation is on the subject and verb that open a new clause, often at the start of a new sentence inside a quote.

529.name: Forms of the verb "have" (have/has/had) right after their subject, whether used for possession, as the perfect-tense auxiliary, or in "have to" obligation. Activation is strongest after pronoun subjects (you, we, I, she). A few possession verbs in other languages or with similar meaning (dispose, develop) fire weakly.

52941.name: Determiners (mostly "the", also "a", "your", "that", and the preposition "of") that come right after a verb or preposition and right before the head noun of a noun phrase. The noun is usually the main entity already under discussion (the product, the organization, the system, the corporation).

52951.name: Unary minus signs marking negative numbers ("-4", "(-1)", "x = -2") in math, code and science text, also the word "negative" and ±. It fires on the sign token right before the number, not on subtraction. A few weak hits land on unrelated tokens.

52965.name: Forms of the verb "consist" (consist, consists, consisted, consisting, and the split piece "ist"), almost always directly followed by "of" or "in" to introduce the components or content of something.
Forms of the verb "consist" (consists, consisting, consisted, consist), typically followed by "of", that introduce what something is made up of or contains.

52967.name: Numeric values that state a statistic, chiefly percentages and proportions. The strongest cases are numbers in parentheses right after a count, e.g. "4,104 (14.6%)" or "39 (95.1%)", where the decimal digits often score highest. Weaker activations appear on other quantities and unit conversions, such as "(525-foot)", and occasionally on words like "percent" or "cent".

52993.name: LaTeX math notation around integrals and dimensional measures, strongest on differential elements and exponents (d^3 x, d^2N, dV, dx, dμ) and on ℝ^n superscripts, integral limits and π factors. Weaker hits come from prose about dimensions or normalizing quantities ('per unit', 'per square', '3 + 1 dimensions').

Mostly math and scientific notation, peaking on tokens that mark what an integral, sum or optimization ranges over. Examples are differential elements (dA, d), operator subscripts such as argmax_, E_ and Vol_{, and phrases like "over all possible" or "integrating over". It also fires more weakly on exponents, superscripts and other structural formula tokens.

53002.name: Coordinating or linking words (mostly "and", also "or", "but", "with", "along with", "coupled with", "alongside other", "and other") that come right after a completed noun phrase or clause, often one ending in a demonstrative like "this/these/that/it". They mark the start of a second item or action joined to the first.

Coordinating conjunctions and connectors (mostly "and", also "or", "but also", "with") right after a completed noun phrase or clause, where they extend it with another item or action. Activation is strongest for additive phrases like "and other reasons", "and many others" and "or any", which add further entities to an established subject.

53010.name: Code annotations/decorators (mostly Java/Spring, e.g. @Component, @Entity, @RestController, @Controller, @Service, @Data), strongest when the annotation sits directly above a class declaration; weaker for method/field annotations (@Test, @JsonProperty), C# attributes in brackets, and decorators in other languages.

53090.name: Line breaks that fall mid-sentence inside boilerplate text, mostly license and template comment headers in code (Apache/MPL license text, NetBeans "To change this template" notes, 42-school header lines ending in " */"). They fire most strongly in Apache license lines, e.g. after "licenses this file" and "Version 2.0". Weak activations also appear on spaces or tokens just before a continuation in other templated, repetitive text.

53104.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature with no clear semantic focus. It fires sporadically on single mid-sentence tokens such as proper-name fragments, word-piece continuations, function words, punctuation and list separators. These tend to appear in formal, technical or noisy (OCR/spam-like) text. Slightly stronger activations occur within noun phrases naming specific entities, such as 'the 1996 American Book Award', 'Mahavir Chakra' and 'graphite'.

53142.name: Restrictive or limiting focus words, chiefly "only" and also "just", "mainly", "exclusively", "exactly", and "than" in "other than" or "no more than". They mark that a quantity, set, or condition is limited to something small or specific.

53164.name: Tokens forming identifiers, field or column names, keys, and labels in structured data or technical text, such as database columns, JSON or array keys, variable or property names, form or UI labels, and named components. Activation is strongest on schema-like field names in code, for example SQL column definitions like ad_id and source.

Tokens forming the key word of a label, field, or attribute name, often completing a compound identifier or name: data/schema keys and column names (published_at, file_stage, _status, .name, -size, ArticleType, HOST), form/metadata labels (Author, Description, Type, Company, job title, publisher), and the head word of compound named items (Rotten Egg, Charcoal, Sigil Stone, Court St, Floor Assembly). Activation is strongest in code and structured-data contexts.

53212.name: The shell command "echo", strongest when it starts a command line in bash, batch, or other scripts. It responds more weakly to other output commands such as print, printf, println and Write-Host, and to echo-related words like echoed, echoing and noecho.

The shell command "echo" (with or without a leading space or tab) used to print output in scripts. Activation is strongest in bash and shell code. Print-like commands in other languages, such as Python "print" and Tcl "puts", activate weakly, as do stray non-code uses of the word "echo".

53263.name: Prime and apostrophe-like marks (′ ″ ’ ' ´) that follow a number, used as notation for things like nucleic-acid ends (3′/5′, often as 3′- or 5′-), inches, decades (1970′s), and arc-minutes. Activation is strongest for the 3′/5′ end notation in molecular biology and weaker for inch and minute marks.

53270.name: Weak, diffuse activation on economic and resource-flow language: supply, demand, capacity, production and quantity. It peaks on words like "supply", "capacity" and "production", on shortages, and on phrases such as "exceed supply", "as much as possible" and "produces more than". It also fires lightly on surrounding context about acquiring, distributing or scaling up amounts of goods, energy or resources.

53333.name: Diffuse feature with no single strong token type. It fires on the word that opens the main content of a statement, item or heading. This is usually the key verb or noun right after a subject, list number, section number or question word: findings, objectives, accusations, titles and questions (e.g., 'found', 'determine', 'Testing', 'What', 'blamed', 'association', 'benefits'). The strongest activations are on clauses stating a claim or issue under judgment or investigation, such as 'whether the government was legally', 'judge was wrong' and 'differed significantly'.

53342.name: Tokens inside the names of specific manufactured products and equipment: brand names, model names and model numbers of vehicles, aircraft, weapons, computer hardware and software. Activation is strongest on military hardware such as aircraft and guns (e.g. 'Ilyushin-96', 'Junkers Ju-390', 'Lewis machine guns', 'Panigale V4'), with weaker activation on consumer tech and cars.

53368.name: The first item in a pair or short list of symbols, mostly single-letter variables or arguments in math and code, that is about to be followed by a comma, 'and', or hyphen and a matching second item (x, y; a, b; k, v; S, T; P and Q). It also fires on paired names like east-west, Mars and Jupiter, and Clinton-Trump.

53399.name: Fractional or secondary parts of compound quantities: the token that adds a fraction or sub-unit to a whole number, such as "half" in "an hour and a half", the digit after a decimal point (2.5), "⅓" or "1/4", and smaller units following a larger one ("5 feet 8 inches", "18 months"). The strongest signal is on "half"/"-half" and fraction symbols.

Fractional or secondary parts of a numeric quantity: digits after a decimal point, the "/2" of mixed fractions like "1 1/2", "half" in "X and a half", and smaller units following a larger one (e.g., "3 years 4 months", "12 feet, 2 inches"). Strongest on "half" and "1/2" completing compound quantities.

53466.name: Runs of whitespace (spaces or tabs) used for indentation or alignment, especially at the beginning of a line after a newline in formatted text, code, addresses, or documents. There is weaker activation on a few scattered tokens in boilerplate or structured text, such as "should" in "Correspondence should be addressed".

Runs of whitespace (spaces or tabs), plus occasional filler such as dot/ellipsis leaders, used as indentation or alignment padding, usually at the start of a line or right after a comment marker (#, //) and just before the line's content. Common in code, tables and messy formatted text.

53533.name: Organization or institution names, often abbreviated, used as domain names in email addresses and URLs. The strongest cases are the part right after "@" in academic or research emails (kit, unipr, u-psud, tudelft, mit, inpe), with weaker activation on website domain parts and institution acronyms in credits.

53535.name: Nouns naming the document or work being described by its own text, mainly "invention" in patents (strongest after "object/advantage of the present"), the "ION" of "INVENTION" in patent section headers, and "paper", "research", "dissertation" or "investigation" in academic aims statements.

53572.name: Numbers (and number words or numerals) that label document sections, chapters, parts, list items or headings, especially after words like "Section", "Chapter" or "Part" or at the start of a heading line. Activation is strongest for in-text cross-references to sections in paper outlines ("Section 3 introduces...").

5359.name: Tokens about language and acquired skills: names of languages (English, Spanish, Python, Go), the word "language" itself, including foreign forms like Czech "jazyky" and Greek "Γλώσσα", and words for speaking, translating, reading, writing or learning. Strongest on explicit language mentions such as "native language skills", "speak a common language" or "Spanish". Weak activations land on loosely related words like learn, play or guidelines.

5362.name: A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no single clear meaning. It mostly lands on tokens inside multi-token names and identifiers: subword pieces, product or model names, code namespaces and methods (::multipart::Form, .assertEquals), URL path segments (/node, /ch), markup fragments and abbreviations in technical or structured text. It fires most strongly on code identifiers.

53635.name: Plot summaries and narrative recaps of stories, films, games or historical events. Activation falls mostly on sentence boundaries and transitions between plot beats (periods, commas, "The", "As", "Ultimately", character names) and on words marking story progression or the climax and ending ("climax of the movie", "at the end", "finally free").

Clause and sentence boundaries in narrative or plot-summary text: sentence-ending periods, paragraph breaks, and the conjunctions, subjects, or opening words that begin the next clause or event (e.g. ". It", "and then they", "After a"). It fires most strongly where a story moves on to a new event or character, often in rambling, semi-incoherent fiction.

53686.name: Structural boundaries where one unit ends and the next begins, mostly in code: closing parentheses/brackets followed by newlines, opening braces, indentation, and the first keyword of a new line or block (e.g. after function signatures). It also fires on prose and document structure such as sentence-ending periods, list numbers, headings and blank lines.

53701.name: A diffuse feature that fires weakly on mostly function words and phrase fragments in passages about practices, procedures, routines and methods. It peaks where established practices or habits are described or evaluated, e.g. 'routine', 'steps', 'measures', 'has been in place', 'shown to be a bad practice' and 'tend not to brush their teeth'.

5372.name: Conditional and control-flow keywords, chiefly "if"/"If" opening a condition in code (if statements, for, match, cfg) and in prose ("If I...", "what if", "Check if"), plus related condition-like words such as "場合", "Where", "as soon as" and "after". Activation is strongest on code constructs (for loops, match, cfg, if blocks).

Conditional keywords, chiefly "if" (also else, elif, when, try, and "If" in prose), that open a condition or branch. Activation is strongest in code (if statements, ternary expressions, if __name__ == "__main__") but also fires on conditional "if" clauses in natural language.

53724.name: Words that open or carry a question or inquiry: interrogatives (what, why, how, who, which, whether, if), question-starting auxiliaries (Does, Can, Is), and the words right after them inside direct or embedded questions. It also fires on title or headline phrases that set up a topic to be explained, such as 'explore how', 'types of', 'common myths', 'Secret To' and 'Promo Codes'. Activation is highest at the start of a question clause.

Tokens inside questions or indirect questions, most strongly in the words that open them or carry them along (wh-words, auxiliaries/modals like 'could', 'would', 'can you', 'is it possible'). Activation is highest on direct questions and query phrasing ('How did this happen?', 'what price tag would I be looking at', 'Can you tell me how to'). It is weaker on embedded clauses of uncertainty ('find out who', 'know what to get') and on content that is speculative or inquisitive.

53727.name: Text right after a statement of success, popularity, fame or some other cause, marking the start of its consequence or follow-up (e.g. "became a hit, and the Fleischers went on", "gained popularity, we have decided", "has made him a hot topic"). The marked words are mostly function words and result verbs (",", "and", "has", "became", "made", "gained", "brought") that open the resulting outcome clause.

53731.name: Numbers or letters that label a document element, such as figures, tables, chapters, sections, appendices, theorems and examples. They usually follow words like "Figure", "Fig.", "Table" or "Chapter" at the start of a caption or heading. Activation is strongest for figure and table numbers that begin captions. Weaker activation appears on section numerals and on the final digit of years in citations.

53753.name: Paragraph-break tokens: sentence-final punctuation (period, closing quote, question mark, parenthesis) fused with a double newline, which ends a paragraph and moves to a new one. These are mostly in news-style prose and often come right after a quote attribution like "he said" or a quoted statement. Activation is strongest when the break follows a quoted remark in reporting.

Sentence-ending punctuation, usually a period fused with one or two newlines, that closes a thought and marks a boundary before a new sentence or paragraph. This is most common in reasoning-style text, where the next paragraph starts with 'Wait', 'In summary', 'Let me', and similar. Weaker activations fall on other boundary tokens such as 'e.g.,', ').', ' like' before examples, '?' and code comments. The strongest case is the '.⏎' in 'he said.⏎' at the end of a quotation.

53761.name: City or town names, especially their final token(s), in addresses and affiliations (academic institutions, companies, manufacturers), typically just before a comma and a state, region, or country.

53801.name: Numeric expressions and their surrounding tokens: leading spaces before numbers, first digit chunks (e.g. "200", "199" in years), and internal separators (commas, periods, hyphens, colons) within quantities, dates, ranges, prices, phone numbers and addresses. It is strongest on counts and ranges preceded by words like "over", "than" or "in" ("over 22,000", "3-4 weeks", "$1").

Tokens right before an upcoming number, mostly the lone space token (or a leading digit chunk, "$", "#", separators like ",", "-", "/"). It fires where a numeral is predicted next, as in years, counts, quantities, ranges, dates, times and addresses, often after words like "in", "since", "than", "between", "within", "and".

53849.name: Structured metadata and boilerplate fields in web/document text (bylines, dates, publisher, codes, versions, member counts, citation fields). Activation falls on the field separators and values after labels like 'by', 'date:', 'published', 'codes:': colons, commas, spaces, date parts, names and bullets.

Fires inside formulaic, boilerplate text where the continuation is highly predictable. Typical cases are date stamps (a month name or the space before a year, often in 'knowledge cutoff June 2024' or 'Last updated' lines), URL and path separators ('://', '/'), and templated code headers like LeetCode's '# Definition for a…'. It also hits stock attribution phrases such as 'contributed by' and stereotyped chat openings like 'User: So' or 'User: Good'.

53881.name: Words naming behaviors, emotions, drives and physiological or psychological functions of organisms (feeding, eating, aggression, mood, motivation, fear, appetite, learning, memory, libido, responses), mostly in scientific or biomedical writing. The strongest hits are terms for behavioral and motivational processes. Weaker hits include cited author names in psychology and biology papers.

53913.name: Content words (mostly nouns and adjectives) that are semantically out of place or unpredictable for their context. It fires most strongly in incoherent, machine-spun or SEO-spam word salad, such as garbled academic or casino/pharma filler text. It also fires weakly on blanks in fill-in-the-blank exercises and on odd word fragments in noisy text.

53922.name: Affiliation markers placed right after author names in academic paper bylines. These are superscript numbers, letters, or symbols such as †, ‡ and §, written as Unicode superscripts, LaTeX \textsuperscript or $^ $, or plain trailing digits. Activation is strongest on markers other than the first (2, 3, b, c), i.e. those indicating a second or later affiliation.

53923.name: Separators and lead-ins inside lists of causes, conditions, diseases or factors. Fires on commas, 'and'/'or', 'such as', 'including', 'caused by' and 'signs of', and sometimes on the first word of the next item, at points where another item is about to follow. The lists are mostly medical, causal or diagnostic (e.g., 'caused by X, Y, or Z'; 'such as A, B and C').

53924.name: Syntax tokens inside code or formula snippets, mostly operators, delimiters and short keywords in terse or unusual languages such as Mathematica, PARI/MAGMA, BASIC-like and Forth-like code. Typical examples are pure-function and application markers (&, ]&, @@, //), statement terminators and control words (End, exit, endif, DUP) and bracket or slash combinations. The strongest activations fall on symbols that mark function application or the end of an expression. Scattered prose and non-Latin tokens activate only weakly.

53932.name: Low-level, diffuse activation on the words of evaluative commentary about an organization's (mostly tech companies like Nintendo, Microsoft, Google, IBM, Amazon) actions, strategy, fortunes or competitive standing. Examples include whether it does enough, gets rich, taunts rivals, changes direction, lags behind or keeps impressing. Activation is strongest on the predicate describing the entity's behavior or rivalry.

53942.name: Words that open or form part of the title of an academic publication venue, especially "Proceedings (of the)", "Proc.", "Transactions of the", "Bulletin of the" and journal or conference names. These appear in citations and bibliographic metadata. The strongest activations are on "Proceedings" and "Proc." and on the following "of the". There is weaker activation on other venue words such as Publications, Report, Review, Rev and Ann, and on phrases like "presented at".

53970.name: Abstract, uncountable nouns naming a quality, property, dimension or concept (mass, speed, trust, humidity, size, breadth/depth, efficiency, flavor), usually bare with no article and acting as a general category. They often appear in coordinated pairs ('X and Y', 'function for form-factor') or as the subject of a generic statement ('Trust is…', 'space is…'). The adjacent 'and', comma or 'is' is also marked.

54065.name: Weak, diffuse feature tied to comics, cartoons, and humor writing: tokens in or near names of comic strips, cartoon characters, cartoonists, and humor columns (e.g., XKCD, Peanuts, Dennis the Menace, Gumball Watterson, Tezuka manga, Wacky Packages, Garbage Pail Kids, Topps) and descriptions of funny/surreal content, often firing on name endings or function words next to these references.

54075.name: Tokens in the opening clause of a direct quotation, mostly a speaker's statement in news-style reporting. Activation starts just after the quote's first word ("We", "It", "The") and runs through the first phrase, typically the subject, verb and complement. It is strongest on the main assertion or verb phrase early in the quote and fades as the sentence goes on.

5415.name: Fires on the position just before or at the start of a year number in bibliographic/metadata contexts (citations, publication dates, DOIs, conference dates). It is strongest on the first three digits of a year ("199", "200", "201") or on the space or " (" right before it, and weakly on other separators in dates, page numbers and identifiers.

54199.name: Numbers used as reference locators in citations, mostly page numbers and page ranges (especially the end of a range), but also verse, line, volume, case-reporter and diff line numbers, plus timestamp minutes. A few weak hits on unrelated tokens like "and" or line breaks.

Numbers that serve as locators inside references, chiefly page numbers in citations (e.g. "p. 199", "Id. at 733", a pinpoint page after a case reporter volume and first page). Activation is strongest for legal case pin cites like "18 Or 126, 138". It also fires weakly on the final digits of timestamps (minutes) and the trailing digits of document or post IDs.

54262.name: A diffuse, low-level feature that fires most strongly and broadly across low-quality, SEO-style or machine-spun web text: promotional and advice copy about dumpsters, casinos and gambling, online therapy, antivirus software and marketing tools, often with awkward synonym substitutions and garbled grammar (e.g., "meet up with their arrangement commitments", "method or significant dumpster"). In these passages it covers long runs of ordinary words, especially second-person "you/your" phrasing. Elsewhere it gives only weak, scattered activations on isolated function words and punctuation in otherwise normal text.

54286.name: Tokens marking the end of a clause, sentence, list item or code statement: final words completing a phrase (e.g. 'Shop Now', 'new growth', 'login') and boundary tokens such as periods, commas, semicolons, closing parens and newlines. Activation is strongest at code statement endings and function calls like '$apply()' and ');'.

Fires at the end of clauses describing a procedural step, especially one that restores, repeats, or keeps a prior state (refresh/reload the page, re-pair, refill, repower, retry, repeat, return, again, maintain the existing profile). Activation usually lands on the final token or punctuation (period, comma, newline, 'and') that closes the step before the next one begins.

54324.name: Fires at the boundary token (is, to, in, a colon or comma, a period) right after a phrase that sets up a superlative, comparison or question, such as 'the best X', 'the highest density of', 'which decade saw the greatest', 'Answer' or 'In conclusion'. In other words, it marks the point just before the answer, winner or chosen item is stated.

54333.name: Fires on the term supersymmetry and its variants (supersymmetric, SUSY, MSSM, supergravity/SUGRA), with the strongest activation on the word-completing pieces after "super"/"sup" (e.g. "ymmetric", "metry"), mostly in particle-physics text. Weak activations also appear on unrelated tokens such as line breaks after "N Pages" headers or document metadata.

54352.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature in expository or encyclopedic prose that describes an entity, such as an organization, product, place or system. It fires mostly on function words and predicate starters right after the subject has been introduced, where the sentence goes on to define what the entity is, has, does or how it operates. Typical tokens include 'is', 'is a', 'has a', ', which', 'functions', 'governed', 'provide the', 'designed' and 'of'. It also fires weakly on sentence boundaries and list bullets in such descriptive text.

54375.name: Fragment tokens within garbled, abbreviated, or symbolic technical strings such as chemical formulas, math/LaTeX notation, variable subscripts, acronyms and codes, OCR noise, and non-Latin characters. The marked token is usually an opaque subword piece in the middle of an unusual alphanumeric sequence, not a normal word.

Fragment tokens inside garbled, nonsensical or corrupted text, such as made-up acronyms, broken identifiers, mangled code and symbol strings. These are mostly subword pieces that continue an unfamiliar or ill-formed word or abbreviation, where the next token is hard to predict.

544.name: Tokens inside or just entering literal, formatted, or quoted content: code lines, shell and SQL commands, config options, preprocessor directives, formulas, rule specifications, and delimiters (colons, newlines, quote marks, bullets) that set off such content. Activation is strongest within command or code snippets that follow an introductory colon or newline.

A diffuse, mostly weak feature that fires at boundaries where literal text is about to be entered or quoted. It is strongest on command or code strings the reader is told to type or add, such as 'net user administrator /active:', 'Add "blacklist', 'PRINT(' and mailcap file entries. It fires more weakly on the colons, quote marks and line breaks that introduce such strings, and on verbs like type, call and search.

54407.name: A weak, diffuse feature of technical, scientific, math and code text. It fires on tokens that open or sit inside a specialized notation or reference. These include citation brackets with author abbreviations (the strongest, e.g. '[YY', '[E'), LaTeX subscripts and symbols, code operators and literals, chemical formulas and nucleotide sequences, answer labels, and spaces before numbers. It occasionally fires on ordinary verbs in expository prose.

Weak, diffuse feature firing on tokens that open or begin a literal/formal expression, mostly in code, math or quoted strings. Typical triggers are assignment and equals signs (=, +=), opening quotes and backticks before a string literal, the first characters of a quoted string, operators, subscripts and coefficients in equations, and letters spelled out as acronyms. Peak activations come where the model must reproduce or track exact symbols.

54466.name: Names of specific events, especially sports competitions, tournaments and races (e.g. Grand Prix, Championship, Invitational meet, Major), along with their locations and the preceding "at the" or "win at the". The strongest activations fall on event-name words and the phrase introducing where a result happened. Weaker activations occur on venues, conferences, places and punctuation around them.

545.name: Words and phrases that express variety, variation, diversity or dependence on circumstances, such as "various", "different", "wide range of", "depends on", "range from", "customizable", "tailored to your needs", "varying degrees" and "from country to country". The strongest activations fall on the core words signaling multiplicity or variability.

Words and phrases expressing variability, diversity, or dependence on conditions: e.g. "varies based on", "depending upon", "different ways/materials", "various reasons/sizes", "a variety of", "regardless of", "dependent on", "ranging". Activation peaks on verbs like "varies" and on nouns marking multiple options or kinds.

54505.name: Tokens inside institutional affiliation and address strings, typically from academic paper author headers. The strongest activations fall on the commas, connectors ("of", "and") and words like "University", "Department" and "Centre" that join nested units (lab, department, university, city). Weaker activation appears on similar organization-name text in prose.

54510.name: The token "(View" opening a parameter list, strongest in Android onClick(View v) click-handler signatures. It is weaker in other methods taking a View argument or in setVisibility(View.VISIBLE/GONE), and also fires on "(View our Privacy Policy)"-style web links.

54602.name: Fires on structural or formatting tokens in highly patterned, repetitive text such as code, HTML tables, LaTeX, lists, dates and data listings. Typical hits are indentation and whitespace before list bullets or numbers, newline runs, closing tags (tr, tbody), repeated identifiers and class names, brackets, and parts of dates (month, year digits, commas). These tokens tend to repeat or continue a pattern already set up earlier in the context.

54623.name: Weak, diffuse feature centered on language learning and linguistic competence: ESL, grammar exercises (e.g. Italian 'grammatica'), translation ('Tradução'), proficiency/course levels (C1, Intermediate), 'linguistically qualified', English/grammar checking, and word choice and usage. Elsewhere it fires faintly on scattered function words, discourse connectors and newlines.

54711.name: Tokens in East Asian (mainly Chinese) contexts: historical dynasties, figures, names, place names, romanized Chinese/Japanese words and their glosses, classical poetry and imagery, cultural items (food, calligraphy, gardens), and xianxia-style translated fiction. Peaks fall on Chinese historical and biographical descriptions and romanized names.

54718.name: Terms for web or app routing and addressing, such as routing, route, navigation, url/uri, path, location, link, address, permalink, pages and controllers. They mostly appear in software, web-development and config contexts. Activation is strongest on "routing"/"route"/"navigation"; there are weak spillovers to other routes (road Route 60, iptables nat, Spanish 'ruta').

Web-framework routing and app-structure terms, mostly Django: the "startapp" command after "python manage.py", and strongest on URL routing words (routing, Route, urlpatterns, django.urls path, URL, navbar, .htaccess).

54730.name: Biographical or historical narration about artists and their creative output (songs, albums, records, films, books, poems), especially passages listing notable works or hits and describing their influence, legacy or pioneering role. Activation falls on connective and descriptive tokens within these discussions ("hits such as", "the band pioneered", "issued his first album", "no records", "originally appeared") rather than on the titles themselves. It is strongest in music-history contexts, with weak, scattered activation elsewhere.

5476.name: Mostly whitespace runs (multiple spaces, single spaces before bullets or values) used for alignment/padding in code, config files, tables and lists; strongest on long space runs between columns or fields. Weak secondary firing on punctuation/newline separators and filler tokens.

A diffuse feature that fires on tokens inside formulaic, highly predictable text, typically mid-phrase where the next token is near-certain. Contexts include newsletter, cookie and signup boilerplate ("Sign up to receive", "like to send you offers and news"), hard line breaks that split common phrases ("According⏎to", "During⏎the"), and line counts in diff hunk headers. It also responds to stretched or repeated characters ("oooooooo", "mm", "))))", dot leaders), and to spacing or field tokens in structured listings such as "$ 6", "Size/Form" and "Join Date".

54760.name: Language about ratings, reviews and aggregate scores, such as review sites (Metacritic, Goodreads), star ratings, averages, vote counts, grades and awards. It fires most strongly on review‑aggregation terms ("ritic", "Reviews", "average of", "score") and on the numbers or prepositions that introduce a rating or count.

54810.name: The "throws" keyword after a method signature's closing parenthesis in Java code, declaring the exceptions the method can raise (weaker on similar post-signature keywords like Solidity "returns").

54858.name: Tokens inside repetitive, structured, list-like or tabular text (numbers, units, dimensions, dates, times, bullets, separators, repeated labels such as "Street", "dislike", "true", "logo", "button"). The feature fires on an element that repeats or continues a predictable pattern set up earlier in the sequence, such as the next item in a series, a repeated field or a boilerplate UI or metadata string, rather than on ordinary prose.

54940.name: A weak, diffuse feature with no single token focus. It fires sporadically on ordinary words and punctuation, most often in informal, TV Tropes–style commentary on fiction and pop culture: monsters, villains, myths, TV shows, games and cartoons. The strongest spans are narrative or evaluative remarks such as "the fascinating twist that…", "just plain weird aspects of" and "famously -".

54948.name: Calls to action that point the reader to more information or a resource, such as 'for more information, visit/see/call', 'you can find more details at', 'check out', 'click/buy/sign up via the link'. Activation peaks on words like 'more', 'information', 'details', 'find', 'visit', 'please' and the comma before the action verb, usually just before a URL, contact or reference.

54953.name: Mostly the word "inside" used as a locative preposition or adverb (contained within something, physically or abstractly, including code contexts like "inside functions"). It also fires on related spatial prepositions in other languages, such as Russian "у", Vietnamese "tại", and occasionally "beside".

54978.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on content words, mostly abstract nouns and descriptive or evaluative adjectives (e.g., diversity, legacy, insight, portrayal, sustainable, noble). These usually complete a noun phrase or clause, often just before punctuation or a preposition. They appear mainly in elevated, academic or figurative prose, with no single topic tying the examples together.

Weak, diffuse activation on content words (mostly abstract or technical nouns and verbs) inside incoherent, word-salad or pseudo-technical text, where phrases sound meaningful but don't make sense. It fires most strongly on long nonsensical jargon runs and only sporadically on isolated words in more coherent prose.

54980.name: Tokens tied to livestock and farming, chiefly cattle: cow, cattle, livestock, steer/heifer, oxen, dairy, beef, pasture, grazing, ranch, farm-raised. Cattle words activate most strongly. It also fires weakly on lookalike subwords and unrelated senses ("cow" in cowardly/cowboy, "beef up", "Beefy") and on loosely related agricultural or industry words (timber, aquaculture, animal science).

54987.name: The consequence clause of boilerplate website consent notices. It fires on the main clause that follows a conditional action ("By continuing to use this site", "if you continue to browse"), most strongly on ", you accept/agree to our use of cookies" and on "you're agreeing to" or "we'll assume you're ok". It also covers the same notices in other languages (Spanish, Italian). Weaker activations appear on similar call-to-action consequences, such as "you can help", "we may receive a commission" and "to keep reading".

55017.name: Move numbers and piece letters in chess notation (e.g. "12 Nd", "39.K") activate most strongly. Weaker activation appears on tokens describing moves or actions in games and puzzles (poker bets, card and board plays, folding steps), and on numbered list or sequence indices.

55023.name: Leading digit tokens of numbers, mainly percentages, decimals or comma-separated figures, that sit in lists of statistics or tables. The strongest activations come after earlier numbers in the same sequence, e.g. the second or third percentage in a breakdown.

55089.name: A weak, diffuse feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires mostly on function words and connectors in the middle of formulaic phrases, such as "and" joining paired terms ("clean and efficient", "maintenance and repair"), "the", "of", "by" and "at". It also fires on predictable word-piece continuations ("-F|actor", "BYJ|US", "Tel|ugu") and on filler such as table-of-contents dot leaders and code indentation. These are tokens where the continuation is highly predictable.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature on ordinary mid-phrase tokens in low-quality, repetitive, garbled or machine-generated text, such as looping strings, word salad, code and math fragments. It is strongest on fluent explanatory or definitional clauses within that noise, like assistant-style self-descriptions ("I can answer questions, provide information, and help") or definitions ("Dichotomous is when there are only two possible outcomes").

55136.name: Final tokens of person names in author lists (mostly academic paper bylines), usually the closing surname fragment or initials, often just before a comma, affiliation marker, superscript, or line break.

55188.name: Double-newline paragraph-break tokens, typically with leading whitespace or punctuation fused in, that come right after a sentence or line ends and before a new paragraph, heading or code block. Activation is strongest when a space is fused before the break (" ⏎⏎") or the break falls after a math or code line.

Paragraph-break tokens: a double newline merged with leading whitespace or other characters (e.g. " ⏎⏎", "  ⏎⏎", "---⏎⏎", tab+⏎⏎). They mark section or paragraph boundaries in prose, code, lists and chat-style answers. Activation is strongest when the break follows a completed sentence and starts a new paragraph.

55272.name: Discourse connectives and sentence openers in formal, academic-style prose. The strongest are words starting a new sentence after a citation or period, especially contrastive "However", plus "Furthermore", "Moreover", "Additionally" and existential "There is/are". Weaker hits are fixed phrase parts of scholarly boilerplate ("et al", "would like to thank", "take into account").

55276.name: Weak, diffuse activation on commentary clauses that follow a mention of a name, word, term or title, i.e. text discussing naming, word choice or a term's origin (e.g. a name being adopted, changed, dubbed, that 'stuck', or 'is simply a fun word'). It also fires on casual, chatty asides in the author's voice, such as 'so I'll just', 'we're fresh out' or 'I have no idea why'.

55286.name: Tokens that close a sentence or heading and start a paragraph break, mostly a period (sometimes "?") merged with a double newline, or a bare double newline after a title. They are strongest in low-quality, SEO-style web text where the next paragraph changes topic.

55391.name: Weak, diffuse activation on wording that describes experimental or testing setups, mostly in scientific prose. It fires most on words for studies, subjects, tasks, tests, conditions, sessions and apparatus, and on the sentence ends or methods phrasing that follow them (e.g. "In the present study", "subjects performed the task", "were tested").

5540.name: Affiliation markers right after author names in paper bylines, mostly superscript numbers, letters, or symbols (¹ ² ³, †, ‡, \textsuperscript{a}) that tie an author to an institution. Weaker activation falls on other byline separators (commas, newlines after names), the word "Affiliations", and occasionally on citation or footnote numbers.

55408.name: Leading whitespace indentation tokens at the start of a line, appearing just before a list bullet or number (•, 2., -) or before code that dedents from a deeper block, such as closing braces/tags, else, or catch. The strongest cases are dedents in code and numbered list items.

55433.name: Fires on the connector or punctuation token that immediately follows a placeholder, variable, or identifier name, mostly in code, templates and formulas. Typical cases are operators, delimiters, colons/equals in key–value pairs, concatenated string suffixes like '.csv' or '>_frames', and method or attribute suffixes. The strongest activations come after template placeholders and variables such as <name>, filename +, and @name. Weaker activations occur on prose linking words ('to', 'for', 'as', 'which') that follow a noun phrase.

55436.name: Code tokens, chiefly indentation whitespace and closing ')', '{', ');' with newline, that come just before a control-flow exit statement such as return, break, continue, raise/throw, exit or an error print. These usually sit inside if, else, except or Err branches handling errors or edge cases. Activation is highest on the indentation directly before a return, continue or break that follows an error message.

55516.name: Numbers in game scores, win–loss records and vote tallies, especially the second number of a hyphenated pair (e.g., the 72 in "77-72"). Activation is strongest on the losing or lower score in reported sports results. It is weaker on first numbers, percentages and units like "points" or "runs".

55519.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly on separator tokens (spaces, periods, commas, colons) inside structured or numeric text such as lists of numbers, decimals, times, dates, tables and DOIs, right before the next number or identifier part. The strongest hits are the periods in DOI/journal identifiers (e.g. PhysRevA.101) and the spaces before numbers in lists. It also fires faintly on code tokens (main, for) and on metadata labels (Created by, Answered by).

5553.name: Location-related words, mainly "where" (and somewhere/anywhere/wherever), plus the clause that follows them, such as "where the physician holds their" or "Where are they". Activation is strongest on "Where" opening direct or indirect questions about a place ("Where can I", "where to go with"). It is weaker on locative relative clauses and on other wh-question phrases.

The word "where" (and variants like Where, wherever, anywhere, somewhere) introducing a location clause or question, plus the clause words right after it (subject, verb, e.g. "where it was coming", "where my mom got"). It is strongest for "where" questions and indirect questions, and weak on related location or question words (places, when, how).

55531.name: Tokens that open a curly-brace placeholder or interpolation, strongest for "${" in shell, Makefile and template variable substitution (e.g. " ${", "=${", "(${"). It fires more weakly on "{" in C#/Python f-strings and format strings, and on "${" starting LaTeX inline math.

55542.name: The right-hand side of an assignment in code, i.e. the value or expression being stored into a variable, strongest on the variable name just after "=" (e.g. "= b;", "= score;", "= tt;"). Weaker activation appears on function arguments, indices and other operands that supply a value.

55569.name: Technical terms in scientific and laboratory writing that name experimental, analytical, or physical methods, instruments, materials, and processes (spectroscopy, chromatography, ionization, desorption, ablation, fragmentation, sample preparation, staining). Activation usually falls on the key word or word-piece of the method or process name.

55594.name: Past participles (and similar verbs) in passive constructions, often following 'is/was/be/can be' and preceding an agent or source phrase like 'by', 'in', 'from', 'through' (e.g. 'controlled by', 'appointed by', 'decided in').

55603.name: Names of terrorist, jihadist, and militant groups, strongest for ISIS / Islamic State / Daesh (including name-completing subword tokens like "esh", "ab", "aida"). It fires weakly on other extremist groups, rebels, cartels and cults, and on "Republic" after "Central African" or "Islamic". It also fires on "ISIS" even when it is an unrelated name, such as a particle accelerator.

55621.name: Separators inside long repetitive sequences, mostly the commas between numbers in number lists and arrays, plus spaces between numbers in columns or rows and repeated filler patterns like " -", "-*" and ";\". Activation is strongest midway through a long run of items, rather than at its start or end.

55634.name: Narrative or report descriptions of how a storm or other natural or physical event behaves and changes over time. The strongest cases are news-style tropical cyclone reports about a named storm's intensity, strength, sustained winds, movement and forecast track (e.g. "has weakened to", "maintained its strength", "forecast to move"). Weaker activation falls on verbs, auxiliaries and connectives describing the progression of fires, earthquakes, eruptions and similar events.

5565.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on awkward, non-native, machine-translated or SEO-spun English. It activates on tokens where the word choice or grammar is unnatural, such as redundant verbs, odd collocations and garbled phrasing. The strongest examples are spammy health copy and broken technical or product descriptions.

55661.name: Formal bureaucratic, legal and policy language, especially wording that describes mandates, authorizations and directives. It fires on words following verbs like directed, required, authorized, prohibits or tasked (often 'to' plus an action verb), on statutory section headings such as 'Declaration of a… emergency' and 'Authorization.--', and on official program or report titles.

55676.name: The word "current"/"currently" (and Current in identifiers like GetCurrent), meaning present or active state, especially in technical contexts (current location, time, buffer, session, directory). Weaker on other present-time words (now, today, right now) and look-alike tokens such as "content".

The word "current" (and "currently") used to mean the present or active instance of something. Activation is strongest in technical and software contexts such as the current document, file, domain, hour, speed or the currently playing station. Weaker activations come from related words like "present", "selected", "now" and "next", and from "Current" used as a name.

55677.name: The separator token (a space, hyphen, opening parenthesis, subscript marker, or similar) placed right after a name or noun and just before the number, label or parenthetical that tags it. Examples are patent reference numerals ("resonator 10", "medium 2"), model numbers (PPSh-41), citations ("et al. (2014)", "Fig. 1"), list items and math variables. Activation is strongest for the space before patent part numerals.

55748.name: Text that states what a system, device, or program displays, reports, or claims, such as error messages, status indicators, and warnings (e.g. "the password is incorrect", "invalid argument", "USB devices not recognized", "the folder is empty"). These usually come right after verbs like says, shows, is telling, or indicates, and are mostly found in tech troubleshooting text.

Text describing technical problems, chiefly error messages, system warnings and status notices from software or devices (e.g. 'unable to save display settings', 'invalid package file', CRYPTO_LIBRARY_INTERNAL_ERROR, 'marked as dirty'). Activation is highest on the quoted or named error and status text, and weaker on nearby troubleshooting terms such as loading, connection, update and powering issues.

55755.name: Inner subword pieces of Latin-style scientific names, chiefly the species epithet of binomial nomenclature (e.g. falc-ip-arum, offic-in-ale, leg-uminos-arum). The middle fragments after the first piece of the word fire most strongly. Weaker hits come from other rare Latinate or foreign words split into odd subwords, such as medical terms and non-English names.

55797.name: Head nouns (often abstract or generic) that complete a noun phrase, typically after a determiner or modifier ("the", adjective, compound modifier) and often followed by "of", a preposition or punctuation. The feature fires on the main noun of a phrase rather than on any particular topic.

Generic common nouns that head a noun phrase, usually right after a determiner or preposition ("the", "a", "its", "an"). They name an entity whose specific identity comes from the surrounding context (the case, the deal, the crisis, an office, the program), and they are often followed by a period, comma or prepositional phrase.

55810.name: Terms from space and geophysical science, especially solar and plasma physics: the Sun, solar flares, sunspots, the corona, photosphere and atmospheric layers, radiation, auroras, fusion and tokamak plasmas, plus related Earth-science terms. Activation peaks on solar phenomena such as flares and sunspots.

5585.name: Temporal expressions, mainly the tokens that open a date or time reference: prepositions and words like "in", "since", "during", "while", "past", "last", month names and "Day", plus the space or leading digits of a year or day number (e.g. "in 201", "March 16", citation years). Activation is strongest on the space just before the day number after a month name.

55886.name: Fires on awkward, unidiomatic or incorrect word choices, typical of synonym-spun SEO text, machine paraphrasing or non-native grammar. Most often these are swapped prepositions or connectives ("within" for "in", "from"/"into" for "of"/"to", "plus" for "and", "along with", "which" for "that"). It also catches odd synonym substitutions ("returning" for "back", "fringe" for "edge", "prosperity" for "well-being", "likelihood" for "odds"). It marks the token where the phrasing deviates from what a fluent writer would say.

55969.name: A diffuse, weakly-firing feature on ordinary mid-sentence tokens, mostly function words and verb-phrase pieces that continue a clause. It favors infinitive or modal-style predicates such as "able to act", "allows them to", "enough to", "must", "could" and "would", plus their objects or complements. It fires most strongly on an incongruous inserted phrase ("drive on" in spam text).

55985.name: Classifier modifiers that come right before the head noun and specify the type or format of a creative or professional work, most often music or film releases (studio, debut, sophomore, full-length, solo, feature, LP). They typically follow ordinals or possessives like "his third", "first", or "debut". Weaker hits are similar category modifiers such as head (coach), lead (role), original (articles), peer-reviewed and oil (paintings).

55993.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on words in phrases describing what something does, provides or contributes: its function, role, purpose or beneficial effect. Examples include 'play a role', 'creates jobs for', 'provide shelter and… while also offering', 'distribute heat, salt', 'feast on… specialize in consuming', 'tax revenues plus economic benefits' and 'committed to supporting'. It usually lands on the verbs, connectives ('and', 'while also', 'for', 'into') and nouns that link an entity to its impact, mostly in expository text.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no clear lexical trigger. It fires on ordinary mid-sentence tokens, mostly content nouns and verbs and short phrases that continue a clause, such as objects of prepositions and predicate phrases ("fund transfers", "memes can", "return to"). Occasional hits fall on code tokens or CJK characters. It is more common in noisy, garbled or synthetic-looking text, and seems to track generic continuation of the sentence rather than any specific meaning.

56007.name: The word "parking" (and related "parked"/"park"/"car park"), especially as a modifier before lot, garage, space, or area. Weaker activation on related vehicle and storage terms like car, vehicles, seat, and moored.
