61533.name: Narratives of combat, warfare and violent or dramatic action, such as battles, attacks, shootings, captures, escapes, kills and military operations. Activation is strongest within descriptions of the action itself and at the sentence breaks between steps of the battle account. Weaker hits appear on related physical-action narration, like finding, seizing or rescuing someone, and sporadically elsewhere.

61550.name: Words expressing difference, distinctness, or sameness/comparison between things ("different", "differ", "unique", "same", "identical", "disparate", "distinction", "homogeneous"), plus tokens completing such comparisons ("from", "between", or the noun that follows). Strongest on "different" after an intensifier like "very" or "completely".

61599.name: Structural boundary tokens in news/web articles: double newlines, periods, colons, and stray spaces that separate headlines, datelines, bylines, and paragraphs. It is strongest on broadcast-media context such as "Radio", "GMT", station call letters, "By" bylines, and "produced/broadcast" credits.

A diffuse, mostly weak feature firing on structural boundary tokens that precede a new segment, such as the '#' starting an indented Python comment line (often after def main():), sentence-final periods, colons or closing brackets before line breaks, list dashes and code-block newlines. It also fires sporadically on parts of acronyms and names. The strongest isolated hit is the year digit in a '© 2024' copyright notice.

61634.name: The middle number segment of dotted classification codes, most strongly the second two-digit field of PACS physics codes (e.g. the "75" in 89.75.Hc). Activation is weaker on similar segments in OCIS, MSC, ACM, EC and industry codes, IP addresses and arXiv IDs.

61662.name: Women's first names (and full-name pieces) in family or relationship contexts, e.g. a wife, mother, sister, girlfriend or the second parent in "X and Y". Activation is strongest on the mother's or wife's name after "and" in parent or couple listings. Words like "wife" and "lady" fire weakly, as do a few unrelated name-like word pieces.

61672.name: Language about filling official positions through appointment, nomination, selection or election. The strongest hits are words like "appointed by", "nominee(s)/nomination" and "selected". It also fires on the officeholders and offices involved, such as judges, justices, secretary, minister, director and administration, and on confirmation hearings. Unrelated tokens get only weak, scattered activations.

61721.name: Strongest on supersymmetry labels in physics notation, such as the "𝒩=4" or "𝒩=(2,2)" count ("N", "=", the number) and the word "supersymmetric"/"super". Weaker activation falls on "=" in quantum-number assignments (S=1/2, I=…, n=…), along with assorted math and LaTeX tokens and scattered formatting whitespace.

61749.name: The word "month" (and its variants "months", "monthly", "Month") as a time-unit noun, most strongly in singular references to a specific or recurring month ("last month", "this month", "every month", "per month"). Plural counts ("three months", "months ago") and other time units like week, day and hour activate more weakly.

The word "month" (and variants like months, monthly, Month) as a time unit, especially singular "month" in relative time phrases like "last/this/earlier this month" or "per month"; weaker on plural "months" and other time units (weeks, hour, tomorrow).

61758.name: Personal names of researchers and authors, especially in academic author bylines, citations, and reference lists. It fires on name pieces such as initials, given names, and surname-ending subword tokens, and on the separators between names (commas, 'and', affiliation superscripts and markers). It is strongest near the end of a name or author list, just before affiliations or the year. It also fires weakly on academic role words like 'professor' or 'senior author'.

Tokens of personal names, especially surnames, initials, and the separating commas and "and" in author lists of citations and bylines. Activation is strongest in long, repetitive bibliographic author sequences and weaker for single names attributed to quotes or credits.

61784.name: The subword token "orig" inside words, strongest in "tumorigenesis/tumorigenic" and also in "origins", "original", "aborigines", "Dorigo". Weak firing on other mid-word fragments such as "rogen" (chondrogenic) and "raft" (xenograft).

61798.name: Formatting and structural tokens in tables, code, and other structured text: row-ending pipes plus newlines, indentation and alignment whitespace, line breaks, and separators that mark cell, line, or column boundaries ahead of the next aligned item.

61810.name: The standalone digit "0" used as a numeric value, most often in code and math (return values, function arguments, comparisons, assignments, binary 0/1 outcomes). Activation is strongest where 0 is a result or output value, as in "returns 0" or "print(0)".

61815.name: Fires weakly on segment boundaries, mostly sentence-final punctuation fused with paragraph breaks (".⏎⏎", "⏎⏎", ":⏎⏎", "...⏎⏎") where a paragraph, heading, title or list item ends and a new section or topic begins. It also fires occasionally on tokens near the very start of a document or line.

Segment boundaries in messy, often prompt-like or chat/system text. It fires mostly on line-break tokens (newlines, often followed by punctuation, closing brackets or code fences) that end one block and begin another. It also fires on instruction or system-prompt phrases that open a new section, such as "You are a helpful AI assistant", "rewrite it to...", "Below is", or Chinese request phrases.

61824.name: Boundaries in SEO spam and keyword-stuffed web text (gambling, pills, essay-writing, downloads, link farms). It fires on punctuation, line breaks, commas between keyword phrases, and tokens like " https", " online", " download", " visit", and " link", right where a junk keyword string or inserted URL begins or ends.

61884.name: The token "Carolina" (or its fragments "olina"/"inas") referring to the U.S. states North/South Carolina, firing most strongly after "North"/"South". It fires weakly on state abbreviations like "NC"/"SC", on related names (Panthers, the name Carolina), and on a few unrelated tokens.

61927.name: Terms for self-referential, iterative or mutually coupled solution methods in scientific and technical writing. It fires most strongly on "-consistent" in "self-consistent" and more weakly on related words such as iterative, coupled, fixed-point, equilibrium, self-sustained and consistency.

61933.name: Sentence-ending punctuation (periods, often merged with paragraph breaks or closing parentheses) in formal academic, scientific, or legal expository prose, marking a boundary just before a new sentence or section. Discourse connectives that open the following sentence (e.g. "That is", "however", "but") and the first token after the break sometimes activate weakly.

61938.name: Sentence-ending punctuation (mainly periods, occasionally semicolons, closing quotes/parentheses or newlines) that ends a complete clause mid-passage, marking a boundary where a new sentence follows.

61949.name: A weak, diffuse feature with no clear semantic focus. It fires mostly on tokens in structured or formatted text: code syntax (brackets, colons, assignments, indentation), markup and citation fields, and section-like headers such as "Media Contact" or "Company Description". It is often near line breaks or the start of a new segment, with only scattered firing on ordinary prose.

A weak, diffuse feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires mostly on highly predictable, low-surprisal tokens in formulaic contexts: the completion of set phrases ("not to mention", "Bill of Rights", "Email Address", "hello-world", "Step 1"). It also fires on boilerplate web text and on structural or syntax tokens in code, HTML and URLs ("https", "<div", "main ()", ";", "time.sleep"), and on line breaks after headers or names. The strongest activations are on code and markup syntax.

61956.name: The final digit of a four-digit year, split as a three-digit prefix plus one digit, especially when it marks the date of a work's publication, release, or founding (often in parentheses after a title or citation).

The final digit of a four-digit year, mostly in release, publication, or creation dates for works such as films, books, and albums. It fires most strongly on years in parentheses after a title or citation. A few weaker hits land on other date-like tokens such as "March" and "this year".

62000.name: The ".ArrayList" token in Java "import java.util.ArrayList;" statements. Other java.util collection classes such as HashMap and Vector activate only weakly, and stray non-code tokens barely activate.

62029.name: A weak, diffuse feature of web blog/article prose (entertainment, sports, movies, opinion pieces), firing mostly at structural and discourse points: sentence ends and paragraph breaks, bylines, author names, photo credits, tags and timestamps, and transitional or reader-addressing phrases like "let's take a look back at", "Here's" and "Let us know".

6203.name: Words completing a description of a person's or thing's age, most strongly "old"/"-old" after a number plus "year(s)" (e.g. "26-year-old", "ten years old"). Weaker on other age words (young, teenage, elderly, born) and on similar measurement completions after a number and unit, such as "long", "distant", "enough".

Words that complete descriptors of age or life stage, chiefly "old"/"-old" after a number plus "year(s)" (e.g. "17-year-old", "12 year old"). Weaker hits are other attributive modifiers that characterize a person or thing, such as "-based", "-century", "aged", "underage", "student", "toddler" and "newborn".

Tokens that complete a descriptive modifier placed before or right after a person or thing, mainly age expressions ("-old" in "X-year-old", "years old", the comma after an age in "Smith, 52,"). Weaker activations come from similar compound or attributive descriptors such as "-based", "-long", "-winning", "-era", "graduate students" and "young". The strongest activations are on "-old" in hyphenated ages describing a person.

62038.name: Head nouns that complete a modifier+noun phrase specifying a tier, scale, or domain of operation — overwhelmingly "level"/"levels" (state level, local level, species-level), also "scale", "layer", "grade", "basis", "side", "domain", "temperature", often in "at the X level/scale" constructions.

62069.name: A weak, diffuse feature on nouns, often word-final subword pieces, naming concrete figures or depicted things, especially representations rather than real objects. Typical cases are characters, creatures and objects shown in artwork, emblems, decorations, toys or fiction: the eagle, arrows and stars of a national seal, the Great Wave, mechanical skeletons and a projected witch, a cardboard traffic policeman, miniature aeroplanes, a raven, a ghostly piper, teddy bears and Star Wars. Activation is strongest on such figurative or depicted figures.

Nouns (and suffixes like "-shaped") naming the visual subject, motif or theme of a depicted design: shapes, characters, mascots and icons shown on products, costumes, cakes, patterns, images or artwork. Examples include Batman, hidden Mickeys, heart-shaped cakes, cloud images, flags, seals and camouflage. Activations are mostly weak and diffuse, peaking on character and shape motifs.

62071.name: Closing delimiters of code or template blocks, often merged with the newlines after them. The strongest case by far is PHP's closing tag "?>", especially when it ends a script. Weaker activations come from other closers such as Jinja/Django "%}", Handlebars "}}", code-fence backticks, triple quotes and XML declaration endings. There are scattered faint activations on ordinary prose words.

Closing delimiters that end an embedded code or template block and switch back to surrounding content, chiefly the PHP closing tag "?>" (strongest when followed by a newline and HTML). Weaker on template closers (" %}", "}}"), multiline string openers (''' or """ plus newline), heredoc markers, and code-fence ends.

62079.name: Visual markers and indicators that point out parts of a figure or image, chiefly the word "arrow"/"arrows". It fires most strongly in parenthetical figure annotations such as "(curved arrow)", "(red arrow)" and "(arrows)". Weaker activations come from other annotation terms like circled, line, boxes, shaded area, bold part, center and Note. The word "arrow" also triggers weakly in non-figure senses (arrow keys, arrow of time).

62085.name: Variables and relation symbols in mathematical statements that define the domain or range of a parameter (e.g., "x \in [0,1]", "d \geq 2", "\epsilon > 0", "for every r > 0"). The strongest activations fall on the constrained variable name and the following \in/\geq/> symbol, especially in LaTeX. Weaker activations appear on prose about ranges and bounds ("less than", "take on a negative value", "will be between").

62088.name: The ".support" package segment in code import paths, strongest in Java "import android.support..." (AppCompat, annotation, v4/v7 libraries) and weaker in other libraries (Spring, Selenium, Elasticsearch). Other package segments after a dot (.validation, .context, .Security) fire only faintly.
The ".utils" submodule token in Python import paths, specifically in "from django.utils import ..." statements in Django code.

62102.name: Weak, diffuse activations on the start of a sentence's main predicate after its subject in formal or expository writing. They fall mostly on auxiliaries, modals and infinitive markers ('has', 'have', 'can be', 'is', 'to') and the verbs that follow them. The clearest cases are present-perfect or passive statements about progress, development or capability, such as 'have enabled', 'has become', 'have been created' and 'can help'. Nearby quantifiers and determiners ('many', 'most', 'the') are also lightly picked up.

62123.name: Continuation tokens that finish a proper name, mostly an organization, company, brand or product name (sometimes a person's name). The token is usually a later subword or word, e.g. a suffix piece like "tran" in Deltran or "Press" in Guilford Press. It fires most strongly on names that repeat in the text.

Non-initial tokens inside proper names, mostly brands, companies, organizations and acronyms (e.g. word-piece endings like 'cker', 'iac', 'ity', or later words like 'Clinic', 'Academy'). They fire on the token that continues or completes the name, not its first piece.

62136.name: Structural boundaries between items in a sequence: list numbers ("3.", "4."), bullets, line breaks and paragraph breaks after a sentence, indentation before a new code line, table row/cell tags, and commas separating names or list items. It marks the point where one item or section ends and the next begins, and is strongest on enumeration numbers.

62170.name: Words built on the root 'condition' (conditional, conditioned, conditionally, unconditional, Condiciones), firing hardest on 'conditional' in probability and logic contexts. It responds more weakly to related words for dependence or qualification, such as contingent, contingency, categorical, qualified and cautiously.

Tokens for the word "condition" and its derivatives, firing most strongly on "conditional" (conditional statements or execution, conditional probability or mean, unconditional) and more weakly on "conditioned", "conditioning" and "conditions". Faint activation also appears on related logic tokens (if/then, implication arrows, "categorical", "contingent").

6223.name: Prepositions and other connecting words (in, for, to, at, when, on) that come right after a completed noun phrase, most often a number or quantity with its unit (e.g. "$928.7 million in 2020", "0.56% within", "n = 22 for"). The word opens a modifier that adds context such as a time, place, condition or purpose. Activation is strongest after numeric measurements, especially "in" introducing a year.

62245.name: Website boilerplate and UI text such as navigation links, button and form instructions ("Press ESC to close", "Hover over the image", "Drop files here", "add to wishlist"), cookie, subscription and risk notices, page-generation stats and date-format placeholders. It activates weakly and diffusely, spread across the template phrases rather than on single words.

62257.name: Fires inside technical, mostly biochemical, compound names. It favors word pieces in the middle or at the end of protein, enzyme and gene names, such as the 'transferase', 'oxid-ase', 'lig-and', 'acetyl', 'glycosyl' and 'kinesin' fragments, and gene symbols like UGT or Ube3a. It also fires on related functional terms like co-activators, transcription factors and motor proteins, and weakly on other jargon or code tokens.

62280.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires most on noisy, garbled, or non-linguistic text: OCR gibberish, ASCII art and box-drawing blocks, runs of dots, pipes, slashes or symbols, and emoticon fragments. It also fires on stray punctuation and formatting tokens such as markdown '**', LaTeX backslashes and dot leaders. In ordinary prose it fires only faintly on scattered function words.

62303.name: The final word or phrase of a title, heading, or question, typically the object of a preposition (in/on/for/of/at), naming the context, domain, platform, place, or version that frames the topic (e.g. 'in Python 3', 'on Ubuntu', 'in India', 'in MySQL 8.0').

The final noun or name that completes a topic phrase in titles, questions, or headings, typically naming the domain, platform, or tool a statement applies to. It most often follows "in" or "on", and fires most strongly on programming languages and software ("in java", "in Python", "on Snapchat", Unity, Android).

62310.name: Padding and separator tokens in tabular or column-aligned text: runs of spaces or tabs between table cells and columns, dotted leaders in tables of contents, dash rules, pipes, and table tags. Weaker activations fall on boundary tokens such as paragraph breaks, stray periods, or navigation words that separate text segments.

62326.name: Tokens right after a statement of an action or choice that begin an explanation of its purpose, reason, or function, such as "to", "so", "because", "in order to", "make sure", "This is so", "as", "used", and opening parentheses. The strongest activations are on purpose and causal connectives in technical or instructional text.

62356.name: Word-initial tokens spelling "gal"/"Gal" (Gal, Gala, Gall, gallons, gal), mostly fragments that begin a longer word or proper name (Galway, Galton, Galois, Galilee, Galatasaray, galactic, gallop, gallbladder). Strongest on the bare "Gal" start of names; weaker on whole words like "gallons" and on similar G-onset fragments (Gol, Gand, aller).

62412.name: The word "magnetic" and its variants (magnet-, -agnetic as in geomagnetic, magnetosphere, magnetized, magnetically), especially when followed by "field(s)" in physics and astrophysics contexts. "Magnetic" activates most strongly, and "field" activates moderately. Related physics terms such as electric, polarization and turbulent activate only weakly.

62471.name: The final digit token(s) of long numeric identifiers (IDs, ISBNs, PMC/HAL/handle numbers, blog IDs, URL parameters) that end a code string. Activation is strongest on blogger.com blog IDs.

62499.name: Legislative leadership and political power roles, firing most strongly on presiding or leading positions in a legislature (Speaker, Speaker of the House, Majority Leader) and the names of people holding them. It responds more weakly to related government vocabulary: party and coalition leaders, politicians' surnames, Congress, constitution, branch, power, and 'led'/'presided'.

Political and legislative leadership terms, mostly titles and roles like "Speaker", "Majority Leader", "President", "Chairman" and "leadership". These often follow an institution name (House, Senate, Council) and come before a politician's name, which is sometimes also marked. Weaker activations cover other governance vocabulary such as parties, majority, coalition, government formation, factions and support. Activation is strongest on "House Speaker" and "Senate Majority Leader".

625.name: Romantic, sexual and marital relationships: words such as partner, spouse, wife, widow, boyfriend, marriage and civil partnership, plus phrases about falling in love, kissing, seduction or impregnation. The strongest activations are on these relationship and intimacy terms. Weak activations fire on loosely related fragments, like the 'Partners' in 'Partnerships', 'Romantic', 'KISS' in 'Kissimmee', 'Wed', 'Singles' and bedrooms.

Words about sex, romance, desire and intimate relationships, such as sexual orientation, libido, lust, partner, husband/wife, weddings, 'screwing someone', condoms and erotic imagery. Activation is strongest on explicitly sexual or relational terms and weak on the many scattered unrelated tokens.

62567.name: Fires on the word "definition" or "definitions" in any capitalization or context: dictionary or glossary headings, formal or mathematical definitions, and code definitions such as class, function or type definitions. It is strongest in programming and technical contexts. It fires weakly on related words like "meanings", "creator" and "TypeDef".

The word "definition" or "definitions" in any casing and sense (meaning of a term, section headings, programming declarations, image or sound sharpness). It also fires on related tokens such as "Def" and "typedef", and weakly on "blueprint".

62573.name: Diffuse, low-strength activation on tokens within passages about investigating, searching, or solving a problem: puzzle and riddle setups, mysteries, game mechanics, and suspenseful step-by-step narrative where a character tries to find out what happens. It falls mostly on action verbs, function words, and clause-ending punctuation in these sequences.

62575.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires at clause and sentence boundaries: mostly sentence-final punctuation (periods, commas, paragraph breaks, also Chinese 。), the noun or word that closes a phrase just before it, and the first words of the following sentence (e.g. 'I', 'However', 'Please'). It is strongest in informal, run-on first-person prose.

6259.name: Number tokens that begin a year or time period, most strongly the leading digits of a decade (e.g. "196" in "1960s", "'80" in "'80s"). They often follow "the", "early", "late" or "mid", and the preceding space can also activate. Activation is weaker for ordinary full years, centuries, age ranges and other numbers after "the".

62595.name: Words expressing refutation, contradiction, denial or negation of claims, ideas or laws (rebut, debunk, contradict, repeal, deny, dispute, reject, veto, critique). Strongest on rebutting/debunking/contradicting arguments.

Words that express contradicting, refuting, negating or opposing something, such as a claim, belief, rule or effort (contradict, counter, debunk, dispel, deny, repeal, undermine, negate). They fire most strongly on verbs of refutation that sit right before the thing being opposed.

62626.name: A weak, diffuse feature centered on sentence and segment boundaries in generic web, SEO and marketing text. It fires mostly on sentence-final periods (often followed by a newline or a new topic sentence), on colons and on stray spaces. It also fires weakly on words in headline-like titles (e.g. "Tips", "Start") and on boilerplate UI phrases ("click", "try again", "enter your comment"). One outlier is a strong activation on "you" in an "If you…" clause.

A diffuse, low-level feature that fires on low-quality web text such as SEO/spam articles, article-spinner output, forum and blog boilerplate, and comment spam. It activates most strongly on sentence-final periods followed by line breaks in generic promotional prose, and on odd words in garbled spam ("ebook", "please", "blog ("). Elsewhere it gives scattered weak hits on boilerplate tokens like "post", "read more" and ":".

62658.name: Fires mostly in news-style prose on the subject and main-verb phrase of a clause reporting what an organization, institution or person did, said or will do, e.g. 'office did not', 'declined to', 'said it was', 'Authority says it's', 'Ravens will continue to negotiate with'. Modals, auxiliaries, negations and reporting verbs that follow such entity subjects are emphasized. There are scattered weak activations on punctuation and structural tokens.

A diffuse feature that mostly fires on verbs, modals, pronouns and function words in procedural or institutional text about handling a problem: who is responsible, who acts, and what steps follow a dispute, report or incident (e.g. 'SAP shall have the right to', 'designate a team to review', 'let them know… ask them to delete', 'Board can take over'). There are scattered weak activations on formatting tokens such as whitespace, dashes and bullets.

62677.name: Expressions of computational complexity and scaling. The strongest activations fall on the argument inside big-O/Theta notation, such as "(n" in O(n), Θ(ndk) and 2^d, and on verbal scaling phrases like "grows linearly with the size of" or "quadratic time with respect to the size of". Weaker activations appear on variables like N and n, other math notation, and "depends on" / "in terms of" phrasing.

62687.name: Tokens for the word stem "numer"/"num" (number-related words such as numerical, numerous, numeracy, numerics, numerator, numerology), firing strongest on the bare "numer"/"Numer" subword piece. There are weak activations on similar-looking stems (nomin-, humer-, iteration) and on foreign equivalents (NUM, 数).

The word stem "numer-" (numerical, numerically, numerator, numerals, enumerate), firing most strongly on the bare "numer"/"Numer" subword piece and more weakly on the whole word "numerical". It also fires weakly on the Chinese character 数/數 (number) and on "numbers".

62706.name: Words describing operations or changes applied to something (replace, add/remove, rearrange, transform, switch, double, modify, tilt, increase), plus the context of whether a result is invariant to or depends on such changes (e.g., "invariant with respect to the renormalization group", "depend on the choice of"). The feature is mostly in technical or mathematical writing and fires weakly on scattered tokens elsewhere.

Words about altering, transforming or freely choosing things: change, transform, deform, move, substitute, transpose, double, cut. It also covers arbitrariness or interchangeability ('any other', 'any two', 'either way', 'same thing on both sides', 'commutative', 'isomorphic'). The shared idea is applying an operation or variation and asking whether the result stays equivalent or invariant. It is strongest in mathematical contexts about equivalence under transformation.

62717.name: Line breaks, closing brackets/tags and separators that end an item in a repeated, list-like or tabular structure, such as code lines, table cells, list entries or repeated phrases. Activation is strongest where the same pattern is about to repeat.

62724.name: Tokens made of several consecutive newlines (usually four or more), often fused with the preceding punctuation such as '.', ')', ';', '}' or '。'. They mark a large blank-line gap that ends one section and starts a new one, e.g. between code functions, after imports, or between paragraphs and headings. Weaker activation appears on wiki boilerplate ('this wiki') and other block boundaries.

62754.name: Weak, diffuse activation on text about physical work done to objects, sites or environments (removal, repair, restoration, expansion, installation, clearing, land or habitat management). It peaks on the action verbs and their objects, plus nearby function words such as 'to', 'and' and 'the', e.g. 'to remove dead and decaying limbs and to prevent'.

62799.name: Subword fragments in the middle of rare, unfamiliar words, mostly foreign proper names (people, places, companies) and drug names, where a word is split into several uncommon pieces; the activation is on an internal fragment, before the word is finished.

Middle subword fragments inside rare, multi-token proper nouns (mostly unusual surnames, foreign given names, and place names), firing on the internal pieces after the first token and before the word ends.

6283.name: The final noun (or noun phrase) of a coordinated list or conjunction, mostly the item right after "and"/"or" or a list comma that closes the phrase, typically just before a period or comma.

The final noun or noun phrase in a coordinated list or pair, usually right after "and", "or", "but", a comma or "+". It marks the second or later item that completes a parallel series, such as "and Cowboys", "Diplo and Bieber", or "heart, lungs, and brain". Commas or periods that close the item are sometimes included.

62923.name: Personal pronouns (especially "us", "you", "them") naming a group after a partitive quantifier, as in "many of us", "those of you", "all of them", "most of us". Activation peaks in these "of"-partitive constructions and is weaker for "like me", "we all", "those people".

62980.name: Words that follow a short imperative verb in website or interface boilerplate, such as "Cite this", "Cite this article as", "Export as", "Share as", "Run as", "Revision as of", "Posting as", "View As". The word "as" after such a command is by far the most frequent, and citation and reference prompts ("Cite this", "cite or link to") activate most strongly.

Function words, chiefly "as" plus "at", "using", "with", "by", that come right after a verb in website boilerplate and UI text, such as "Flag as inappropriate", "Revision as of", "referenced as", "Published at", "Log in using" and "Give as a gift". The words that complete a citation or attribution instruction ("cite the", "Preferred Citation") also activate. In each case the token links an action to the category, format or timestamp that follows it.

63085.name: Words about founding or creating an organization, institution, place, or group: "found/founded/founding/founder(s)/co-founder/foundation". Weaker activations go to near-synonyms like "established", "opened", "formed", "institution of", and "origins". The verb uses "founded" and "found" (as in "to found") are strongest.

6314.name: Tokens inside proper names of places, mostly the later or completing subword piece of a geographic name (city, county, region, district, river, valley). Typical cases are Onondaga, Kitsap, Kingstown, Pradesh and Cape. Activation is weak and also spills onto a few other proper-name fragments, such as person or era names.

Geographic place names (cities, counties, states, regions, countries), with activation mostly on the final or later subword token of the name; strongest on regional/county-level names, especially those followed by words like "County".

63145.name: Units of measurement that follow a number, covering length, time, angle, pixel and screen, percent and dosage units (inch, cm, px, ms, °, pixels, DPI, mg, yrs, %). The strongest cases are display and size units such as px, pixels and inch.

63146.name: The word "plain" (strongest) and its forms (plains, Plain-, plaintext, plaintive), plus the related word "bare" (barefoot, bare metal, barely). Activation peaks on "plain" meaning simple/unadorned/obvious, as in "just plain", "plain and simple" or "plain text", and is weaker for geographic plains and "bare".

63262.name: A weak, diffuse feature found in expository scientific and engineering prose about physical phenomena such as optics, fluids, materials, acoustics and circuits. It fires mostly on structural connectors where the explanation continues: sentence boundaries followed by a new sentence start ('. But', '. A', '. The'), clause commas, parentheses, and prepositions or articles like 'of', 'on the', 'that'. Occasionally it fires on technical nouns such as 'behaviour', 'distribution', 'design' and 'scenarios'.

A diffuse, weak feature that fires across expository science and engineering text, such as research summaries, technology descriptions and environmental or physics explanations. It peaks on words that describe how something works, is designed or is studied: method and purpose phrases ("using", "so that", "to enhance", "included replacing", "aims at studying concepts to"), mechanism nouns ("noise reduction", "charge modulation") and fragments of technical names.

63279.name: Separators in lists of people's names (commas, "and", newlines, list numbering, closing parentheses or affiliation markers) that come right before the next personal name, as in author lists, credits, rosters and committees. Activation is strongest in long runs of comma-separated full names.

63297.name: Spam/SEO keyword phrases abruptly spliced into unrelated prose, e.g. product or search queries like drug names, CBD gummies, casino bonuses, forex, shoes, 'essay on…', 'near me', 'where to buy'. The strongest activations fall on the start and core words of the injected keyword string where it breaks the surrounding sentence.

63324.name: The ".beans" token in Java package paths, overwhelmingly in Spring imports like "org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired". It fires much more weakly on the singular ".bean" in other package names, and only sporadically elsewhere.

63349.name: Tokens sitting right before a predictable number, especially inside numeric expressions. The strongest cases are hyphens in numeric ranges (40-50%, 39.7-81.3), the space before the second number in pairs like 'X% and 60%', and year prefixes like '200'/'202' in dates. Weaker cases include decimal points, thousands commas and other separators. Faint, scattered activations also appear on sentence-ending punctuation and newlines before list items.

63473.name: The token right after a command, function name or operator where an argument begins, in code and shell commands. These are usually space-prefixed symbols that open the argument: $ for variables, quotes, brackets, (&, <, /, a URL scheme, or line-continuation backslashes and backticks. The strongest cases are shell or Perl arguments such as `$1` and string concatenation like `"+str(`.

63531.name: Fires on verbs, prepositions and connectives in expository, technical or academic prose. It is strongest where the English is awkward or non-native: agreement and tense errors ('it has also ensure', 'has lead to', 'the excitation system perform', 'the appearance help for'), odd verb or preposition choices ('quantify significant', 'require to count', 'consists in'), and run-on clause linking ('which involves', 'can precisely capture').

63572.name: Words for dead bodies and the lifeless leftovers of former life or activity: corpses, bodies, human remains, skulls, bones, fossils, mummies, ruins, debris, artifacts. Related words also activate, such as dead, lying prone, asleep, ghostly figures and silhouettes, and statues. Activation is strongest on 'remains', 'body', 'corpse(s)' and 'skull(s)'.

63588.name: The last token of a citation reference in academic text. This is most often the final digit of a publication year in author-year citations (e.g., 'et al., 201|6;'), and also the closing numbers in bracketed reference lists and the ends of BibTeX cite keys. It typically comes right before the punctuation that closes or separates citations.

63731.name: Phrases naming the institution, department, or person that a patient, case, or request is directed to, especially clinical case-report wording such as "was admitted/referred/presented to the [emergency department / clinic / hospital]". Activation peaks on the admission verb, the following preposition and article, and the facility noun. Weaker activation appears on general recipients of a referral, contact, or commission ("called me", "commissioned us", "hired by", "to a nearby hospital").

63772.name: Tokens inside runs of repeated characters or symbols, such as strings of the same letter or digit ("000", "111", "CCDD", "WWLLW"), elongated interjections ("yeeeah", "ooooh"), placeholder X's, repeated stars, daggers or block glyphs, and doubled backticks. The feature fires partway through the run, where a character or chunk repeats what came just before it.

63819.name: Variable names, parameters, or quantity labels (often single letters in math/code, or words like speed, level, dose, version, frequency) that are about to be assigned or paired with a specific value, typically right before '=', a number, or a relation like '<'.

63846.name: Separators and connecting words (mostly colons after labels like "Date", "Published", "Created", "Filed"; also "on", "(", table-cell tags) that directly precede a date or timestamp value in metadata-style text.

63856.name: Structural delimiters in structured or code-like text, chiefly the HTML "<thead" tag that opens a table, plus assignment operators (" =") after variable names in code and other separators such as table-cell tags, colons after keys or labels, and whitespace or newlines before list items. Activations are weak overall.

63872.name: Punctuation that closes a direct quotation (mostly a comma fused with a closing quote mark, e.g. ,” or ,") at the end of a quoted statement, just before the speaker attribution such as "he said" or "says [name]". It is strongest on the comma+quote token in news-style quotes, weaker for periods, question marks or exclamation marks ending quotes.

63877.name: Relational connective tokens linking two sides of an expression, especially in math/LaTeX. Activation is strongest on “to” / “\to” denoting convergence or mapping (e.g. “converges weakly … to”, “u_n \to u_0”). It is moderate on “=”, “\equiv”, “\cdot” and the start of a right-hand side. Weak, diffuse firing appears on ordinary verbs or prepositions that link a subject to its object or complement (“depends on”, “has a”, “as”, “with”).

63894.name: The final digit of a publication year in an academic citation (e.g. the "6" completing "201" in "Smith et al. 2016"), occasionally with the closing punctuation. The feature also fires weakly on other closing citation markers, such as reference numbers and closing brackets.

63928.name: Tokens in scientific or technical prose about chemical or physical transformations, such as reactions, compounds forming, materials changing state, minerals and their composition. Activation is strongest on words that describe a process or its products (e.g. "reaction", "formed", "fumes", "-shift", "to" in "turn to"/"to a liquid"), and on connecting words inside these process descriptions.

63939.name: Separators (commas, semicolons, slashes, newlines) between items in lists of classification codes or identifiers. Activation is strongest for commas and semicolons separating subject codes in academic paper front matter (PACS, MSC, AMS, JEL), and weaker for separators in patent class lists, product model numbers, emails and similar code lists.

6402.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly on function words, punctuation and delimiters at clause or list-item boundaries, such as semicolons, colons followed by line breaks, underscores in variable names, and newlines between dated entries. It is strongest in repetitive, templated text, like the repeated n_1, x_1, arr_1 assignments, cast lists, numbered sections and code. There it marks the point where the next parallel item or segment is about to begin.

64024.name: The word "many" right after "How"/"how", opening a question that asks for a count or quantity (math problems, unit conversions, factual trivia). Activation is strongest when "How many" begins a standalone question or heading. Rare weak hits land on other quantity-phrase tokens, such as "of" in "number of".

64026.name: The first number or code segment in a hierarchical reference or identifier, such as section, rule, figure and chapter numbers ("§ 5.360", "Section 2.3", "Fig. 15.8"), classification codes (patent, JEL, MSC, OCIS), version numbers and phone or room codes. It typically falls on the leading part just before a period, slash or hyphen separator.

64043.name: Steroid drug names, mainly the word "steroid(s)" and the steroid-related subword pieces of longer names ("oster"/"oids" in corticosteroids, "one" in hydrocortisone/prednisolone, "ortic" in glucocorticoids). Activation is strongest on corticosteroids used against inflammation and weaker for brassinosteroids and NSAIDs.

64055.name: Identifier names in code and structured data: the first word of a field, key, parameter, column, or method name right after a declaration context (def, pub, struct field indent, quote/backtick for dict/SQL/JSON keys), plus similar label-like names in math variables, table headers, and web UI links.

64080.name: Opening delimiters of code documentation: triple-quote docstring openers (""" or ''') and, more weakly, comment markers (#, //, ///) that begin a description of a function, class, or module. Activation is strongest for docstrings placed right after a def/method signature and weaker for module-level docstrings and plain comments.

64120.name: Fires on the right-hand side of math equations: equals signs, the space after them, and the value or term just past an operator. It also fires on operators, arrows (⇒, \rightarrow) and leading whitespace in formulas and code, i.e. the point where a result or next term is about to be written. Weaker activations occur in ordinary prose, on determiners or function words (a, some, these, those) that precede the next noun phrase.

64141.name: Words within names of organizations and institutions (universities, institutes, societies, councils, companies, clubs, associations, parties, groups), mostly the head nouns such as Institute, Society, Council, Company, Club and the 'of the…' parts of multi-word institutional names. It also fires weakly on generic collective nouns like group, industry and organizations, and often appears in membership or affiliation contexts.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on the token completing a multi-word name or fixed compound term. It is strongest on organization and institution names (World Bank, World Trade Organization/WTO, Institute, Association, Alliance, UN/Nations, OpenAI, JSTOR, TradingView). It also fires on head nouns of set phrases (answer options, Final Answer, PEP 8 guidelines, core module, interface). Scattered activations on function words and punctuation in lists suggest it is otherwise generic.

64206.name: Continuation tokens inside institutional names and postal addresses, especially in academic affiliation lines. The strongest cases are German or other European compound words and street names, such as -straße, -universität and -medizin. It also fires on nouns ending institution names (Center, Institute, University, Technology), on postal codes and phone digits, and on the word "version" in "Citation for published version".

64210.name: Leading whitespace (runs of spaces or tabs) at the start of a line, mostly in source code, that indents the line. It fires most strongly on continuation lines of a statement split across lines, such as wrapped arguments, chained method calls, or wrapped conditions, and also on ordinary block indentation. There are weak, sporadic hits on non-whitespace tokens.

Leading indentation whitespace (spaces or tabs) at the start of a line in code or structured text, especially right after a line opening a block (e.g. a line ending in ':', '{', '(' or 'then'), where the indent shifts to a new level.

64225.name: Weak, diffuse activations on ideologically or politically charged concepts, especially groups, movements, nations and contested social and political ideas (leftism, communism, victimhood, positive discrimination, Soros, Sharia, progressive or establishment politics). These terms typically appear in opinionated or polemical commentary. The strongest hits are victim-status and identity-politics framing.

64245.name: Words that express opposition or being against something, e.g. "oppose/opposed/opposing", "opposition (to)", "opponents of", "against", along with weaker antonymic or obstructive relations ("antithetical to", "obstructed", "in favor"). The strongest activations fall on forms of "oppose".

Words expressing opposition or a stance against something (oppose/opposed/opposing, against, opponents, opposition, at odds, object to), with the strongest activations on verbs like "opposed". Weaker activations appear on support or favor terms (support, favor, backs, all for) and on "opp" letter strings in unrelated words (Oppenheimer, Stoppard, oppression).

64251.name: Mostly numeric tokens in sequences or references: list/part numbers, citation superscripts, page numbers, years' final digits, dates and counts. These are often items in an ordered series (Part 8, 9, 10…; refs 16, 17). Weaker activation on sentence-ending periods/paragraph breaks and a few ordinal words ("second", "five").

Numbers (or the final digit/ordinal suffix of a number) that act as an identifier in a sequence or index: dates (day after a month, last digit of a year), citation/figure/item/issue numbers, "N of M" counters, list numbering and ordinals. Month names that precede a date also activate weakly.

64362.name: Enumeration markers that open the items of a list, mostly the first one (letters like a/A/(a)/i or numbers like 1, plus the following period or parenthesis), especially answer choices in multiple-choice questions or sub-parts of problems. Weaker activation falls on similar separators that introduce an item or answer, such as speaker colons, bullets, and the question-ending comma or colon just before the options.

64383.name: Tokens that sit mid-sequence inside repetitive, structured content such as numeric tables, grids, lists, arrays, code literals, filenames and enumerations. Numbers are the most common case, e.g. table cells, grid values, complex-number components and digits in IDs. Some non-numeric list items also fire, such as list entries, table field names and repeated characters.

6440.name: Boundaries in author-affiliation and address blocks, mainly in academic paper headers. It fires most strongly on line breaks or punctuation right after a country or postal code, and on the affiliation markers (numbers, †, ‡, superscripts) that start the next entry. It also fires on the start of the next header element, such as Department, Email:, Received, Abstract or footnotes, and on email domain endings like .edu or .id.

64440.name: Names of diseases, medical conditions and phenotypes/traits (e.g. cancers, heart disease, PD, HIV, asthma, obesity, aggressive behavior), typically at the point where the condition is named after words like 'treatment of', 'patients with', 'forms of', 'associated with'; weaker activation on other scientific/biomedical topic nouns.

64451.name: Discourse connectives and conjunctive adverbs that link clauses and signal contrast, consequence or addition. "however" dominates, firing most strongly when it falls mid-sentence after a comma or semicolon rather than starting a sentence. Weaker activations come from "therefore", "hence", "otherwise", "moreover" and "nonetheless", and from the final word of multiword connectives such as "in fact", "on the other hand", "of course" and "at the same time".

64460.name: Mostly weak, diffuse activations on the predicate words right after a subject, e.g. passive verbs like named, termed, inserted and issued, and tokens like this, that and only. The strongest activations fall on meta-discursive phrases where the writer comments on their own statement or sets up a justification or explanation. Examples are 'Why am I pointing this out?', 'what makes me think', 'my theory is that', 'I'm just saying' and 'How is that useful?'. These are often followed by 'because' or an explanation.

64489.name: Location and institutional affiliation context: tokens in phrases giving where someone or something is based, such as prepositions (in, at, of, from) and names of places, universities, institutes, departments, or organizations, especially right after a person's name or role (e.g., 'professor at UC Davis', 'in Toms River', 'in the city').

64525.name: Separator and formatting tokens (line breaks, comment markers like #, //, *, pipes, bullets, indentation) in document headers and metadata blocks, usually right after or before items such as titles, dates, authors and filenames. Comment-prefix tokens inside file header comments are the strongest cases.

64563.name: The first value or number token right after an assignment/equals sign, operator or opening bracket, usually in math or code (e.g. "x = 1", "n = 77", "[2, 3"). It fires most on the first numeral or digit of the value being set. There are weaker, sporadic activations on other tokens.

64648.name: Tokens in the last columns of grid-like, tabular, or repetitive structured text (matrices, ASCII art, tables, number grids, LaTeX arrays, repeated symbol rows), especially the last cells right before a line break or row terminator such as \\, |, or ]. It also fires weakly on the last item of repeated patterns in prose.

64665.name: Tokens immediately following an author's surname in academic author lists and citations, most strongly "et" (as in "et al."), plus separating commas, "and", affiliation superscripts and markers, and the citation year. It fires especially after East Asian surnames (Chen, Wang, Li, Zhang).

64691.name: Tokens that repeat or mirror an earlier token within a parallel, list-like or symmetric structure (e.g., the second item in a pair like "t1[1] == t2[1]", "eddie smith and joan smith", "opposite face", repeated values in parallel lines or code). The activation falls on the copied element that completes the parallel pattern.

64693.name: Division operators and markers in math, code, and prose: the slash "/" (including "//", ")/", "/("), LaTeX fraction separators like "}{" and "\frac", and words like "divide"/"divided by". Activation is strongest for arithmetic division in code and formulas (e.g. pi / 2, len(x)//2, W/2). It is weak for non-mathematical slashes such as category separators or unit notation like ms/call.

64707.name: Words that introduce source attribution, citation or provenance information: e.g. "quoted in/by", "reprinted", "reproduced", "posted", "retrieved from", "via", "licensed under", "Wikimedia/Commons", "see", "author of". They usually follow a source name or comma in credits, bylines and references. Strongest on "quoted"; weak, scattered activation on other connective words.

Words in attribution, sourcing and provenance phrases, mostly passive verbs and prepositions saying where content was published, quoted, credited, found or distributed (e.g. via, quoted by, published, posted, seen, referred to, Associated Press, License Photo, Supported by). Strongest on 'via' and 'quoted by'.

64717.name: First names or initials of people, mostly in author/contributor lists (academic papers, bylines), with the strongest activation on given names that come after the first entry in a list of several people and sit just before the surname.

First names (or their first subword/initial token) of people, especially a second or later person in a list of authors, researchers or credited contributors (after commas, "and", "Dr.", or a line break), usually followed by a surname and affiliation.

64735.name: The word "Python" or "python" used as the name of the programming language, in prose, code fences, shebang lines, package names and language lists. It fires weakly on unrelated tokens such as the snake sense or docstring quotes.

64771.name: Separator tokens inside email addresses and URLs, chiefly the "@" between user and domain, plus "://", ".com" and ".gov". They typically appear in contact or attribution boilerplate such as repository notices and author lines. There is weak activation on similar attribution or affiliation contexts (e.g., "by", "(", a trailing country name).

Single connective or operator tokens in technical, code, or math contexts that link a left-hand item to a right-hand item, such as "=", "%", "@" in an email address, or "is" in a key-to-value mapping. Occasionally the token is a function word like "the" inside technical prose.

64787.name: Tokens that open a variable placeholder or interpolation in code, shell commands, URLs, or templates, such as "(!" field references, "${", "={", "{{", "%" format specifiers, and "$". These are the positions where a variable name or value gets substituted into a string or expression. Much weaker activations occur on scattered ordinary tokens, notably "page" in the boilerplate "top of page".

Template placeholders and variable slots: the opening delimiters ({{, {, [[, [, <, $) and names of fill-in fields where text is meant to be substituted (e.g. {{amount}}, {table_name}, <name>, [post_name], [insert ...], $search). It fires most strongly on the opening bracket of these slots and also weakly on other code-like syntax and odd fill-in tokens.

64872.name: Diffuse, mostly weak activations in expository technical writing, mainly programming, math and software docs. They fire on words that define or describe an abstract entity and how it is referenced, passed or made available, e.g. "is an object", "available to your scripts as the context object", "a symbol (like x, y, or z)", variables, placeholders, arrays and values. The strongest hits fall on explanations of what an identifier or object represents.

Mostly technical/programming documentation describing what role an entity plays or where it goes, such as how a value is passed, represented, added or placed. It fires most on role nouns like 'argument', 'variables', 'parameter', 'Context', 'slots' and 'pronoun', and on role-assigning phrases like 'passed as the first argument', 'is represented by a' and 'added as a'. It also fires weakly on placeholder-like tokens such as 'None' and 'XXXX'.

64891.name: Tokens tied to conditional or boolean logic: conditions, comparisons, and checks that evaluate to true or false, such as if-statement comparisons, stop criteria, true/false values, and outcomes. These appear mostly in code and technical or mathematical text. The strongest activation is on the phrase "condition turns into False".

649.name: Diffuse, low-level activation across tokens of generic, formulaic web prose, strongest and densest in SEO/marketing-style or boilerplate explanatory text (e.g., product pitches, business advice, health claims), with weaker spikes at sentence boundaries and transitional phrases (". This", "In fact", "Moreover"). Specific narrative or news content activates only sparsely.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires broadly on ordinary tokens (content nouns, verbs, connectives, punctuation) in generic expository or assistant-style text, such as tech and code explanations, tutorials, product descriptions, and essays, including garbled or non-English text. It has no specific lexical trigger. It peaks mildly on runs of descriptive or explanatory prose, for example marketing claims like 'boxes are both durable and safe'.

64903.name: Function words and predicate phrases directly following a named scientific entity (often a molecule, hormone, or chemical such as ATP, insulin, dopamine, or hydrogen) that describe its role or function, e.g. "is the key", "works as a regulatory molecule", "can be used as a", "responsible for", "played a role". Activation is weaker on scattered subword tokens inside technical names and acronyms.

64909.name: Acronyms of sports governing bodies, leagues and competitions (FIFA, NASCAR, ICC, UEFA, FA, NCAA, WTA, FIA), often firing only on the later subword pieces of the acronym. Activation is strongest on FIFA, especially before "World Cup". There is weak noise on unrelated tokens.

64978.name: Long runs of dot leaders (and similar filler like underscores or ellipses) that sit between an entry title and its page number, as in tables of contents or form fields. Activation is strongest on the first leader chunk after the title and drops on later chunks. Weaker activation appears on other separators between a label and its value, such as a <td> cell before a page number or a blank line after "Leave a Reply".

65030.name: Scientific and taxonomic descriptive prose, mainly species and taxon descriptions in biology and paleontology (Latin genus and species names, family suffixes like -idae, author/year citations, statements of distribution, habitat and morphology). Activation lands on the function words, punctuation and name fragments inside these passages and is strongest in dense species-description text. Weak, scattered activation also appears on general academic and technical writing.

65054.name: Tokens forming bird names (swallows, hawks, woodpeckers, pigeons, owls, doves, loons, Taillow), usually word-piece fragments inside the name, plus broader wildlife and nature terms such as "Wildlife" in organization names, wetlands and ecology.

65080.name: Programming/markup language names used as code labels, strongest as the language tag right after a markdown code fence (```js, ```python, ```bash, ```yaml). Weaker on other language mentions like class='java', <?php, shebang/path segments (/perl, /java), and inline names such as 'Python snippet'. There are faint hits on similar metadata labels (Pages, bib, -review).

65114.name: Forms of the word "disclose" (disclose, disclosed, disclosure(s), undisclosed, and the "losure" piece of non-disclosure) in any sense: revealing information, legal or financial disclosure, and affiliate disclaimers. Weak activations appear on related revealing verbs such as "divulge" and "discussed".
Forms of the word "disclose" (disclose, disclosed, disclosure(s), undisclosed, Disclosure headers), i.e., revealing or making information known; weakly also fires on the similar-looking "discourse".

65144.name: Function words and discourse markers in subjective, evaluative commentary (often review-style), where the writer gives an opinion, concession, or recommendation. Typical spots are stance phrases like "I highly recommend", "to be fair, it is actually", "I'm just not happy with that", hedges and modals (may, will likely, must), and contrastive or concessive connectives (but, so it, since), with peaks at the start of the judgment clause.

65152.name: Equality assertion function names in unit-test code (assertEquals, Assert.AreEqual, assert_eq!, self.assertEqual, ASSERT_EQ, XCTAssertEqual), with the highest activation on Java-style assertEquals and weaker activation on other assertions such as assertTrue and assertNotNull.

65191.name: The final digit of a year in a full date, typically a dateline or header at the top of a blog post, article or archive page (e.g. "Tuesday, May 8, 201[2]"). It fires most strongly when the date begins with a weekday name. There is weak activation on spaces after titles.

The final digit of a four-digit year in a date (e.g. the last digit of 2002, 2009, 2021), often at the start of garbled or noisy text. Occasional weaker hits land on stray tokens in similarly incoherent text.

65196.name: Boundary tokens that close a sentence, paragraph, or section: final punctuation (period, question/exclamation mark, closing parenthesis) fused with line breaks, or bare newlines. Activation is strongest on ".⏎⏎" paragraph breaks right before a new topic, heading, or section begins. Weaker activation appears on the first word of a new paragraph.

6521.name: Interrogative words (what, why, how, who) that open a question or a wh-clause, plus the words right after them (e.g., "What more could you", "What's wrong", "How to"). Activation is strongest on rhetorical or conversational questions and on free relative "what" clauses ("what really matters is"). It is weaker on headings such as "How to…" or "What is X?".

65215.name: Tokens inside repetitive, patterned sequences, mostly numeric or mathematical: comma-separated number lists, series, matrix entries with & separators, arithmetic expressions, and indexed variables. Activation is strongest deep in long regular lists or series, where the next element follows from the established pattern. It fires weakly on repeated words or list structure in prose.

65293.name: Long runs of whitespace (many spaces or tabs) used for alignment or indentation, mostly in code: continuation lines aligned under an opening parenthesis, padding before trailing comments, centered titles in legal documents, and table or box padding. Activation is strongest on these wide space tokens. Weak secondary activations occur on long dot leaders in tables of contents and on occasional punctuation or conjunctions in prose.

65394.name: Technical/scientific text about classifying constituents into types, families or multiplets, firing most strongly on particle-physics content: quarks and fermions, their generations and flavors (up/charm/top), doublets, and left-handed doublet fields (Q_L, L_L) in LaTeX operators. It fires weakly on similar category terms in other fields (cell types, semiconductor family, ligand, units, bipolar cells).

Names of particle categories in physics (quarks, leptons, fermions, bosons, gravitino), firing most strongly on these taxonomy words. Weaker activation appears on words that classify or join kinds of things, such as 'of various types', 'and' between paired categories, and '+' combining components. Much of the remaining activity is low-level noise in technical or math text.

65400.name: The first symbol or token after an equals sign (or similar relation) in math, physics or code expressions, firing most strongly when the right-hand side repeats the variable or function name from the left side (e.g. u(0,x)=u(x), V=V_per+V_ω, ξ=ξ_S, f(x)=f(0)+…, y(0)=y(h), dp[i]=dp[…]).

The first token(s) on the right-hand side of a mathematical equation or definition (right after "=" or another relation), firing hardest when that symbol repeats the variable or function named on the left (e.g. "u = u(x,t)", "W = WΦ", "a = a'"). It fires weakly on similar relational slots in prose and code.

Math/code variables at the start of an expression's right-hand side (just after '=' or a relation), especially when they repeat a symbol from the left side, as in v = v_0 or f(a) = f(b). More weakly, any token that copies an earlier word or identifier (sacrificed the sacrifice, mute/unmute, repeated function names in code).

65418.name: The middle subword token "theros" (and occasionally "ther") inside "atherosclerosis"/"atheromatous", following a split-off "a"/"A". The activation is strongest in medical and vascular contexts. Weak activations also occur on mid-word or mid-number fragments, such as trailing digits of project IDs and "-arrow" in "more-arrow".

65492.name: Separator tokens (commas, spaces, dots, newlines, <td> cells, 'x') placed between items in repetitive lists or sequences of numbers/values/words, firing most strongly when the same item is repeated many times (e.g. '50, 50, 50…').

Separator or delimiter tokens (commas, spaces, newlines, hyphens, semicolons, pipes, slashes) between items in highly repetitive sequences, such as number lists, data tables, or repeated strings. Activation grows as the repetition continues and the next item becomes predictable.

65504.name: Number tokens made mostly of zeros (like "000", "00", "0", "001") inside identifiers, codes, decimals, timestamps, and matrices. Activation is strongest on leading-zero runs that start a padded number or code (e.g., "00000", "(0002)", "[0001]", ISSN/DOI prefixes).

65521.name: A diffuse, weakly-activating feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires mostly on structural or connective tokens in technical, code, or formatted text: separators and operators (->, |, :, =, commas, quotes, brackets, " ("), code indentation and syntax pieces, line breaks, and short function words or prepositions (of, on, to, from) that link a label to what follows.

65532.name: The trailing numeral or letter suffix (e.g., 1, 3, 21, A, E, R) that completes an alphanumeric identifier, most often a gene/protein name (Cas1, Stat3, katG, MnmE), and also cell lines, wells, and model codes. Letter suffixes on gene names activate most strongly.

6564.name: Weak, diffuse feature on structural and technical text. It fires most strongly on generic placeholders or templates that describe a format rather than real content, such as "[Author names]. [Article title]", "name of author, name of recipient", "(ACCOUNT_LENGTH + 1)", "foo: f("foo")" and "/path/to". It also fires weakly on punctuation and delimiters in structured text: colons introducing a spec ("Received:", "rulestring: B"), braces, equals signs, tags, and code or math syntax.

6574.name: Words tied to schooling and education levels, such as school names, grade or year levels (high school, 10th grade, Class XII, elementary, varsity), degrees, majors and university names. Activation is strongest on terms for school stages like high school, grade and class, and weak on scattered unrelated word fragments.

6647.name: The conditional keyword "if"/"If" that begins a condition, strongest in code if-statements (e.g. "if (" / "if ($") and also common in sentence-initial prose "If" clauses. Weaker activation spreads onto the tokens of the condition expression, with faint scattered hits on other tokens.

Words opening a conditional clause, mainly sentence-initial "If"/"if" (also "Should", or a bare condition after "If"), especially when they lead into a branch or alternative outcome such as "If not…" or "if unsuccessful…". The pattern extends to comparison and condition operators in code ("!==", "<", "=").

6673.name: Words tied to the submission, filing, pending or publication status of documents. It is strongest on patent filings ("application", "Ser. No.", "divisional of", "filed") and also covers manuscripts or papers "submitted", "received", "preliminary", "ongoing", "pending" and "Manuscript". It also fires weakly on other metadata nouns such as paper, dissertation, publication, doi and arXiv.

670.name: A weak, diffuse feature firing on the opening words of a new sentence, title, or clause, often right after a heading or paragraph break. It covers the framing lead-in (subject, verb, and function words such as "I believe that if you want to", "Those who want to", "The funny thing is,", "Know Your Credit") up to, but usually not including, the main content noun.

A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires across stretches of ordinary running prose (function words, verbs, noun phrases mid-clause) rather than on specific tokens. It is strongest within explanatory or narrative clauses and is common in noisy, incoherent, or machine-generated-looking text, including prose fragments mixed into code or web boilerplate.

6702.name: A diffuse, weak feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires on ordinary mid-sentence tokens in running prose (and occasionally code), mostly function words and phrase-building words such as "the", "of", "to", "is", "with" and commas, plus verbs and nouns that open a continuing clause. Typical cases are "consider becoming a", "the options is to", "discover the most efficient one" and "impact of aquatic organism". Activation tends to rise slightly in multi-word stretches that lead into a complement or object, rather than on any particular topic or word.

6741.name: Fires most on the word "Sort", both as a capitalized command or label ("Sort by:", "Sort code") and in "a sort of". It fires more weakly on synonyms like "kind" and "type". It also responds weakly to related ideas of classifying, separating and working things out ("separation", "clustering", "discern", "figure out", "solved"). Scattered low activations elsewhere, often on verbs, appear to be noise.

6780.name: Clause or sentence boundaries, mostly the period (or period plus newline) ending a sentence and sometimes the first word of the next sentence, plus commas, semicolons and parentheses that close a clause. The strongest firing is on a sentence-final period after a completed statement, especially where the text continues with a new sentence.

Sentence and clause boundaries: mostly the period (or other end punctuation, often with following newlines) that closes a complete statement, plus clause-joining commas and conjunctions ("and", "while", "though", "But", "And") where one idea ends and the next begins. Activation is strongest at the end of short factual or listing statements.

6887.name: The second element of a hyphenated compound modifier (e.g., "-solving", "-energy", "-gas", "-quality"), i.e., the hyphen-prefixed token joining a word to the preceding word to form a compound adjective/noun modifier, usually before a head noun; weak scattered activations on other modifiers.

Tokens that join a word to the noun or word it modifies, mostly hyphenated compound pieces ("-meter", "-end", "-hour", "-abuse") forming compound modifiers. Possessive apostrophes ("trainers'", "day’s") also fire because they link a possessor to the following noun.

6889.name: Weak, diffuse feature that fires most on words expressing equivalence, sameness or correspondence between things (equivalent, equal to, synonyms, identical, interchangeable, comparable, proportional, mappings, transformation, rename). It also gives faint activations on scattered word fragments and technical terms.

Words expressing sameness, equivalence or similarity between things (equivalent, same, isomorphism, synonyms, similarities, tantamount, twin, homogeneous, interchangeably, "amount to"), strongest on "isomorphism"; other activations are weak and scattered.

6912.name: Tokens deep inside long random-looking alphanumeric strings such as hex hashes, UUIDs, API keys, encoded URL parameters and long digit runs. Activation is strongest partway through the unpredictable character sequence, especially in hex and mixed letter-digit chunks. Weaker activation appears on IDs, DOIs, postal codes, numeric data and garbled-encoding text.

6981.name: References to the people or agents responsible for something: names of creators, founders, authors and speakers, along with the agentive phrases attached to them ("by the same authors", "co-founder", "producer of", "he established", "I"). Activation is strongest on personal names and creator or founder roles, especially after "by" or in appositives that introduce a person.

70.name: The very first token of a document, whatever it is (a title word, heading, byline, navigation text, newline or whitespace), marking the start of the text.

Fires on the very first token of a document or text sequence, whatever that token happens to be (a word, word fragment, symbol, code keyword, or whitespace/newline). Where the text opens with repeated filler like newlines or asterisks, the leading run is marked as well. The feature tracks sequence-start position, not content.

700.name: A broad, diffuse activation over ordinary running text: it covers long stretches of fluent prose, mostly in mid-sentence descriptive or explanatory clauses (marketing copy, narration, technical how-to). Activation tends to rise toward content words late in the clause. It is weaker or absent on code, boilerplate and identifiers, and is not tied to specific words.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature that spans runs of substantive content tokens in LLM/assistant-style technical text, such as code and markup, math formulas and worked calculations, problem statements, and clarification requests. It does not single out one specific word, and it is strongest on the core phrase of an explanation or definition.

7004.name: Words about updating or keeping current. The strongest are forms of "update" (updated, updates, Update), especially in "Last updated"/"Updated:" metadata, and "date" in "up to date". Weaker hits include related recency and newness terms such as latest, refresh, recent, upgrade, modern and advances.

7072.name: Weak activations on tokens inside predictable, boilerplate web and code text: navigation links and site chrome ("Skip to main content", "Login | Register", "Connect with us", "Leave a Reply"), metadata and licensing phrases ("Open Access", "Copyright", "Last Updated", "Issue"), and code file headers ("-*- coding", "Created on", package/import lines). The marked token is typically the word that completes the stock phrase.

7079.name: Marks where a conditional clause ends and its consequence begins: the comma, 'then', colon or brace and indentation after an if/once/given condition in prose or code (if…:, else, ') {'), plus the closing word of the condition itself (e.g. 'so', 'True', 'achieved'). Strongest on code colons and newlines following if statements.

7199.name: Section/chapter numbering and identifier tokens in structured references: digits and separators in chapter/section numbers, LaTeX \label{sec:intro}/{s1} keys, figure filenames, DOIs, URL path IDs, and index codes. Peaks on the number or key that names a section or item (e.g. the "1" in \label{s1}).

7216.name: Names of LaTeX text- and font-formatting commands written right after a backslash, such as \text, \mathrm, \operatorname, \mathbf, \textbf, \rm and \textit, usually in math mode just before a braced argument. Activation is strongest on \mathrm, the "name" part of \operatorname, and \text used in subscripts, units or labels. Other LaTeX command names (\url, \bibitem, \emph, \,) and HTML entities like ' activate only weakly.

7219.name: Past-participle attribution or permission words in legal and boilerplate notices (licensed, published, sponsored, certified, authorized, powered by, distributed). It is by far strongest on "Licensed" opening an Apache-style license comment at the top of a source-code file, and moderate on "licensed under" Creative Commons notices.

722.name: Boundaries between text segments, mostly newlines and sentence-ending punctuation followed by line breaks. It fires most strongly in structured metadata, such as citation and DOI blocks, key-value fields (Size:, Issue, Classification:) and section headers (Keywords, Index Terms). The first word of a new field or section often activates as well.

724.name: Fires on the tokens leading up to and starting a person's name (usually a surname): first names, initials, titles (Dr., Capt.), role nouns (historian), and introducers like "by", "said", "see", "and", commas and parentheses. It is strongest in academic citations and author lists, where it peaks on the opening parenthesis, list number, separator or "by" right before an author surname.

7271.name: Pieces of web and document metadata, especially URL parts ("://", "www", domains like ".com"/".org"/".edu", path segments), which activate most strongly. Weaker activations land on DOI numbers, file paths, citation fields (journal names, vol), site navigation, headers and names of sites or shows. Overall it tracks boilerplate reference and link text rather than ordinary prose.

7300.name: Boundary tokens (newlines, often fused with closing punctuation like '.', '?', '!', ')', '}', or stray spaces) that end one text segment, list item, or section right before an unrelated new segment, heading, or field begins. Strongest at abrupt topic/document shifts, e.g., before a new '###' heading or after a timestamp or "more" link.

7397.name: Weak, scattered activations on word pieces, often fragments, evoking hippie, new-age or wellness lifestyle culture: hippie, bohemian, Taoist, holistic, mindfulness, CBD, vegetarian/veggies, 'med' (as in meditate), harmonize, chill out, calm, trippin', workout/gyms and fasting. The strongest activations are on HIPPIE, med, mindfulness, CBD and Taoist.

7403.name: A weak, diffuse feature. It fires on words about whether something exists, is present, or can be found. Typical cases are finding, seeing, searching for or locating things, and existing or no longer existing. It also covers deleting, removing or destroying things, membership checks ('if … not in', 'exists', a count of 0), and memory or persistence ('memory', 'souvenir', 'toujours', '思念'). This holds in both prose and code.

744.name: Weak activation on attribution and credit text naming people or organizations: author bylines, affiliations, contact details, signature lines, credits like "produced by" or "photo credit", and spokesperson or title attributions. It fires mostly on parts of personal names (often the final subword), titles, affiliation markers (commas, numbers, asterisks) and the line breaks between them.

7459.name: Operators and connective symbols that come right after a number (or variable) in math, LaTeX, or code. The strongest cases are multiplication signs (*, \cdot, ×) and the backslash starting a LaTeX command such as \pi or \times, especially in coefficient patterns like "2\pi" or "2 *". There is weaker activation on other separators that follow a numeric token.

7468.name: Tokens that close or end a structure, block, or segment, mainly closing markup: LaTeX \end{align*}/\end{eqnarray} (strongest), HTML closing tags (, , ), code fences, comment and region terminators, and closing brackets or quotes. It also fires weakly on the whitespace or newline at a boundary just before a new section or list item, such as the space before "1."

7482.name: Tokens that close a structured block: HTML/XML closing-tag openers ", , ), the brace after LaTeX \end, final closing braces of code classes/functions, and "End"/#endregion. Also weakly fires on boundary text after a section ends (e.g., "Leave a Reply", list labels).

7555.name: Weak, diffuse activations on tokens that cite or attribute information to media and publication sources: news articles, journals, press and source lines, URLs (https://www…), bylines, transcripts, interviews and 'according to'/'told'/'said' attributions.

Language about news media and the sourcing or attribution of reported information: news outlets and press items (news, media, press release/conference, story, edition, report, interview), attribution phrases ("according to", "reports say", "as the Guardian reports", "courtesy of", "via the", "photo credit"), and the punctuation or byline points where such a citation would begin or end.

7568.name: Separators (commas, newlines, spaces, " in", " (") that come right after the name of an institution, department, organization or address component, marking the boundary to the next part of an affiliation or address line (e.g. "Department of X, University of Y, City, Country"). Activation is strongest after university and department names in academic author affiliations.

7577.name: A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no single clear trigger, scattered across arbitrary tokens (word pieces, punctuation, nouns) in noisy web text. It is somewhat stronger on keyword-stuffed or SEO/spam-like passages, such as repeated search phrases, tag lists and scraped titles (e.g., "Visual keyboard windows", "corticosteroid-induced", "environmental pollution"), especially on the repeated terms and the commas between them.

Tokens inside incoherent, garbled, or machine-generated word-salad text (spam, nonsensical sentences, broken grammar, random keyword lists). Activation is strongest where text loses coherence entirely and weak or sparse in otherwise fluent passages.

7676.name: Places just before a name, label or identifier is given, mostly in code and technical text. It fires on words like "name", "title", "id", "class", "called", "Identifier:" and "username". It also fires on syntax that introduces a named value, such as function-call openings, string concatenations in paths, URL and DOI segments, and phone-number endings before an email address.
